catalogTitle: שמחת אדר ע"י "פקודי ה' ישרים משמחי לב"

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that the simcha of Adar comes to a Jew through "pikudei Hashem yesharim mesamchei lev": the joy of learning with clarity, of davening well and of giving tzedakah, after first explaining why a Jew should be content to serve Hashem where He has placed him.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with "mishenichnas Adar marbin besimcha" and with the many people traveling to Eretz Yisroel for Purim. Purim was created in galus, he says, and a Jew should be content where he is: great tzaddikim such as the Ba'al Shem Tov, the Vilna Gaon and the Chofetz Chaim wanted to go and were held back from Heaven. Galus is a shlichus to raise sparks of holiness, and one must know where a desire to travel comes from. Turning to Adar, he contrasts the goy's joy from a bottle with the Jew's joy from "pikudei Hashem yesharim mesamchei lev". Learning a blatt Gemara until it becomes clear brings great simcha; Adar, when the Torah was accepted anew after prophecy ended, is the time of Torah she'be'al peh. Simcha is the sign of good learning and good davening, which feed each other, and tzedakah given beyond one's means also brings simcha. He closes with Torah, tefillah and tzedakah as the joy of Purim, and a brachah.

en: A goy seeks happiness in a bottle and ends up more depressed, while a Jew's simcha comes from "pikudei Hashem yesharim mesamchei lev": doing Hashem's will through learning and davening.
When a blatt Gemara becomes clear and new understanding opens up, it brings tremendous simcha, and the clearer it becomes the greater the joy.
Adar is the time of Torah she'be'al peh: after prophecy ended with the first Beis HaMikdash, the miracle of Purim brought a new acceptance of the Torah with love and joy.
Simcha is the sign of proper learning and proper davening, and the two feed each other: Torah is of the mind and tefillah of the heart, and a person needs both.
Giving tzedakah beyond one's means brings simcha afterwards, and Torah, tefillah and tzedakah together are part of the joy of Purim.
A Jew should be content where Hashem has placed him: galus is a shlichus, and the circumstances that keep a person where he is show that this is what Hashem wants.

Torah she'be'al peh and ruach hakodesh

title.en: Purim in Eretz Yisroel or in galus

summary.en: The Rav opens with the simcha of Adar and the many who travel to Eretz Yisroel for Purim. He says Purim was created in galus, that Purim in a walled city belongs to higher levels, and that a Jew must be content where he is, bringing the Ba'al Shem Tov, the Vilna Gaon and the Chofetz Chaim, who wanted to go and were held back from Heaven.

title.en: Galus as a shlichus

summary.en: The Rav explains that Hashem sent the Jews into galus to gather "converts", which the Arizal reads as sparks of holiness, and compares every Jew's home to a shliach's Chabad house. One must know where the desire to travel stems from, not imitate others, and if the means are lacking, Hashem is telling him to stay.

title.en: Contentment with Hashem's plan

summary.en: The Rav tells of shluchim sent back from 770 and says each person must make an honest reckoning, never borrow money for such a trip or burden his parents. He describes the level of wanting nothing but what Hashem wants, notes that the Talmud Bavli and the great works of Torah came about in galus, and says no one knows Hashem's plans in what is happening now in Eretz Yisroel.

title.en: Pikudei Hashem yesharim mesamchei lev

summary.en: Turning to his topic, the Rav asks how one increases simcha in Adar. He contrasts the goy who drinks to become happy and wakes up depressed with the Jew whose joy comes from "pikudei Hashem yesharim mesamchei lev", and describes the tremendous simcha of a blatt Gemara that becomes clear.

title.en: Adar, Torah she'be'al peh and ruach hakodesh

summary.en: The Rav explains that learning is a wondrous union with Hashem, and that Adar is the time of Torah she'be'al peh: after prophecy ended, the Torah was accepted anew with love at Purim, and ruach hakodesh now means arriving at the truth in the Gemara. The test of whether one learned properly is simcha.

title.en: Tefillah, learning and deveikus

summary.en: The Rav says learning needs siyata dishmaya and therefore tefillah, brings the Ba'al Shem Tov that the sign of good davening is simcha afterwards, and explains that Torah (mind) and tefillah (heart) bring each other. Deveikus is for everyone at his level, as he shows from the Sanzer Rav and Rabbi Pinchas of Koretz.

title.en: Good davening and the joy of tzedakah

summary.en: The Rav says that with Hashem's help there is good davening in the beis medrash, and one who does not take advantage of it is wasteful, especially in Adar. He describes the simcha felt after giving tzedakah beyond one's means, brings "pasoach tiftach" and the teaching that tzedakah is central in the time before Mashiach, and concludes that Torah, tefillah and tzedakah are part of the simcha of Purim.

title.en: Matanos la'evyonim and a closing brachah

summary.en: The Rav brings the Rambam that matanos la'evyonim are meant to gladden the hearts of the poor, says Adar is a time of Torah, tzedakah and tefillah when prayers are accepted, and blesses all to merit the full simcha of the redemption. The end turns to the festive gathering with cake and wine; the last stretch is barely intelligible.

title.en: End of recording

summary.en: A long stretch with almost no transcribed speech at the end of the recording.

catalogTitle: מעלת השנה שחל בו פורים המשולש

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains why a year of Purim Meshulash, when Erev Pesach falls on Shabbos, is a rare time ripe for geulah, and calls on the lowest generation to bring Mashiach through Torah, tefillah and a clean mouth.

abstract.en: The Rav opens after Chanukah: Purim belongs to Mashiach ben Yosef and Nissan to Mashiach ben David, and Adar prepares for Nissan. This year is rare: the Imrei Noam, citing the Rimanover, writes that the final geulah will come in a year when Erev Pesach falls on Shabbos. He links Purim Meshulash to Yosef revealing himself to his brothers. He then explains 'velo ya'avor': Purim cannot pass the fifteenth, since from the sixteenth the waning moon is the domain of Eisav and Amalek, which cannot be entered before Mashiach; only in Purim Meshulash is the seudah held on the sixteenth. Why did such years pass without Mashiach? There was a hole in the pocket. Yet our generation, facing unprecedented trials, is asked for less and can bring Mashiach. He urges hasmadah, kavanah and guarding the mouth, warns against pressuring fathers to pay for Purim trips, and closes that the lowest generation's task is to bring Mashiach.

en: A year of Purim Meshulash is always a year in which Erev Pesach falls on Shabbos, a kevius the Imrei Noam, citing the Rimanover, ties to the final geulah.
Purim may not be held after the fifteenth ('velo ya'avor') because from the sixteenth, as the moon wanes, is the domain of Eisav and Amalek, which cannot be entered until Mashiach comes.
In Purim Meshulash the seudah in Yerushalayim falls on Sunday, the sixteenth, so once in decades the Jews do enter Eisav's domain.
Earlier generations had such years and Mashiach did not come, because there was a 'hole in the pocket' through which the merit fell out.
Our generation faces trials earlier generations never had, so only a little is asked of it, and its small efforts give great nachas ruach.
The Rav calls for learning with hasmadah, davening with kavanah and guarding the mouth, so that the Torah and tefillah that pass through it are pure.
Every generation has its task, and the task of the lowest generation, the 'heel' of the generations, is to bring Mashiach.

candidateTopics: velo ya'avor and the waning moon

title.en: A rare year: Erev Pesach on Shabbos

summary.en: The Rav says Purim is Mashiach ben Yosef and Nissan Mashiach ben David, with Adar preparing for Nissan. He reads the Imrei Noam, who brings from the Rimanover that the final geulah will come in a year when Erev Pesach falls on Shabbos, as this year does.

title.en: Yosef's revelation and the waning moon

summary.en: The Rav ties Purim Meshulash to Yosef's 'Ani Yosef', a sign that Hashem will reveal that the whole galus was for the good. He then asks why Purim may not pass the fifteenth, and explains that from the sixteenth the moon wanes and the sitra achra, whose head is the angel of Eisav, rules, as shown by the Shulchan Aruch's limit on weddings.

title.en: Entering Eisav's domain on Purim Meshulash

summary.en: The Rav brings Edom's refusal, 'lo sa'avor bi', and explains the Gemara's 'velo ya'avor': before Mashiach one cannot enter Eisav's domain on the sixteenth. Only in Purim Meshulash, when the seudah in Yerushalayim is on Sunday the sixteenth, does one cross over, and such a year always has Erev Pesach on Shabbos.

title.en: A hole in the pocket; Hillel becomes Nasi

summary.en: The Rav asks why such years came before without Mashiach, and answers with the havdalah segulah for sons and the 'hole in the pocket'. He brings that Hillel became Nasi through a Shabbos Erev Pesach, a nesius from Beis Dovid that is a sign of Mashiach, and says the generations keep growing smaller.

title.en: Why Mashiach can come in our weak generation

summary.en: The Rav brings R' Chezkel of Kuzmir's statement that Mashiach would come in his time, which drew laughter since he had not come in the days of the Ba'al Shem Tov and the great tzaddikim. He answers that less is expected of later generations, whose trials, such as kavanah in tefillah and guarding the eyes, are far harder, so a little gives great nachas ruach.

title.en: Mending the pocket: Torah, tefillah, a clean mouth

summary.en: The Rav brings R' Avraham of Slonim that Jews must be told how strong they are, and says this year may be the time of Mashiach if the pockets are mended. He calls for hasmadah, kavanah and guarding the mouth from lashon hara, since Torah and tefillah pass through the mouth, and turns to the bochurim's plans to travel for Purim Meshulash, warning against a mitzvah haba'ah ba'aveirah.

title.en: Purim trips, the rabbanim and tzedakah

summary.en: The Rav says fathers in his shul of poor kollel yungeleit and melamdim must not be pressed to pay for a trip to Eretz Yisrael, since Mordechai himself kept Purim outside Yerushalayim, and one should do what the rabbanim say. He discusses the rabbanim's plan for the busy Friday and a Sunday gathering for tzedakah, and the Shulchan Aruch on when a Chanukah meal is a seudas mitzvah.

title.en: The lowest generation's task

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara that Yosef's five garments to Binyamin hint at Mordechai's five royal garments, and urges using the three months until Erev Pesach for learning and tefillos. He asks each person to make a cheshbon hanefesh about why he was sent into the world now, and answers that the lowest generation, the 'heel', is meant to bring Mashiach.

catalogTitle: 8 Days Ruled by the Timeless Light of משיח (connection to פרשת וישלח)

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that the eight days of the Chanukah miracle were one long day in the Mikdash, a glow of the light of Yemos HaMashiach that stands above the seven-day order of time.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Gemara that wicks and oils unfit for Shabbos may be used for Chanukah, and explains that the light of Chanukah reaches souls that Shabbos cannot ignite. Chanukah is a foretaste of Yemos HaMashiach, when the seven-stringed harp of the Mikdash will have eight strings. Time is built of seven days, while Mashiach will be above time. He notes the strange wording of the Beraisa and the Mechaber, 'on the 25th of Kislev the days of Chanukah are eight', which the Rama corrects with 'begin'. He asks how the Kohanim could fulfil the mitzvah with miraculous oil, and answers that in the Mikdash the eight days were one long day, so the first lighting stretched over all eight. This explains why Chanukah is named for the 25th, why the Kohanim cried and then stopped, the word 'mitzvah' in Haneiros Halalu, and how Hashem moved the nature of the future into that time. He closes that Chanukah is a time of thanking Hashem, above all for being a Jew.

en: Wicks and oils that do not burn well on Shabbos may be used on Chanukah, because the light of Chanukah reaches souls that Shabbos cannot ignite.
Chanukah is a foretaste of Yemos HaMashiach, the eighth string beyond the seven notes of the present world.
Time is built of seven days, while the light of Mashiach, from which the Chanukah miracle came, is above time.
In the Mikdash the eight days of the miracle were one day eight days long, so the Kohanim did not have to light again.
Chanukah is a time of thanking Hashem, and above all for being a Jew, which is what the Chanukah war was fought for.

the eighth string of the harp
thanking Hashem for being a Jew

title.en: Chanukah light for souls Shabbos cannot ignite

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara that wicks and oils unfit for Shabbos may be used for Chanukah, and explains that the Shechinah comes down on Chanukah to souls that Shabbos cannot ignite. He then calls Chanukah a foretaste of Yemos HaMashiach, when the seven-stringed harp will have eight strings.

title.en: Above time: 'the days of Chanukah are eight'

summary.en: The Rav says time is built of seven days while Mashiach will be above time, and Chanukah too is not bound by the order of time. He points to the difficult wording of the Beraisa and the Mechaber, 'on the 25th of Kislev the days of Chanukah are eight', which the Rama corrects by adding 'begin'.

title.en: Can a mitzvah be done with miracle oil?

summary.en: The Rav asks how the Menorah could be lit with oil that refilled miraculously, since such oil is not olive oil squeezed from olives. He brings the Derech Pikudecha that a mitzvah cannot be done through a miracle, and describes the Kohanim crying over it.

title.en: Time in Yemos HaMashiach and the eighth note

summary.en: The Rav explains that in Yemos HaMashiach the order of time will change and days will be like years, comparing it to the year of the Mabul when the constellations did not function. Creation follows seven notes, as the seven days and the seven mizmorim of Kabbalas Shabbos show; Mashiach will bring an eighth, Binah, and the Chanukah miracle was a glow of that light above time.

title.en: One day eight days long in the Mikdash

summary.en: The Rav explains that Hashem gave the Mikdash one day that lasted eight days, so the Kohanim's first lighting continued and they did not need to relight; the Chashmonaim's mizmor ending 'orech yamim' alludes to this. This answers the Beis Yosef's question why all eight days are called by the name of the 25th, and the wording without 'begin'. He then asks why the Kohanim stopped crying if the stretched day were not so.

title.en: The Menorah above and the stretched mitzvah

summary.en: With the parable of two pianos, the Rav explains that whatever is done below registers above: the Menorah burning in the Mikdash below meant the Menorah above was burning, and the Kohanim cried for fear of darkness in the world. The miracle was that the single lighting remained a mitzvah, which explains the word 'mitzvah' in Haneiros Halalu, kept by the Ba'al HaTanya, and he concludes that Hashem moved the nature of Yemos HaMashiach into the time of the Chashmonaim.

title.en: Chanukah's blessing: thanking Hashem

summary.en: The Rav says each Yom Tov has its own blessing to take along, and that of Chanukah is hallel and hoda'ah; the Rambam waits until the laws of Chanukah to give the laws of Hallel. He calls for a cheshbon hanefesh of all Hashem's kindnesses, and above all thanks for being a Jew, since on Chanukah the Jews fought for Torah, Shabbos, Rosh Chodesh and milah.

catalogTitle: זמן שאפילו שוכחי ה' ישובו (שייכות לז' אדר ולפ' ויקרא)

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that the month of Adar, bound up with Moshe Rabbeinu's humility and his Mishkan, is the time when even the Jews who have forgotten Hashem are called back with love, and that Purim draws down hidden chassadim on Klal Yisrael.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the custom of recalling Moshe Rabbeinu's merit in Adar and with the idea of 'borrowing' from a better future, illustrated by a story of a Kotzker chassid. From the small alef of Vayikra he explains Moshe's humility and how every Jew who shares it is called closer, even in the hiddenness of Adar, when Hashem's name is missing from the Megillah. He then ties Adar, and especially Adar Sheni, to the forgotten Jews outside the camp: the extra silver of the shekalim that Moshe forgot became the hooks of the pillars, which stood outside the courtyard and will yet be joined back. Moshe's Mishkan, he says, was never truly destroyed; every Mikdash is a copy of it, and its holiness still shields Klal Yisrael. He speaks of Amalek in place, soul and time, reads from Yesod Yosef about Taanis Esther and the light revealed at the Megillah reading, and ends with the Name of Hashem hidden in the Megillah, showing that Purim is chessed for Israel and din for its enemies.

en: The Rav says that one who accepts upon himself in Adar to keep and learn Torah, 'kiyemu v'kiblu', gains a connection to Moshe Rabbeinu, whose soul is spread through every Jew.
Moshe wrote Vayikra with a small alef because he held himself smaller than everyone; a Jew who takes on that humility is called in by Hashem with a call of love.
Adar, and especially Adar Sheni, is the time of those outside the camp who have forgotten Hashem, and Purim is when they are brought back in.
Every Mikdash and every sanctuary a Jew builds for Hashem is a copy of the Mishkan Moshe made, and its holiness still protects Klal Yisrael.
Adar is the time of Amalek in the year, and the mitzvos of Purim are what equip Jews to wage war against him.
Hashem's Name is hidden in the Megillah in a form that brings chassadim to Israel and judgment to its enemies, and every year the same kindness returns.

Amalek in place, soul and time
Hashem's name hidden in the Megillah

title.en: Moshe's merit and borrowing from the future

summary.en: The Rav opens with the custom of recalling Moshe Rabbeinu's merit and the teaching that the final redemption will come in his merit, through Torah. Since Jews are not yet fully devoted to Torah, he explains that they 'borrow' from the future, as in the Kotzk story of a chassid who called Hashem 'Father', and as in the 'kiyemu v'kiblu' of Purim.

title.en: The small alef of Vayikra

summary.en: From this week's parsha the Rav explains Moshe's reluctance to enter the Ohel Moed and the small alef of Vayikra, citing the Baal HaTurim and Rashi, and the Midrash that the leftover ink gave Moshe his radiant face. He adds that Moshe is the inclusive soul of all Israel, present in every Jew.

title.en: Called close even in hiddenness

summary.en: The Rav explains that through Moshe's humility a Jew is called in with love, even in the hiddenness of Adar, when Hashem's name is absent both in 'vayikra el Moshe' and in the Megillah. A large alef is seen from afar, a small one only from close; the Megillah is Mordechai's message to the distant, and on Purim even those who forgot Hashem return.

title.en: Pekudei, Adar Sheni and the forgotten silver

summary.en: The Rav notes that Moshe's name is missing in Tetzaveh but appears thirteen times in Pekudei, and ties this to a leap year's second hiddenness and greater revelation. He calls Adar the time of those outside the camp, and brings the Midrash that Moshe forgot what he did with the 1,775 extra shekels until he remembered they became hooks for the pillars.

title.en: The hooks outside the courtyard

summary.en: The Rav explains that the six hundred thousand whose shekalim made the silver sockets are the core of the camp, while the extra Jews are the forgotten ones, connected to the forgetting of Torah that Osniel ben Kenaz restored through pilpul. The hooks stood outside the courtyard, yet will be joined back to the pillars, since every Jew is a 'head' in some way.

title.en: Every Mikdash is Moshe's Mishkan

summary.en: On 'eileh pekudei haMishkan, Mishkan ha'Eidus' the Rav brings Rashi's reading of the double word as a pledge for the two destructions, and the Yismach Moshe's answer that every Mikdash is really the Mishkan Moshe made. He illustrates with a poet's original manuscript and its copies.

title.en: The diamond that saved a life

summary.en: The Rav asks how Moshe's Mishkan could be lost when the Gemara says Moshe's handiwork cannot be destroyed, and answers with the mashal of a son who gave his father's diamond to save his life. Moshe's holiness absorbed the wrath meant for Israel, and Mordechai, a spark of Moshe, likewise saved the Jews.

title.en: Amalek in soul and in time

summary.en: The Rav explains that Amalek exists in soul, in souls that spread heresy and doubt in emunah, especially before Moshiach, and in time, at the end of the year farthest from Nisan. Just as the mitzvah of wiping out Amalek applies to a known Amalekite, so in Adar one must wage war with Amalek, and the mitzvos of Purim equip Jews for it.

title.en: Yesod Yosef on Taanis Esther

summary.en: The Rav introduces the sefer Yesod Yosef and reads from it that on Taanis Esther Mordechai and Esther come down to join the Jews. Mordechai saw the inner root of Haman's power, and Esther stood in the inner courtyard above; the scepter of chessed was extended to all who join her, and one should say 'Al Ayeles HaShachar' and then pray in their merit.

title.en: The hidden light of the Megillah reading

summary.en: Continuing the Yesod Yosef, the Rav describes a hidden holy world that opens on Purim, whose light lasts the whole day, unlike the moment of 'Ayeh' in Shabbos Kedushah. Because it comes from a concealed place, Hashem's name is hidden in the Megillah; 'mikra Megillah' means calling that light down, with great awe at the reading.

title.en: Hashem's Name hidden in the Megillah

summary.en: The Rav explains that Hashem's Name in order means mercy and reversed means judgment; Nisan carries it forward, while Adar is a time of din. Haman's 'v'chol zeh einenu shoveh li' carries the Name reversed in its final letters, Esther's 'yavo hamelech v'Haman hayom' carries it in its initials, and Hashem gave chassadim to Israel and dinim to Haman. He ends that the Megillah is a flow of chassadim that recurs every year.

catalogTitle: יו"ט ליהודים בעלי מדריגה' ומרדכי לא יכרע- היה בטוח בה'' יו"ט של לעתיד לבא' פעמונים בשולי המעיל- דור אחרון

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains Shushan Purim as the Yom Tov of the higher levels, Mordechai's refusal to bow as a deeper standard of emunah, and Purim as a foretaste of the complete wiping out of Amalek in the days of Moshiach.

abstract.en: The Rav asks why new Amalekites rose against the Jews in Shushan on the second day and why Esther asked only then for Haman's ten sons to be hanged. He answers that Purim reaches the lowest Jews while Shushan Purim belongs to the higher ones, the walled-city Jews tied to Jerusalem; what is no sin for one is a sin for another, so finer Amalekites and the ten sons, the soul's ten powers, are destroyed on the second day. He then reads the Targum on Mordechai's refusal to bow to Haman and resolves its contradiction with the Divrei Yoel: Avraham's tractate Avodah Zarah had 400 chapters, and for Mordechai believing that Haman provides one's bread is idolatry. Every Jew, he says, must know this truth and never despair. Turning to Megillah 7a, he explains that the Megillah holds the light of Moshiach, links Shushan Purim to a bris milah, and closes with Esther's wish that the Yom Tov bind the Jews of the last generation to Jerusalem.

en: Purim reaches down to the simplest Jews, while Shushan Purim is the Yom Tov of the higher levels, the walled-city Jews connected to Jerusalem.
Each Jew is judged by his level: what is permitted for one is a sin for a higher one, so there are Amalekites that count as Amalek only for the higher Jew.
Haman attacks the basic belief in Divine providence that every Jew has, while his ten sons are the soul's ten powers, which only the Shushan Purim Jew is expected to uproot.
For Mordechai, believing that one must bow to Haman because he controls one's funding is itself avodah zarah, a chapter in a higher tractate of Avodah Zarah.
Every Jew must know that wealth and honor come only from Hashem, and must not despair over his low state, just as Jerusalem will be rebuilt.
Amalek was written in Scripture only three times because it was never fully destroyed; the Megillah carries the light of Moshiach and lets Jews grow used to it.

title.en: Amalek's brazenness and the second day

summary.en: The Rav describes Amalek's brazenness, which made Haman's descendants reveal themselves by rising against the Jews. He asks why new Amalekites appeared in Shushan on the second day and why Esther asked only then for Haman's ten sons to be hanged.

title.en: Purim for the low, Shushan Purim for the high

summary.en: The Rav explains that Purim reaches the lowest Jews while Shushan Purim belongs to the walled-city Jews tied to Jerusalem. He brings the Targum Sheni that Mordechai came to Shushan only to raise Esther, because his light could be revealed only in a place of hiddenness.

title.en: Each by his level, and finer Amalekites

summary.en: The Rav teaches that what is permitted for one Jew is a sin for a higher one, and so there are finer Amalekites who count as Amalek only for the higher Jew; these sprang up on the second day. He connects Shushan with Jerusalem through the Shushan gate of the Temple Mount.

title.en: Esther and Shoshanah; rejoicing together

summary.en: The Rav contrasts Esther, hiddenness, with Shoshanah, the rose whose beauty is revealed. He says both days must be kept: Jews outside rejoice with the higher Jews tied to Mordechai, and the Jews of Jerusalem rejoice with the Jews of exile.

title.en: Haman, his ten sons, and inner Torah

summary.en: The Rav explains that Haman attacks the basic emunah in Divine providence that every Jew has, while his ten sons are the soul's ten powers, which the Shushan Purim Jew must uproot. He notes that where inner Torah took hold, among the Ba'al Shem Tov's disciples, Shushan Purim became a real Yom Tov, and in the days of Moshiach it will spread to the whole world.

title.en: The Targum on Mordechai's refusal to bow

summary.en: The Rav reads the Megillah with the Targum: Mordechai bowed neither to the idol nor to Haman, who had sold himself to him for a loaf of bread. Later the Jews complain, and Mordechai answers that Haman wore images on his garment; the Rav points out the contradiction and asks why Mordechai's Sanhedrin sat at the king's gate.

title.en: Avraham's 400 chapters of Avodah Zarah

summary.en: The Rav brings the Divrei Yoel on the Gemara that Avraham's tractate Avodah Zarah had 400 chapters while ours has five: idolatry has many levels, and what is not idolatry for a simple person is idolatry for a greater one. He insists the Targum's contradiction cannot be dismissed as differing midrashim.

title.en: The king's funds and Mordechai's emunah

summary.en: The Rav suggests that Achashverosh supported religions, so Mordechai's Sanhedrin, funded by the king, sat at the king's gate, and Haman administered all the funds. Everyone bowed to Haman, but Mordechai stood firm in emunah that wealth and honor come from Hashem, and the Jews complained that his refusal brought the decree.

title.en: Haman's garment: idolatry from front and back

summary.en: The Rav explains Mordechai's answer through the Divrei Yoel: believing one must bow to Haman because he provides one's bread is idolatry on a higher level, and even forgetting for a moment that Hashem rules is the image 'from behind'. Mordechai hinted that he feeds Haman, since all blessing comes first to Israel.

title.en: Knowing the truth, and the dance

summary.en: The Rav says the Jews fell silent because they understood: even one not on Mordechai's level must know the truth and recall it in hard moments, when tempted to flatter whoever seems to give his livelihood. He compares this to dancing at a simcha, when a person jumps above his own height though he will come down again.

title.en: Every Jewish heart is Jerusalem

summary.en: The Rav asks what Shushan Purim means to Jews outside Jerusalem and answers that every Jewish heart is Jerusalem. A Jew who feels he wasted Purim should remember that ruined Jerusalem will be rebuilt, and so will he; he closes with 'layehudim haysah orah' and a blessing that the beauty of a Jew be revealed.

title.en: 'Three and not four': the Megillah's place

summary.en: The Rav opens with the Gemara in Megillah where Esther asks to be written for generations and the Sages answer that Amalek is written three times and not four, and with the dispute whether Esther defiles the hands. He explains the 24 holy books as the 24 ornaments of the bride, the Shechinah, each prophet bringing down an ornament already prepared in heaven.

title.en: The light of Moshiach in the Megillah

summary.en: The Rav brings the Likkutei Torah of Chernobyl that the Megillah holds the light of Moshiach, given so that Jews can grow used to that great light. Purim will remain when other festivals are annulled because its essence is the wiping out of Amalek, the preparation for Moshiach; until that is complete the Megillah's full holiness is still 'in heaven'.

title.en: The seudah of Shushan Purim as a bris

summary.en: The Rav brings the Bnei Yissaschar that the Megillah needs the laws of holy writings only as an object of the mitzvah on Purim. He explains that a bris milah, like Purim, gives a glimmer of the days of Moshiach as the orlah is removed and the holy point is revealed, so the seudah of Shushan Purim is a seudas bris milah.

title.en: Blessing for the bris; why only three times

summary.en: The Rav blesses the newly circumcised child, whose bris falls on Shushan Purim, and all present. He then returns to 'three and not four': Amalek was only weakened by Yehoshua, Shaul left Agag, and in the Megillah too Hashem's name is hidden, so the Sages hesitated to write it until they found it in a passuk.

title.en: Bells on the hem: Esther's Yom Tov for the last generation

summary.en: The Rav explains that the bells and pomegranates on the hem of the Kohen Gadol's robe hint at the last generations, the simple Jews 'full of mitzvos like a pomegranate'. Esther could not ask Achashverosh for a Yom Tov for Jerusalem, so she asked for Shushan, knowing Shushan would vanish while Jerusalem remains; the day binds the last generation to Jerusalem.

catalogTitle: גדולת מרדכי. גראמען (מר' שלמה לעזער שליט"א)

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains why Mordechai, whom the Gemara ranks lower for leaving Torah study to save lives, was in truth the head of all tzaddikim and the Moshe of his generation, whose bond with Torah was never broken.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Gemara that Mordechai, listed after four men in one passuk and after five in another, dropped in rank once he left Torah study for public affairs, from which Rav Yosef learns that Torah study is greater than saving lives. He asks why, then, only some of the Sanhedrin separated from him, and shows Mordechai's stature: the Gemara finds him in the Torah as mor dror, the Midrash calls him head of all tzaddikim, and the Zohar calls him the soul of Moshe. The greatest tzaddikim, like Yaakov and the Avos, stay bound to Torah even in worldly affairs. The Gemara and Ezra wrote by pshat, each tzaddik according to his soul's root; the minority of the Sanhedrin were souls of pshat, like the Beis Yosef. Mordechai is mor dror, misjudged by some, and every level is true. The recording ends with grammen by another speaker.

en: From Mordechai's lower ranking in the second passuk, the Gemara learns that Torah study is greater than saving lives.
Mordechai is the head of all tzaddikim and the soul of Moshe Rabbeinu, and on Purim his great light comes down into the world.
The greatest tzaddikim, like Yaakov at Lavan's house and the Avos, can be busy with worldly matters while their whole occupation remains Torah.
Every tzaddik writes according to the root of his soul, so Ezra's placing of Mordechai reflects Ezra's level of understanding.
The minority of the Sanhedrin who separated from Mordechai were souls of pshat, while the majority understood that he never left the depths of Torah.
Opposing views of a tzaddik can each be true on its own level, as the Chiddushei HaRim says of the Midrash and the Zohar on Yaakov bowing to Esav.

candidateTopics: Mordechai as the soul of Moshe

title.en: Mordechai's lower ranking and Torah versus saving lives

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara that Mordechai is listed after four men in one passuk and after five in another, because he became the king's second and could no longer learn as before; from here Rav Yosef learns that Torah study is greater than saving lives. He raises the difficulty that saving a life overrides the whole Torah, and asks why Mordechai's situation should show a weakness in his Torah.

title.en: Mordechai, head of all tzaddikim

summary.en: The Rav asks why the rest of the Sanhedrin did not separate from Mordechai, and shows his stature: the Gemara finds him in the Torah as mor dror, the Midrash calls him head of all tzaddikim, and the Zohar says he was the soul of Moshe. He explains that the greatest tzaddikim, like Yaakov tending Lavan's sheep and the Avos, never interrupted their bond with Hashem in worldly affairs, and that Mordechai's way was hidden.

title.en: Each tzaddik writes by his soul's root

summary.en: The Rav explains that the Gemara speaks by pshat. With the Zohar and the Rema MiFano on Hadar, the eighth king, whose death the Torah does not record but Ezra's pesukim do, he shows that each tzaddik writes by his soul's root, so Ezra's ranking of Mordechai reflects Ezra's level. Moshe too did not truly die, and Haman, who knew Moshe died in Adar but not that he was born in Adar, did not know that Mordechai was the Moshe of his generation.

title.en: The minority of the Sanhedrin: souls of pshat

summary.en: The Rav explains that the minority of the Sanhedrin who separated were souls of pshat, which does not make them smaller, just as the Arizal told the Beis Yosef that his root was teaching halachah. The majority understood that Mordechai, like the Avos, never left the depths of Torah; he adds a hint from the initials of the names in the passuk, whose shin alludes to the three Avos.

title.en: Mor dror, and every level is true

summary.en: The Rav brings the dispute of the Rambam and the Raavad over musk, mor dror, and says Mordechai is like it: some cannot understand him and judge him unfit, and mor dror equals in gematria that Moshe was born on the seventh of Adar. With the Chiddushei HaRim on Yaakov bowing to Esav he explains that each level is true, and closes that the Megillah ends with Mordechai seeking the good of his people, as in every generation Mordechai brings salvation to Jews.

title.en: Announcements and grammen on doubled words

summary.en: Another speaker makes announcements, then begins rhymed Purim grammen asking why words are doubled in the Megillah and in tefillah.

title.en: Grammen: the tale of the new chassid

summary.en: The grammen continue with a rhymed tale about a simple chassid brought to Vizhnitz and the passages he wished to skip in davening.

title.en: Grammen: threefold mercy and Mashiach

summary.en: The grammen conclude with rhymes on remembering the Creator, His mercy and the coming of Mashiach, with a closing appeal for tzedakah.

catalogTitle: Lighting the Extinguished Candles

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Chanukah, a Yom Tov of the galus set in the darkest place and time, calls on every Jew to go out and relight the extinguished neshamos, while Hashem, behind the darkness, is preparing Mashiach.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the idea of good and less good times: Jews prefer the first half of the month, when the moon grows, and the right side, the side of chesed. Chanukah breaks every rule: it falls at the end of the month, in the long nights of Teves, its lamp stands on the left of the door, below ten tefachim, out in the public domain. He explains that Chanukah and Purim are Yomim Tovim of the galus, and that the extinguished candles stand for the many neshamos blown out in the galus; Chanukah teaches a Jew to go out into the dark and relight them. He then takes up the questions people ask about the darkness of our time and answers them from the Midrash on 'Vayehi ba'eis hahi': while everyone was busy with his own troubles, Hashem was preparing the light of Mashiach. He closes by asking each listener to prepare himself and others for Mashiach, since every mitzvah lights more than one can see.

en: Jews prefer the first half of the month, when the moon waxes, and the right side of chesed, yet Chanukah falls at the end of the month and its lamp stands on the left side of the door.
Chanukah and Purim are Yomim Tovim of the galus, weekdays with a full Shemoneh Esrei, and Chanukah sits in the lowest place of the galus: end of the month, left side, the darkest nights of the year.
The extinguished candles are the neshamos blown out in the galus, and Chanukah teaches a Jew to go out into the public domain and relight them.
Behind the dark events of the parsha, and of our own time, Hashem is preparing Mashiach.
Every mitzvah is like a button whose effect a person cannot see, and lighting the Chanukah candle lights one's own neshamah and those of others.

title.en: Favorable times and the right side

summary.en: The Rav explains that there are favorable and unfavorable times, that the first half of the month is an eis ratzon because Jews are compared to the waxing moon, and that most Yomim Tovim fall on the first or fifteenth of the month. Chanukah is the exception, at the end of the month, and Jews also always give priority to the right side.

title.en: Chanukah in the lowest place of the galus

summary.en: The Rav lists how Chanukah stands against the usual rules: its lamp is on the left side, at night in the long nights of Teves, in the public domain outside Hashem's 'atmosphere', and below ten tefachim where the Shechinah does not rest. He explains that Chanukah and Purim are weekday Yomim Tovim of the galus, and that Chanukah signifies the deepest galus.

title.en: Relighting the extinguished neshamos

summary.en: Using 'ner Hashem nishmas adam', the Rav explains that many neshamos are blown out in the galus, and that on Chanukah a Jew goes out to the public domain to relight them. He says this is the darkest hour before dawn, and lists the questions people ask about the darkness of our time.

title.en: The troubles of the Avos and the light of Mashiach

summary.en: The Rav asks why Yaakov Avinu had to bow to Esav, why Dina was taken, and why the brothers sold Yosef. He answers with the Midrash on 'Vayehi ba'eis hahi': while everyone was busy with his own matter, Hashem was preparing the light of Mashiach.

title.en: No free choice: everything leads to Mashiach

summary.en: The Rav brings that the Shevatim had no free choice in selling Yosef, citing the Ohr HaChaim, and shows how Mashiach ben Yosef came from the episode of Dina and Mashiach ben David from Yehudah and Tamar, while the galus of Mitzrayim prepared the nation. He applies this to the confusing events of today.

title.en: Lighting your own neshamah and others'

summary.en: The Rav tells his listeners to prepare themselves and others for Mashiach: lighting the Chanukah candle lights one's own neshamah, and like a button that lights a whole building, every mitzvah does more than one can see. He calls bringing light to the lost neshamos the task of this generation, and ends with a brachah.

catalogTitle: שושן פורים הוא תחילת וסוף נס של מגילה

oneLiner.en: The Rav shows that the miracle of the Megillah begins and ends on Shushan Purim, and that the mitzvos of Purim are the Jews' weapon against Yishmael in the last stage of exile.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with two stories of tzaddikim whose Purim joy brought salvation: the Lubavitcher Rebbe's farbrengen before Stalin's fall, and Rabbi Elazar of Amsterdam during a flood. He then brings the Ya'aros Devash that Vashti was killed on the night of Pesach, the yahrzeit of her father Belshazzar, and the Chasam Sofer that the Beis Hamikdash could be rebuilt right after the war on Amalek on erev Pesach. This explains why Shaul counted the people with Pesach lambs, and, with the Ruzhiner's words, why Shaul spared Agag and what Shmuel cried about all night. The kings timed their feasts for after Pesach, but the wise men told Achashverosh that the day was in fact Shushan Purim, so the Megillah opens and closes with Shushan Purim. From 'vaya'avor Mordechai' and the Akeidah he teaches that mesiras nefesh crosses the Satan's barriers, and closes that the Purim mitzvos defeat Yishmael today.

en: According to the Ya'aros Devash, Achashverosh's feast was timed so that its climax fell on Pesach, the night Belshazzar was killed.
Following the Chasam Sofer, the war on Amalek is to be on erev Pesach and the Beis Hamikdash could be built that same night, so the kings waited until Pesach passed before celebrating.
The wise men told Achashverosh that the day Vashti was killed was not Pesach but Shushan Purim, so the Megillah begins and ends with Shushan Purim.
The first miracle of the Megillah is the downfall of Nebuchadnezzar's house, and the Rav calls it the main miracle of the Megillah.
Like Avraham on the way to the Akeidah, Mordechai crossed the Satan's 'water' with the cry 'hoshi'eini Elokim', and this gives Jews the strength to pass the barriers of the final exile.
The Rav says the Purim mitzvos of tzedakah, reading the Megillah, the feast with wine and the gifts are the weapons that defeat Yishmael.

candidateTopics: war on Amalek on erev Pesach

title.en: The Purim farbrengen before Stalin's fall

summary.en: The Rav tells how, fifty years earlier, while Stalin was plotting against the Jews, the Lubavitcher Rebbe at a Purim seudah told a story of an old chassid who shouted 'hurrah' three times at an election, and shouted it with the crowd. Two days later Stalin was announced ill, and he soon died.

title.en: Rabbi Elazar of Amsterdam and the broken dike

summary.en: The Rav tells how the queen of Holland sent to Rabbi Elazar of Amsterdam when a dike broke, and was saved; coming to thank him she found him drinking and singing, and he told her that on Purim drinking does more than a year of Tehillim. He then speaks of the present seudah of Shushan Purim and the need for great salvations.

title.en: Vashti and her father's yahrzeit on Pesach

summary.en: The Rav brings the Ya'aros Devash that Achashverosh's feast fell on Pesach and that Vashti had an excuse: it was the yahrzeit of her father Belshazzar, killed on Pesach night, and whether it was a leap year decided the matter. The proof is from the piyut of the Haggadah, and the Rav asks how the paytan knew it.

title.en: Why wait for Pesach: the Chasam Sofer

summary.en: Since kings counted their years from Tishrei, the Rav asks why the feast celebrating that the Beis Hamikdash would not be rebuilt was held after Pesach. He brings Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakai's decree that the whole day of the omer waving is forbidden for new grain, and the Chasam Sofer's explanation: the war on Amalek will be on erev Pesach, and right after it the Beis Hamikdash can be built.

title.en: Shaul's war on Amalek and the Pesach lambs

summary.en: With the Chasam Sofer the Rav explains the haftarah of Parshas Zachor: Shaul counted the people with lambs, which the Targum Yonasan says were the Pesach lambs, since the war was on erev Pesach. Leaving Agag alive while the war was still going on was not yet a sin, but once erev Pesach ended the time for wiping out Amalek had passed, and Shmuel cried to Hashem all night.

title.en: The Ruzhiner on Shaul and Agag

summary.en: The Rav brings the Ruzhiner's answer to the Chiddushei HaRim: Shaul left Agag alive one night so that Haman would be born, the Jews would have Purim and accept the Torah anew; but a king may not bring his people into danger. The Rav adds that Shmuel's night of crying was a tefillah that Shaul's plan should succeed.

title.en: Shushan Purim opens and closes the Megillah

summary.en: Belshazzar and Achashverosh both counted from Tishrei but held their feasts after Pesach, knowing the Beis Hamikdash could only come after the war on Amalek on erev Pesach. When Vashti refused and Achashverosh asked whether it was her father's yahrzeit, the wise men answered that the day was not Pesach but Shushan Purim; the Megillah thus opens with Vashti's death on Shushan Purim and closes with Shushan Purim, and its first miracle, the end of Nebuchadnezzar's house, is its main one.

title.en: 'Vaya'avor Mordechai' and the Akeidah

summary.en: The Rav asks why the Gemara stresses that Mordechai crossed water when he went to gather the Jews. He brings the Midrash that the Satan turned himself into a river to stop Avraham on the way to the Akeidah, and Avraham cried 'hoshi'eini Elokim'; the Akeidah answered Yishmael's boast about his milah, and Mordechai crossed the Satan's water the same way, making Purim for all generations.

title.en: Ikvesa deMeshicha and the wine of Purim

summary.en: Bringing the Chiddushei HaRim that Purim sustains the Jews in the trials before Moshiach, the Rav describes today's exile, with its politics, parties and elections, as a great 'water' meant to keep Jews from serving Hashem, and Esther's 'I have not been called' as the smallness of that time; the answer is tefillah with mesiras nefesh. He brings the Midrash that 'oil for the light' is Moshiach and explains that the Satan of Yishmael hates wine because his fall will come through the Jews' wine on Purim.

title.en: Esther's plea and the Purim 'breaking news'

summary.en: The Rav mentions a Slonimer custom of singing 'Vatosef Esther' and says this verse holds the whole strategy against Yishmael: to plead again and again, with more davening, learning and tzedakah. He closes with 'breaking news' that Yishmael has been struck down by the tzedakah, Megillah reading, wine and gifts of Jews everywhere, the final victory and end of exile, and asks for a niggun.

catalogTitle: צד א: אור המגילה יורד למדרגות הכי נמוכות ביותר.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Targum is the 'back side' of holiness, and that the Megillah, with its Targum Sheni, carries the light of kedushah down to the very lowest places, to strengthen the emunah of those who are far.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the idea that Targum is the 'back side' of holiness, which is why Kaddish is said in Aramaic: to subdue the sitra achra and reveal Hashem's kingship even among the shedim. Following the Arizal, Targum equals tardemah, deep sleep: holiness now seems asleep. The Megillah, unlike the Torah, descends to the lowest levels, and so it has a second Targum, just as Adar has a second Adar. He shows this in Esther's cry in the house of idols, in Shlomo Hamelech who went down into the strongholds of the sitra achra, in Esther sending a shed as her messenger, and in Yaakov leaving Lavan's last sparks for Gilad, the place of Eliyahu. Amalek's denial is answered by the Megillah's hidden miracles. He closes with an appeal for an organization that draws distant Jews close, and with the joy of Shushan Purim.

en: Targum is the 'back side' of holiness, and Kaddish is said in Aramaic to subdue the sitra achra and reveal Hashem's kingship everywhere.
Unlike the Torah, which begins on high, the Megillah descends to the lowest places, and therefore it has a second Targum.
Shlomo Hamelech dared to go down into the lowest places to reveal Hashem's kingship, and that is why so much of the Targum Sheni speaks about him.
Esther drew holiness down even into the house of idols, and even used a shed as her messenger, revealing Hashem's kingship even over shedim.
Amalek casts doubt into emunah by calling everything chance, while the Megillah, with no open miracle, teaches that everything is a miracle.

title.en: Targum, Kaddish and the back side of holiness

summary.en: The Rav explains that Targum is the 'back side' of holiness, close to the sitra achra, and brings the Beis Yosef that Kaddish is said in Aramaic to subdue it. Kaddish asks that Hashem's kingship be revealed even in the place of shedim, and Purim brings holiness down to the lowest point.

title.en: Targum as tardemah; Targum in Torah and Megillah

summary.en: The Rav brings the Arizal that Targum equals tardemah, deep sleep, and explains that holiness is now as if asleep; Avraham's prophecy came in tardemah and 'machazeh'. The Megillah goes down into the weekday world of Targum to give hope to the lost, and he brings the Gemara on where Targum appears in the Torah and in the Megillah.

title.en: The Megillah goes down: Targum Sheni and Esther's cry

summary.en: The Rav explains that the Megillah, unlike the Torah, comes down to repair the 'stragglers', and therefore has a second Targum, as Adar has a second Adar. He asks why Esther cried out when the Shechinah left her in the house of idols, and answers that she had to draw holiness down even there, as in our generation.

title.en: Shlomo Hamelech and the Targum Sheni

summary.en: The Rav explains that Shlomo Hamelech dared to go down into the strongholds of the sitra achra to reveal Hashem's kingship, which is why the Targum Sheni speaks about him at length. Shlomo ruled with wisdom, not war, as a mark of Moshiach ben David; the Megillah, rooted in Mordechai's Chochmah, reaches the lowest places, and Esther even used a shed.

title.en: Who carried Esther's words? A shed as messenger

summary.en: The Rav brings the Manos HaLevi's question about who delivered Esther's answer to Mordechai, and gives his own answer: no one could know Esther was Jewish, as shown by her seven maids, one for each day, so she sent a shed. This explains the plural 'vayagidu' and why Mordechai had to go through water.

title.en: Yaakov, Lavan and the sparks left for Gilad

summary.en: The Rav brings the Ba'al Shem Tov that Yaakov spent his years with Lavan raising sparks of holiness, and asks why he left before finishing. He answers that the deepest klipah holds the highest sparks, which needed the power of Eliyahu at Gilad, where Yaakov also repaired the Targum 'yegar sahadusa'.

title.en: Bilaam, Amalek and the edge of the camp

summary.en: The Rav explains that Bilaam sought to rule over 'ketzeh ha'am', those who had fallen outside the camp, like Amalek, and that the Megillah addresses exactly these, the level of Targum Sheni. Amalek casts doubt into emunah by calling everything chance, even the splitting of the sea.

title.en: Emunah at the Shushan Purim tish

summary.en: The Rav says that Jews sitting at a Shushan Purim tish in the lowest of times is itself emunah: over a Megillah with no open miracle they bless 'she'asah nissim', which the Ramban calls the foundation of emunah. He ties this to Yaakov at Gal-ed and to the coming revelation that will end the sitra achra.

title.en: Drawing the distant close; the joy of Shushan Purim

summary.en: The Rav speaks about an organization that draws distant Jews close, tells of bachurim in Eretz Yisrael it rescued, and says that one must daven daily for one's children in these dangerous times. He ends by calling to rejoice with Shushan Purim and the Targum Sheni, through which even the lowest give honor to Hashem.

catalogTitle: צד ב: במגילה נתגלה אורו של מלך המשיח

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Mordechai belonged to the world of the future redemption, beyond Ezra's level, and that Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak, by deriving the Megillah's holiness from 'u'zichram lo yasuf', grasped this light of Mashiach that is revealed on Shushan Purim.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the five days on which the Megillah can be read, corresponding to the five final letters, which the Midrash calls letters of redemption; the last, tzaddik, is the future redemption, and so Shushan Purim, the Purim of walled Yerushalayim, belongs to it. He then asks why only some of the Sanhedrin parted from Mordechai, and why Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak proves the Megillah's holiness from 'u'zichram lo yasuf'. Through the Rambam's ruling that the Prophets will lose their force in the future but not the Torah and the Megillah, the Chasam Sofer's words on the Megillah, the eighth king Hadar whom Ezra recorded as dying, and the Ba'al haTanya's distinction between prophecy and wisdom, he explains that Mordechai lived in a world of the eradication of Amalek, above Ezra's prophecy. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak, a special soul, grasped this, and it is the deeper light of Shushan Purim.

en: The five days of reading the Megillah correspond to the five final letters, letters of redemption; the last, tzaddik, is the future redemption, and so Shushan Purim, the Purim of walled Yerushalayim, belongs to it.
In the future the Prophets will lose their force before the greater understanding Jews will have, but the Torah of Moshe and the Megillah will not, and will be understood even more.
Each prophet wrote according to the level of his prophecy; Ezra did not reach the level at which the eighth king lives, so he wrote 'and he died' of Hadar.
Mordechai lived in a world where Amalek was already eradicated, and so he grasped what Ezra could not; Ezra recorded him as having fallen only because his book does not reach that level.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak, a special soul, derived the Megillah's holiness from 'lo yasuf', likening it to the Torah of Moshe, and this reflects the deeper level of Shushan Purim.

title.en: Five days, five final letters, and Shushan Purim

summary.en: The Rav links the five days of reading the Megillah to the five final letters that the Midrash calls letters of redemption, and explains that the last day, Shushan Purim, is the tzaddik, the future redemption of walled Yerushalayim. He brings the Arizal via the Bnei Yissaschar on Haman and Zeresh drawing from these letters, and ties the gallows of fifty cubits to the fiftieth gate.

title.en: Mordechai, Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak, and what will remain

summary.en: The Rav asks why only some of the Sanhedrin parted from Mordechai, and why Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak proves the Megillah's holiness from the end of the verse, 'u'zichram lo yasuf'. He brings the Rambam that the Prophets will lose their force in the future but not the Torah of Moshe or the Megillah, explains what that loss means, and brings the Chasam Sofer that the Megillah reveals greater light than the Torah given under compulsion.

title.en: The eighth king, Ezra, and prophecy versus wisdom

summary.en: The Rav brings the Zohar on the parsha of the eight kings: the eighth, Hadar, has no 'and he died', yet in the book Ezra wrote it says he died, because Ezra wrote according to his level of prophecy. He then brings the Ba'al haTanya's answer about the Arizal grasping more than Moshe: wisdom can grasp beyond prophecy, though Moshe's prophecy is far greater, and nothing more can be grasped while Amalek is in the world.

title.en: Mordechai in a world without Amalek

summary.en: The Rav explains that Mordechai was a soul of the time of Mashiach who lived in a world of the eradication of Amalek and so reached what Ezra did not. This answers why most of his brethren accepted him and why Ezra listed him as fallen: Ezra wrote according to his own prophecy, while Mordechai belongs to the world of the eighth king, above all those counted there.

title.en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak and the two levels of Purim

summary.en: The Rav tells how the Chozeh of Lublin and the Satmar Rav rejoiced at a teaching of Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak and brings the Imrei Yosef's gematria for his name. He explains that Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's proof from 'lo yasuf' likens the Megillah to the Torah of Moshe and the secret Moshe placed 'in the ears of Yehoshua', and distinguishes Purim from Shushan Purim, closing with a blessing to see the redemption with our own eyes.

catalogTitle: חנוכה Connects us to the אור הגנוז in the תורה

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Chanukah, born of mesiras nefesh and completing the mitzvos of the Torah, holds the hidden light (ohr haganuz) concealed in the Torah, a light of eight that is above nature and points to Mashiach.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Rambam's unique praise of the Chanukah lights as a very beloved mitzvah. He explains that Chanukah came through the Chashmonaim's mesiras nefesh, and whatever comes with suffering is more precious, as Rashi shows from Avraham's milah and a mishnah about a cow and her calf; like the Akeidah, it is remembered by Hashem. Chanukah is also the last of the seven rabbinic mitzvos that complete the 620 letters of the Aseres HaDibros, the siyum of the Torah's mitzvos. He then describes the ohr haganuz, which Adam enjoyed for 36 hours and which Hashem hid in the Torah, where tzaddikim find it, illustrated by a story of a Rebbe and a wealthy visitor. The 36 Chanukah candles carry this light. Eight is above nature, like the Jewish people's existence and the Torah, and on Chanukah a light of Mashiach appears, hidden in unexpected ways.

en: The Rambam calls the Chanukah lights a very beloved mitzvah because Chanukah came through mesiras nefesh, and what comes with suffering is more precious.
Chanukah is the last of the seven rabbinic mitzvos that complete the 620 letters of the Aseres HaDibros, so it is the siyum of all the mitzvos.
The ohr haganuz, the hidden light of creation, was concealed by Hashem in the Torah, where tzaddikim who learn lishmah can find it.
As the siyum of the mitzvos, Chanukah holds the ohr haganuz, and its 36 candles match the 36 hours Adam enjoyed that light.
Eight stands above nature, which was created in seven days; the Jewish people, the Torah and Chanukah's eight days all belong to this level.
On Chanukah a light of Mashiach appears, and Mashiach comes in hidden, unexpected ways, as shown in the parshiyos read before Chanukah.

title.en: Why Chanukah is a beloved mitzvah

summary.en: The Rav asks why the Rambam calls the Chanukah lights a very beloved mitzvah, a praise he gives no other mitzvah. He explains that the Chashmonaim went out with true mesiras nefesh, expecting no miracle, contrasts Avraham with Haran in Ur Kasdim, and brings Rashi that Avraham's milah was precious to him because it came with pain.

title.en: What comes with suffering is precious

summary.en: The Rav brings a mishnah in Shabbos about farmers who poured salt on a cow after calving so that she would cherish the calf born with pain. Chanukah, unlike Pesach, was itself the product of suffering, so it is beloved to Yidden and to Hashem, and like the Akeidah it is remembered for merit.

title.en: Chanukah as the siyum of the mitzvos

summary.en: The Rav compares Chanukah to the Akeidah, the last test that sealed Avraham. He explains that the 620 letters of the Aseres HaDibros match the 613 mitzvos and the seven rabbinic mitzvos, the last of which is Chanukah, so Chanukah completes the Torah's mitzvos like a siyum or the completion of the Beis HaMikdash.

title.en: The ohr haganuz hidden in the Torah

summary.en: The Rav brings Rashi that the light of creation was hidden for tzaddikim in the future, and the Midrash that Adam enjoyed it for 36 hours, since Shabbos pleaded for him to stay in Gan Eden. Following the Zohar as the Ba'al Shem Tov explains it, the light is hidden in the Torah, and tzaddikim who learn lishmah see everything through it.

title.en: The Rebbe and the shortcut

summary.en: The Rav tells of a wealthy man from America who complained to a Rebbe about his long walk to his office; the Rebbe told him of a shortcut in his own city, and when asked how he knew, answered that he looks at the whole world when he says Melech HaOlam in a brachah. The Rav adds that what was once mocked, that every word and movement is recorded, is now seen in technology.

title.en: A glimpse of the hidden light; 36 candles

summary.en: The Rav says that even ordinary people who learn lishmah sometimes catch a flash of a new insight in a Gemara, a reflection of the ohr haganuz. The 36 hours of that light match the 36 masechtos of Gemara, and since Chanukah is the siyum of the mitzvos it holds the light too, which is why the sefarim count 36 Chanukah candles.

title.en: Gazing at the candles; eight above nature

summary.en: The Rav describes a neglected minhag to sit by the Chanukah lights for the first half hour and gaze at them to absorb their kedushah and the hidden light. He then brings that the harp of the Beis HaMikdash had seven strings and that of Mashiach will have eight, and explains that seven is nature and eight is above it, which is why milah is on the eighth day.

title.en: A nation above nature

summary.en: The Rav explains that the Jewish people's survival, outliving every empire without a homeland, is above nature, and that the Torah, received after the seven weeks of the Omer, belongs to the level of eight. Every stage of the nation's growth, from the Avos to the 600,000, happened outside Eretz Yisrael, so Chanukah's eight days show the eternity of the Torah and a light of Mashiach.

title.en: The light of Mashiach comes hidden

summary.en: The Rav cites the Rokeach that on Chanukah the light of Mashiach appears, and the Malbim that the eighth pasuk after seven of nature speaks of the Torah. Chanukah is a time to learn Torah in depth; shemen, oil, is linked to eight and rises above all liquids. He closes with Asnas, born from the episode of Dinah and Shechem, and with Yehudah and Tamar, to show that Mashiach comes in ways nobody expects.

catalogTitle: מלכות של אסתר ע"י רוח הק'

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Esther's 'malchus' was ruach hakodesh, and that this was her answer to the Chachamim when she asked them to write the Megillah for all generations.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Gemara in Megillah: Esther asked the Chachamim to write the Megillah for all generations, they feared arousing the envy of the nations, and she answered that it was already written in the chronicles of the kings of Madai and Paras. He finds this dialogue in the verses at the end of the Megillah and asks why the verse about Achashverosh's tax interrupts it. He rejects reading Esther's words as a queen's command: she always submitted to Mordechai and the Chachamim, and a queen has no such authority. Rather, Esther's malchus was ruach hakodesh, like the kingship of Shlomo HaMelech that will be revealed in the future Yerushalayim. Achashverosh, written without a vav, was a taker and not a true king; Mordechai and Esther were the true kings. He ends with Shushan Purim, the Kosel Maaravi in every Jew's heart, and a tefillah for Yerushalayim.

en: The Gemara's dialogue between Esther and the Chachamim is hinted in the closing verses of the Megillah: her request in 'umaamar Esther' and her answer in 'halo hem kesuvim'.
Esther did not press the Chachamim with a queen's authority; her 'malchus' was ruach hakodesh, and with it she revealed that the Megillah must be written.
Achashverosh was not a true king but a taker; the true kings of Madai and Paras were Mordechai and Esther.
Shlomo HaMelech's kingship over the upper and lower worlds came from ruach hakodesh and is a model of the kingship that will be revealed in the future.
The Jews of Shushan, who sinned more, received a greater day, Shushan Purim, because the inner point of a Jew, like the Kosel Maaravi, is never destroyed.

title.en: Singing at the seudah

summary.en: Singing before the Rav begins to speak; the transcript holds only fragments of the songs.

title.en: Esther asks the Chachamim to write the Megillah

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara in which Esther asks the Chachamim to fix the Megillah for all generations and answers their fear of the nations' envy, and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's proof that the Megillah was said with ruach hakodesh. He finds the dialogue in the verses at the end of the Megillah and asks why the verse about Achashverosh's tax stands between the question and the answer.

title.en: Did Esther speak with a queen's authority?

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gra, who explains that Esther spoke to the Chachamim with the authority of a queen, and asks: she always obeyed Mordechai and asked the Chachamim her questions, and a queen, unlike a king, has no law of obedience. He then notes that Achashverosh's name in the interrupting verse is written without a vav.

title.en: Malchus as ruach hakodesh: Esther and Shlomo

summary.en: The Rav explains that Esther's malchus means ruach hakodesh, as the Gemara reads 'Esther clothed herself in malchus', and compares it to Shlomo HaMelech, whose kingship over upper and lower worlds came from ruach hakodesh. Shlomo's rule without war is a model of the future Yerushalayim whose wall will be Hashem Himself, and the 'sixty mighty men' around him were, in the Midrash, sixty masechtos.

title.en: Achashverosh the taker, Mordechai and Esther the kings

summary.en: The Rav explains that Mordechai and Esther were the true kings and Achashverosh only an imitation, so Esther's answer about the 'kings of Madai and Paras' refers to their own kingship of ruach hakodesh. The interrupting verse sets this up: a Jewish king gives, while Achashverosh, who levies a tax, is a taker, and like Efron he loses a vav from his name.

title.en: Why the Jews of Shushan received an extra day

summary.en: The Rav explains Esther's request for another day for Shushan: its Jews had an added sin, so even Purim was not enough for them and they needed a greater day. The love of Hashem hidden in every Jew, revealed on Purim, is a point that can never be burned, and Shushan Purim is Yerushalayim's day, when only Yerushalayim reads the Megillah as its Hallel.

title.en: The Kosel Maaravi in every heart, and a tefillah for Yerushalayim

summary.en: The Rav explains 'the city will be rebuilt on its ruin' as the Kosel Maaravi, which remains in every Jew's heart, and tells what he heard about the Satmar Rav's last drasha in Yerushalayim. He closes with a tefillah that all turn to Yerushalayim and soon see it surrounded by a wall of fire.

catalogTitle: מרדכי תיקן קצת חטא עץ הדעת

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains how Mordechai, by refusing to bow to Haman, repaired on the level of drush a flaw left by the sin of Adam and by Yaakov's bowing to Esav, bringing a tikun of the future world that makes the Megillah and Purim eternal.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Manos HaLevi: Mordechai's refusal to bow repaired Yaakov's bowing to Esav. The Midrash criticizes that bowing while the Zohar praises it; the Chiddushei HaRim resolves this through the four worlds matching sod, drush, remez and pshat, which Adam's sin set out of line. Yaakov chose a great tikun in the world of sod at the cost of a flaw in the world of drush. The Gemara's criticism of Devorah and Chulda shows a similar flaw: a time when men had to submit to women and din ruled over chesed. Adar is a reversed month, and the Purim miracle began with 'let every man rule in his house', the turn from din to chesed. Mordechai, from the world of tikun, repaired the drush flaw, which is why the Megillah becomes an iggeres on Purim, will never be nullified, and is expounded by the Gemara from beginning to end.

en: Mordechai, a spark of Yaakov's soul, repaired by refusing to bow to Haman what Yaakov did in bowing to Esav.
The four levels of Torah, pshat, remez, drush and sod, correspond to four worlds, and because of Adam's sin they do not always fit one another, so the Midrash and the Zohar can disagree.

A situation in which a man must submit to a woman, leadership through the attribute of din, is itself a flaw in creation; this, not the women's conduct, is the target of the Gemara's criticism of Devorah and Chulda.
The Purim miracle began with the first letters, 'let every man rule in his house', which set up a new order turning din into chesed, 'v'nahafoch hu'.
Mordechai came from the world of tikun and brought down a tikun of the future that did not exist even at Matan Torah, which is why Purim will remain when all else is nullified.

On Purim the Megillah is no longer one of the books of Kesuvim but an iggeres bound up with the world of tikun, and therefore it may not be written together with the other Kesuvim and will never be nullified.
Because Mordechai repaired the world of drush, the Gemara expounds the Megillah from beginning to end, which it does for no other book of Tanach.

title.en: Yaakov's bowing to Esav: Midrash and Zohar

summary.en: The Rav brings the Manos HaLevi that Mordechai repaired Yaakov's bowing to Esav, then contrasts the Midrash, which criticizes that bowing, with the Zohar, which praises it. He resolves the contradiction with the Chiddushei HaRim: the four worlds match sod, drush, remez and pshat, Adam's sin set them out of line, and Yaakov chose a tikun in the world of sod at the cost of a flaw in the world of drush.

title.en: Devorah, Chulda and the order of honor

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara in Megillah that haughtiness does not befit women, shown by the unflattering names of Devorah and Chulda, and asks why only women, and what they did wrong at all. He lays out the order of honor between navi, kohen gadol and king, and how a king must stand before the kohen gadol who brings the word of Hashem through the Urim v'Tumim.

title.en: The flaw is the situation, not the women

summary.en: The Rav shows that Chulda and Devorah acted correctly, since a prophecy and a judge appointed by Hashem's word demand that the man submit, as Tosafos explains. Following the Chiddushei HaRim he answers that the complaint is against the situation itself: leadership through din, a man submitting to a woman, is a flaw in creation, while chesed must be joined over din, as many halachos that give the right side precedence show.

title.en: Adar reversed and the first letters

summary.en: The Rav calls Adar a reversed month, citing the Bnei Yissaschar and the Arizal on its letter combination, in which din precedes chesed. The miracle begins with the first letters, 'let every man rule in his house': against Rashi's reading, which the Chasam Sofer calls forced, the Rav explains them as the start of a new order turning din to chesed. Mordechai, of the world of tikun, brought a tikun never seen before, not even at Matan Torah.

title.en: Mordechai's tikun and the Megillah as an iggeres

summary.en: The Rav returns to Yaakov: he knowingly left a flaw in the world of drush for a greater tikun in the world of sod, and Mordechai repaired that flaw, preparing the days of Moshiach. From the Rambam's ruling that a Megillah written with the other Kesuvim is invalid, he explains that on Purim the Megillah is an iggeres of the world of tikun, which is why it alone will never be nullified.

title.en: Doresh tov l'amo and Shushan Purim

summary.en: The Rav explains that the Gemara expounds the whole Megillah, unlike any other book, because Mordechai repaired the world of drush, as its closing words 'doresh tov l'amo' hint. Shushan Purim is the Purim of Yerushalayim, written in the Megillah in its complete form, and Mordechai was beyond the grasp of others. He closes with a tefilah for the coming of Moshiach and the rebuilding of Yerushalayim.

title.en: Untranscribed gap

summary.en: A long stretch of about twelve minutes with almost no transcribed speech, likely singing or noise at the seudah.

title.en: Purim remarks on Haman and Amalek

summary.en: A speaker, apparently not the Rav, makes light Purim remarks about saying Haman's name three times and how Amalek spoils the mitzvos of Purim, then introduces a rhymed song.

title.en: Rhymed Purim song on serving Hashem with joy

summary.en: A long rhymed recitation, apparently by another speaker, with a recurring refrain about taking joy from Purim, through vignettes of a Jew who keeps his good cheer through the trials of the year.

catalogTitle: תשנ"ו - שפע אור המגילה יורד כדי להחיות בן מלך

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that the great light of the Megillah came down into the lowest places, like the Baal HaTanya's parable of the jewel poured out to revive the ill prince, in order to give hope to the Jewish people in a time of hiddenness.

abstract.en: The Rav discusses why Rav was displeased with a man who planted flax on Purim. Flax, the Pri Tzaddik explains, grows each stalk alone and signifies separation; it was Kayin's offering, while Purim gathers all Jews together. He contrasts Yaakov's household, called 'nefesh' in the singular, with Esav's 'nefashos', and explains through the Baal HaTanya that division comes only from bodies. He then asks why the Megillah, recorded in the Persian chronicles, did not bring darkness as the Greek translation of the Torah did. He tells how the Maggid fell ill over his teachings' writings lying on the ground, and how the Baal HaTanya's parable of a jewel poured over an ill prince brought him to recover. So too, the Rav concludes, the Megillah's light descended into the lowest places to revive the prince, bringing hope to every generation.

en: Flax signifies separation, since each stalk grows on its own, and so planting it on Purim, a day of gathering all Jews together, displeased Rav more than other work.
Among bodies there is division, but among souls there is unity, so a person for whom the soul is primary can truly love every Jew.
Unlike the Greek translation of the Torah, which brought darkness, the Megillah being recorded in the Persian chronicles brought a great light.
Like the prince who could only be saved by pouring out the whole jewel, the highest Torah must be poured out to revive a very low generation, even if some of it falls on the street.

What happened to Esther, the soul of the Jewish people hidden in Achashverosh's palace, happened to the light of the Torah in the Megillah, which went down so low that Hashem's name is not even mentioned in it.

title.en: Flax on Purim and the idea of separation

summary.en: The Rav asks why Rav was displeased with a man who planted flax on Purim. He brings the Midrash that Kayin's offering was flax and the Pri Tzaddik that flax signifies separation, the opposite of Purim, a time of gathering all Jews, and notes that flax was used only in the Beis HaMikdash.

title.en: Unity of souls, and the Megillah in Persian chronicles

summary.en: The Rav brings Rashi contrasting Yaakov's 'nefesh' with Esav's 'nefashos', the families gathering on Purim, and the Baal HaTanya that division is only of bodies. He then contrasts the darkness that followed the Greek translation of the Torah with the Megillah written in the Persian chronicles, citing the Ibn Ezra, and brings that the highest holiness descended into the lowest places.

title.en: The Baal HaTanya's parable of the ill prince

summary.en: The Rav tells how the Maggid was displeased to see copied writings of his teachings lying on the ground and became ill, and how the Baal HaTanya answered with a parable of a king who finally let a doctor grind up the whole jewel of his crown and pour it over his unconscious son. The Baal HaTanya applied it to the high words of Torah that must be poured out to revive the Jewish people.

title.en: The Megillah's light poured into low places

summary.en: The Rav explains that the Maggid recovered through this plea, and applies it to the Megillah: its light, which the Chasam Sofer calls greater than the light of the Torah of Moshe, went down into Achashverosh's feast and the Persian chronicles, as Esther, the soul of the Jewish people, was hidden in his palace. Instead of darkness it brought 'light and joy', and the Rav calls on his listeners to draw hope, bitachon and emunah from it and to thank Hashem.

catalogTitle: A Time for הודאה

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Chanukah, the time of hoda'ah, is a time of bracha in the sense of increase, tied to Yosef, to the number six and to Parshas Toldos, and he calls for real thanks and tefillah for Klal Yisrael in dangerous times.

abstract.en: Continuing from Mizmor l'Todah, the Rav calls Chanukah the zman of hoda'ah, set for Hallel and thanks, and defines hoda'ah as awareness of receiving more than one deserves, as Leah felt at Yehuda's birth. After the story of the Maggid of Mezritch and the Ba'al HaTanya on how each sedra fits its week, he explains that Chanukah's mitzvah grows from night to night, which is bracha: increase, as the letters of the word bracha show. Yosef, whose name means addition, is the sixth and embodies bracha; Toldos is the sixth sedra, full of bracha, and Yavan is addition in tumah. The Rav then speaks about the daily miracles behind Modim and Mizmor l'Todah, Kayin's and Hevel's offerings, the danger facing Jews in Eretz Yisrael and everywhere, and the need for tefillah, zechusim and teshuvah, since Chanukah is a time for yeshuos.

en: Chanukah is the zman of hoda'ah, set by Chazal for Hallel and thanks, and its gift for the year is thankfulness.
Hoda'ah is a person's awareness that Hashem gives him more than he deserves, as Leah said at the birth of her fourth son.
Bracha means increase, and Chanukah, whose lights and blessings grow each day, is entirely bracha.
Yosef, the sixth, is the embodiment of bracha, and the strength of Yosef is what earned the miracle of Chanukah.
Saying Mizmor l'Todah with thought is like bringing a korban todah, and saying it with one's mind elsewhere is like a flawed korban.
Jews in Eretz Yisrael and everywhere are in danger, and the Rav says one must daven, gather zechusim and do teshuvah, since Chanukah is a time for yeshuos.
