title.en: Chanukah, the time of hoda'ah

summary.en: Continuing from Mizmor l'Todah, the Rav calls Chanukah the zman of thanks, notes that the Rambam puts the laws of Hallel in the laws of Chanukah, and explains that each Yom Tov leaves a gift for the year. Chanukah's gift is hoda'ah, the awareness of receiving more than one deserves, as Leah felt at Yehuda's birth.

title.en: The Maggid's ba'al korei

summary.en: The Rav says each sedra is woven into the events of its week, and tells how the Maggid of Mezritch chose the future Ba'al HaTanya as his ba'al korei because he knew why each aliyah belongs to its day and to the person called up. He adds that Toldos is the first Shabbos of Kislev, the month of hoda'ah.

title.en: Bracha means increase; Yosef the sixth

summary.en: The Rav explains that the mitzvah and the brachos of Chanukah are mosif v'holech, ever increasing, and that this is the meaning of bracha, shown by the letters of the word, each a doubling. Yosef, the sixth, became two shevatim, and his name means addition, so he embodies bracha, with the word bracha appearing six times in Yaakov's blessing of him.

title.en: All of Kislev is Chanukah; Toldos the sixth sedra

summary.en: The Rav says the whole month of Kislev, the month of bracha, is Chanukah, which came from the mesiras nefesh of the Kohanim, like the readiness to give one's life in Shema. He then shows that Toldos is the sixth sedra, the sedra of bracha, with the word bracha in every aliyah, and ties Yosef to the sixth aliyah.

title.en: Yosef against Yavan

summary.en: The Rav brings the Shelah that the strength of Yosef earned the Chanukah miracle, and explains that Yosef is addition in kedushah while Yavan is addition in tumah, invading what is not theirs, as the letters of the name Yavan show. On Chanukah Jews in turn go into the domain of tumah, lighting at night on the left side of the door; Toldos and the sixth aliyah carry the quality of Yosef.

title.en: Sixes of bracha

summary.en: The Rav shows the number six in Toldos: Yitzchak was sixty at the twins' birth and reaped a hundredfold in a year of hunger, and 666 is six in every place, the bracha of increase. Chanukah's thirty-six lights are six times six, the sixth aliyah holds the greatest bracha, Rosh Chodesh Kislev is the sixtieth day of the year, and the sixth middle bracha of Shemoneh Esrei is the one called bracha.

title.en: Daily miracles and the korban todah

summary.en: The Rav says Hashem makes miracles every day, so whoever thanks in Modim without believing it says something false. He explains why 'evening, morning and afternoon' was placed after 'Your miracles', that saying Mizmor l'Todah with thought takes the place of a korban todah, and contrasts Hevel's offering with Kayin's, which lacked a pure heart.

title.en: Caring about Jews in danger

summary.en: Bringing in his rebbe Reb Shraga Feivel Mendlowitz, who rebuked people for not caring what happens to Jews everywhere, the Rav describes the danger to Jews in Eretz Yisrael, surrounded by enemies arming themselves, and in New York too. He recalls how in the war a German general's advance was turned back through miracles, and says that Hashem will make miracles but Jews must daven and not sit in apathy.

title.en: Chanukah, a time of yeshuos

summary.en: The Rav says Chanukah is a time of yeshuos: the reading of the twelve Nesi'im on Chanukah is a zechus against the twelve princes of Yishmael. He calls for tefillah, zechusim and teshuvah, tells of a relative who wanted to leave Eretz Yisrael for America just before the Twin Towers fell, and brings the Gemara that a plague in Eretz Yisrael obligates Jews outside it too.

catalogTitle: תשנ"ז - לעתיד לבא ישתלשל פורים בתוך תחום עשו

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Purim, a taste of the days of Mashiach, stops at the fifteenth of Adar because beyond it lies the border of Esav, and that in the future Purim will extend into that realm as well.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Gemara that the ten sons of Haman are read in one breath, and the Chasam Sofer's explanation: they were the ten forces of the side of impurity, each taking over when the one before fell, until all of it was nullified with Vayzasa. He then explains that Esther is likened to the moon, and the full moon falls on the fifteenth, so Shushan Purim, kept in Yerushalayim, is the deeper Purim. The Gemara asks why Purim cannot be extended to the sixteenth and answers 'v'lo ya'avor'; the Rav explains that from the sixteenth the moon wanes, and that is the realm of Esav, who said 'lo sa'avor bi'. Purim is only a sample of the days of Mashiach. In the future, when the moon becomes whole, Purim will enter Esav's realm too. He ends with Mordechai stepping on Haman and the custom of stamping at Haman's name.

en: According to the Chasam Sofer, the ten sons of Haman were the ten forces of impurity, and only when the last of them, Vayzasa, was killed was the whole structure nullified; therefore they are said in one breath.
Esther is likened to the moon, and the moon is full on the fifteenth, so Shushan Purim is the essential Purim, and Yerushalayim, which corresponds to the full moon, keeps it.
From the sixteenth the moon begins to wane, and that diminishing is the power of Esav; the words 'v'lo ya'avor' mean that Purim cannot cross into Esav's border.
Purim is a level of the days of Mashiach, but only a sample of it, since the power of Esav still rules the world.
In the future, when the moon becomes whole, Purim will extend into the sixteenth and seventeenth as well, the realm of Esav.

title.en: The ten sons of Haman in one breath

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara that the ten sons of Haman are said in one breath, and the Chasam Sofer's explanation, built on how Moshe, Aharon and Miriam passed away: the ten sons were the ten forces of impurity, and only with Vayzasa was the whole structure undone.

title.en: Esther, the full moon and Shushan Purim

summary.en: The Rav explains that Esther is likened to the moon, which is full on the fifteenth, making Shushan Purim the essential Purim, kept in Yerushalayim, the place of the full moon. He asks why the Gemara's answer to extending Purim is the strange phrase 'v'lo ya'avor', and notes that from the sixteenth the moon wanes.

title.en: Purim stops at the border of Esav

summary.en: The Rav calls Purim a level of the days of Mashiach, yet only a sample of it. Esther asked for 'tomorrow' too, but she could not ask for the waning days, because they belong to Esav, who told the Jews 'lo sa'avor bi', and Hashem did not give them his land.

title.en: Haman's ten sons and the future redemption

summary.en: The Rav explains 'v'lo ya'avor' as Esav's cry at his border, which will fall when 'saviors ascend Har Tziyon to judge Har Esav'. He links the lower seven sons of Haman to the seven shepherds, and Vayzasa, the last, to Dovid HaMelech and Mashiach, so that the full end of Haman's structure is still to come.

title.en: Treading on Haman: 'midrach kaf regel'

summary.en: The Rav says that in the future Purim will enter the sixteenth and seventeenth, and reads 'ad midrach kaf regel' as the footsteps of Mashiach. He tells how Mordechai stepped on Haman and answered him with 'v'atah al bamoseimo tidroch', Moshe Rabbeinu's last words, connects this to the custom of stamping at Haman's name, and closes with a wish for today's Shushan Purim.

title.en: The animals Yaakov sent to Esav

summary.en: After a gap in the recording, the Rav brings the Akeidas Yitzchak that the animals Yaakov sent to Esav were the souls of simple Jews, and asks what became of them; he suggests they went to Amalek and were the animals Shaul did not kill. The recording ends with brief, mostly unclear remarks about the hour.

catalogTitle: ע"י הפור שהיפל המן נתגלגל נס של פורים

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Purim is named for Haman's lot because Haman's casting of the goral aroused the world of the goral, where Klal Yisrael is judged by its hidden inner point, and so it was Haman himself who brought about the miracle.

abstract.en: The Rav asks why Purim carries the name of Haman's lot rather than of the salvation. Citing the Siddur of the Ba'al HaTanya, he explains that a goral is above reason and reveals the inner point of a Jew that only Hashem understands, as on Yom Kippur. Angels, as pure intellect, cannot grasp it, which is why Menashe's teshuvah came through a hidden tunnel. He then asks how the decree of the Purim era was annulled, and answers with the Ba'al Shem Tov's teaching of several courts: the heavenly court ruled against Klal Yisrael, but Haman's casting of a lot aroused the world of the goral, where Jews are judged by their hidden love. This is a taste of the days of Mashiach, so Haman caused the miracle. After a break he shows that Jews, like terumah, can never be redeemed or exchanged, which is what Haman sought to deny.

en: A goral is above reason: it reveals the inner point of a Jew that only Hashem understands, which is why both Yom Kippur and Purim are tied to a lot.
Angels are pure intellect and judge correctly by reason, but the point of a Jew that is above reason cannot be explained to them, so Hashem accepted Menashe's teshuvah through a hidden tunnel.

Following the Ba'al Shem Tov, there are several courts above: the decree of destruction passed in the heavenly court of angels, but before Hashem Himself the Jews are judged by their hidden love, which never wanted to sin.
When Haman cast a lot to destroy the Jews, it aroused the world of the goral above, where no externality reaches, and there the Jews were judged by their hidden root, so the decree was annulled.
The whole salvation came through Haman's lot, since the decree itself came from the Jews' own sins; therefore the day is called Purim, after the pur.
Purim is a taste of the world to come and will not be nullified even when the other festivals are, because the inner point it reveals belongs to the days of Mashiach.
Jews are Hashem's terumah, holy in their very being, and can never be redeemed, sold or exchanged for another nation; Haman sought to deny this.

title.en: Tarshish, Amalek, and the eternal bond

catalogTitle: The Greek War Against Faithfulness

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that the Greek war against Klal Yisrael was a war against emunah, which is faithfulness, the bond of Klal Yisrael to Hashem like a wife to her husband, and that tumah is what breaks that bond.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the principle that what happened to the Avos is a sign for their children: the episode of Dina and Shechem foreshadows the Greek decrees, and Levi, not Shimon, led the fight, as the Kohanim and Yehudis did at Chanukah. He asks why, according to the Rashbam, the women were the main part of the miracle. Greek philosophy accepts only what the mind understands; emunah is faithfulness, an instinctive bond like that of a wife to her husband, which the Avnei Nezer uses to explain why a woman is trusted to remarry on one witness. The name Yisrael expresses that bond, and tumah is a barrier that destroys it, so the Greeks set out to defile. The pach shemen came from the place where the dust for the sotah was taken. Yaakov needed the name Yisrael before facing Shechem. The Rav ends with today's war of tumah brought in through electronic devices.

en: The episode of Dina and Shechem was a sign for the Greek decrees, and Levi and the Kohanim, not Shimon, were the ones who won that war.
Greek philosophy accepts only what the mind can understand and prove, which is the opposite of emunah.
Emunah is faithfulness: an instinctive bond between Klal Yisrael and Hashem, like that of a wife to her husband.
Tumah is a barrier that destroys that bond, so the Greek war against emunah was a war of tumah against taharah.
The Greeks tried to erase the name Yisrael, which expresses Klal Yisrael's bond with Hashem, and Yaakov needed that name before his encounter with Shechem.
The Rav says the war of Yavan is being replayed today through tumah that enters Jewish homes, and calls for mesirus nefesh against it.

title.en: Greek philosophy versus emunah as faithfulness

summary.en: The Rav describes the Greek idea of accepting only what the mind understands, shows its illogic with an example from medicine, and defines emunah as faithfulness, an instinctive bond like a wife's to her husband. He brings the Avnei Nezer on why a woman may remarry on one witness, and explains that Levi felt this bond more, rallying to 'Mi laShem elai' with Moshe and later with Matisyahu.

title.en: The name Yisrael and tumah as a barrier

summary.en: The Rav explains that Klal Yisrael carries the name Yisrael as a wife takes her husband's name, joining 'yashar' with Hashem's Name. Since Hashem is pure, the bond exists only with taharah; tumah is a barrier that destroys emunah, which is why so many mitzvos require taharah.

title.en: The Chazon Ish and the dentist's hands

summary.en: The Rav tells how the Chazon Ish, treated at night by a dentist who rushed over before washing his hands, felt the tumah of his fingers affect his learning. He adds that Torah must be learned in purity, and concludes that the war of Yavan was emunah against kefirah, tumah against taharah.

title.en: The Greeks in the Heichal and the hidden pach shemen

summary.en: The Rav explains that the Greeks entered the Heichal not to destroy but to defile, and that what is said of a woman applies to Klal Yisrael, who is pure. He asks how the pach shemen could be hidden under the Heichal floor without breaking its stones, answers from the Gemara in Sotah about a loose marble slab with a ring, from where the dust for the sotah was taken, and concludes that the pach symbolizes the purity of Knesses Yisrael.

title.en: Why Yaakov wanted the name Yisrael from the angel

summary.en: The Rav asks why Yaakov wanted the angel of Esav to call him Yisrael rather than wait for Hashem at Beis El. He brings Rav Tzadok HaKohen that emunah includes knowing one is a Yisrael, the Radbaz that one may not even say he is a Yishmaeli in a time of persecution, and explains that Yaakov knew he would first face Shechem, which stands for the battle of Yehudis.

title.en: Shechem, Yavan and the separateness of Yisrael

summary.en: The Rav explains that Shechem's idea, like Yavan's, was that the Jews are not separate, and that the Greeks forced Jews to write that they have no portion in the G-d of Yisrael. He brings 'ki nevalah asah b'Yisrael', the breaches the Greeks made in the barrier of the Temple Mount, and connects Chanukah to the twenty-five letters of Shema Yisrael and to the mezuzah.

title.en: The war of tumah today

summary.en: The Rav concludes that Yaakov needed the name Yisrael for his fight with Shechem, which stands for Yavan. He then says the war of Yavan is being replayed in the times before Mashiach through tumah brought into Jewish homes by electronic devices, mentions his shul's rule about cell phones, and calls for mesirus nefesh for taharah.

catalogTitle: ע"י פורים זוכים לשושן פורים; מפלת המן ממדריגת חמישים

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that keeping Purim properly lifts a Jew into the higher light of Shushan Purim, and that Haman fell because he tried to reach the level of fifty, the root of Jewish unity revealed in kriyas shema, which reaches down to the lowest Jew.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Maharal: Esther wanted a greater Purim, on the fifteenth, when the moon is full, like the other Yomim Tovim. He tells how the Ba'al HaTanya's mezuzos were special only because the sofer wrote them on the fifteenth. Shushan Purim belongs to the walled cities and is earned by one's service, while the fourteenth came to the weaker Jews through the goral; one who keeps the fourteenth properly is raised into the fifteenth. He then turns to Haman, who, on Zeresh's advice, wanted to stop Mordechai's kriyas shema. Kriyas shema is emunah above understanding and the unity of all souls in 'echad', the level of fifty that Haman tried to reach and fell from, hanged on a tree of fifty on the day of the omer. That root reaches down to the last word of shema, to the lowest Jew, and this is the joy of Purim. He closes with why Purim was not extended to the sixteenth and seventeenth, and with Purim's power to lift a Jew from the dust.

en: According to the Maharal, Esther wanted Purim on the fifteenth, the full moon, the day of the month on which the Yomim Tovim fall.

The fourteenth was given to the weaker Jews through the goral, from a place no sin reaches; Shushan Purim is for the walled cities and is earned through one's service, and keeping the fourteenth properly leads into it.
Haman wanted to stop kriyas shema, which is emunah above understanding and the unity of all Jewish souls in the word 'echad'.
Haman fell because he tried to climb to the level of fifty, the place of Kodesh HaKodashim beyond understanding, and so he was hanged on a tree of fifty cubits on the day of the omer harvest.

The root of kriyas shema reaches down to its last word, 'Elokeichem', which stands for the lowest Jew in the last generation; even the suffix of Hashem's Name may not be erased, and Amalek, who tried to erase it, is himself erased.
The joy of Purim is that the Ribono shel Olam tells even the lowest Jew 'I am your G-d', binding him to Shema Yisrael.

Purim was not extended to the sixteenth and seventeenth because the waning half of the month belongs to Esav; when Moshiach comes, that border will be crossed, and the Gemara's question is in truth a tefillah.

oneLiner.en: Through the Musaf piyut of Parshas HaChodesh built on the words 'Rishon l'Tziyon', the Rav explains that Nissan is the month of renewal and redemption, given to the Jewish people who stand above time.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Musaf piyut of Parshas HaChodesh, whose stanzas begin with the seven words of 'Rishon l'Tziyon'. He contrasts Nissan, the month of chesed and renewal from which the Jewish kings count, with Tishrei, the month of din from which the nations count: the nations have only a 'shanah', a repetition, while the Jews have a 'chodesh', a renewal like the moon. Even a rose reddened by sin stays beloved, and the Jews, who sanctify the months themselves, stand above time, as the early redemption from Egypt showed. Nissan wakes the sleepers, for the heart of Yisrael, Hashem Himself, never sleeps. He explains why the hidden light of creation lacks 'vayehi ken', why Nissan brings salvation on credit and lifts even the lowest, how the spiritual rain of Nissan enters the matzah and the four cups, and closes with the hidden end, the four cups against the four kingdoms, and the four craftsmen of the redemption.

en: Nissan, from which the Jewish kings count, is the month of chesed and renewal, while Tishrei, from which the nations count, is the month of din.
The nations have only a 'shanah', a year of repetition, while the Jews have a 'chodesh', a renewal like the moon that is reborn after darkness.
Because the Jews sanctify the months themselves, they stand above time and set it, rather than being ruled by it.
Nissan wakes the sleepers: there is a point in every Jewish heart, Hashem Himself, that never sleeps and from which revival comes.
In Nissan salvation can come 'on credit', as the redemption from Egypt was granted on the merit of the Torah the Jews would later receive.
The spiritual rain that pours down in Nissan enters the matzah and the four cups, which carry Torah, emunah and blessing for the whole year.

title.en: Nissan and Tishrei: renewal against repetition

summary.en: The Rav contrasts the two Rosh Hashanahs: Nissan, for the Jewish kings, the month of chesed and spring, and Tishrei, from which the nations count, the month of din. The nations have only a 'shanah', repetition, while the Jews, likened to the moon, have a 'chodesh', renewal, and like the bald man of the Midrash can shed their sins.

title.en: The red rose and a people above time

summary.en: The Rav explains that the rose, even when red with sin, stays beloved and gives off a good scent, because the Jews stand above time. He brings the redemption from Egypt before the four hundred years and the mitzvah of sanctifying the month, through which the Jews set time themselves.

title.en: Waking the sleepers: the heart that stays awake

summary.en: On the stanza about waking those who sleep, the Rav explains 'Ani yeshenah v'libi er': the heart of Yisrael, Hashem Himself, never sleeps. In Nissan the covenant of the Avos is renewed, every individual can renew himself, and Hashem hides the sins of the Jews.

title.en: The hidden light and 'lo ken haresha'im'

summary.en: The Rav brings a Midrash that the light of the first day lacks 'vayehi ken' because it was hidden on account of the wicked, and reads 'lo ken haresha'im' in this light. He notes that this Shabbos Parshas HaChodesh falls on the twenty-fifth of Adar, the day of 'Yehi ohr', and calls it a time to daven.

title.en: The chasimah, and Nissan at the center of salvation

summary.en: The Rav explains why the stanza must return to the theme of 'Magen Avraham' before the blessing's close, then turns to the stanza of 'l'Tziyon': Hashem hastened the redemption, and the precious light of creation shines from the twenty-fifth of Adar to Rosh Chodesh Nissan. Nissan stands between Adar and Iyar at the center of all salvations.

title.en: Salvation on credit

summary.en: The Rav explains 'mekupos' as borrowing: Moshe asked in what merit the Jews would be redeemed, and was told they would receive the Torah, so the redemption came on credit. Nissan, the month of creation and chesed and head of the four seasons, feeds the whole year, and he prays that the hidden light made for Adam be renewed.

title.en: 'Zeh' and the month that lifts up

summary.en: On the stanza of 'hinei zeh', the Rav explains 'zeh' as pointing at Hashem with a finger, as at the Yam Suf. Every Nissan brings a possible redemption, and even a Jew in the lowest depths is lifted up, since Nissan means to raise; the clouds then pour spiritual plenty.

title.en: Spiritual rain in the matzah and the four cups

summary.en: The Rav explains why Nissan's mitzvos are mitzvos of eating: the plenty comes through rain into grain and wine, and per the Midrash grain is halachah and wine aggadah, so the matzah and four cups carry Torah for the whole year. Whoever opens his heart is filled, even if he feels like an empty pit.

title.en: Planting emunah in children; the Hallel of Pesach

summary.en: The Rav compares the young plants of spring to small children and says, citing sefarim, that the Seder night is the best time to plant emunah in them. He brings that the Hallel of Pesach 'cracks the roof' and that the four parshiyos, of which HaChodesh is the last, correspond to the four letters of Hashem's Name.

title.en: The hidden end, the four cups and the four craftsmen

summary.en: The Rav explains that the end is hidden in Hashem's heart, that the four cups give the strength to be freed from the four kingdoms, and that if nature renews itself in Nissan, Klal Yisrael surely does. He closes with the Egyptians plowing over hidden Jewish children as a symbol of the exile, and the four craftsmen of the redemption.

catalogTitle: “קול דודי דופק פתחי לי אחותי רעיתי שראשי נמלא טל”

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that in Nissan Hashem knocks on the heart of every Jew, 'kol dodi dofek... pischi li', opening the gates of blessing, and that the avodah of the month is to remove the chametz of the yetzer hara and take in emunah through the matzah.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with Nissan as the month of renewal, when the world was created and all of nature wakes from the sleep of winter in a kind of techiyas hameisim, because the Jewish people were reborn as a nation at the Exodus. Nissan brings down love, song and blessing, and each person chooses how to use them. The gates above open: Hashem knocks on every Jewish heart, 'kol dodi dofek... pischi li', bringing the tal of blessing. He explains the small aleph of Vayikra, matzah as 'patir', opening, the chesed of Nissan against the din of Tishrei, and the Chozeh of Lublin's pinkas. The avodah of the month is removing chametz, the yetzer hara, and eating matzah, the food of emunah. He ends with leaning on Hashem as the root of simcha, and with Avraham Avinu, the first of the believers.

en: Nissan is the month of renewal: nature's rebirth after winter reflects the rebirth of the Jewish people as a nation at the Exodus, and Nissan is a time of techiyas hameisim.
In Nissan the gates above and below open; Hashem knocks on each Jew's heart, 'kol dodi dofek, pischi li', because He comes filled with tal, the blessing of the month.
Nissan's guidance is chesed, in contrast to the din of Tishrei, so its avodah is through song, Hallel, matzah and acts of kindness.
The avodah of Nissan has two parts: removing chametz, which hints at the yetzer hara, and eating matzah, which brings emunah.
Matzah is 'the food of emunah'; its physical form is only a capsule for its spirituality, which is the same as the matzah eaten in Egypt.
Leaning at the Seder expresses that a Jew leans on Hashem; this reliance is the root of simcha, while sadness comes from having no one to lean on.
Pesach is the yom tov of Avraham Avinu, the first of the believers, and the time to take in emunah and bitachon for the whole year.

title.en: Nissan, the month of renewal

summary.en: The Rav opens with the idea that a Jew can renew himself and that the world was created in Nissan. Nature sleeps through the winter and wakes in Nissan as a kind of techiyas hameisim, which is why the haftarah of the dry bones is read on Pesach.

title.en: Salvations circling; rebirth of nature and nation

summary.en: The Rav explains the piyut's words that salvations circle in Nissan like birds, and that the spring rains fill the empty pits, as spiritual flow fills empty people. Since what happens in heaven shows itself below, the rebirth of the Jewish people at the Exodus is mirrored in the rebirth of nature, and Nissan brings a flow of love and chesed.

title.en: Shir HaShirim and the song of Nissan

summary.en: The Rav explains why Shir HaShirim is said on Pesach: Nissan pours love and song onto all of creation, and each person chooses where to direct them; Shlomo HaMelech caught that song for Hashem. Everything opens in Nissan, the treasury of tal included, and among the things that open is the Jewish heart, to which Hashem calls 'kol dodi dofek, pischi li'.

title.en: Pischi li: 'my head is filled with tal'

summary.en: The Rav compares Nissan to the opening of the aron, an eis ratzon when the Zohar's Brich Shmei is said, and explains that Hashem knocks on each Jew's heart and asks him to open because He comes with gifts: His head is filled with tal. Through the gematria of the Name with its milui he shows that tal is the flow of blessing, and calls on the listeners to wake from the sleep of winter to the true sweetness of Torah.

title.en: Vayikra's small aleph: no chance

summary.en: The Rav explains that Vayikra opens with a language of chibah because Hashem is close, a relative of the Jewish people. Amalek is the power of 'mikreh', chance, and Adar is a time of hester panim; the small aleph of Vayikra is seen only from close by, while one who is far reads 'vayikar', coincidence. In Nissan a Jew draws near and sees that Hashem runs everything.

title.en: Matzah as 'patir', the key that opens

summary.en: The Rav brings that the Targum calls matzah 'patir', from 'peter rechem', an opening; matzah is a key to the blessings of tal on Pesach night. He brings the Targum Yonasan that the gates of heaven opened on the night Yaakov took Yitzchak's blessings, suggests this is the source of stealing the afikoman, and says matzah opens the heart, which is why the door is opened for Eliyahu.

title.en: Nissan's chesed and the kingship of Hashem

summary.en: The Rav explains that Nissan's tzeruf is 'yismechu hashamayim vesagel ha'aretz', the Name in its straight order, pure chesed, so its avodah is through song, matzah and kindness, as Hilchos Pesach opens with maos chittin. Nissan is Rosh Hashanah for kings and the time the nation was created, which answers why the Aseres HaDibros say 'who took you out of Egypt'; he hopes for the day when even the nations will say 'Hashem malach'.

title.en: Nissan holds the whole year

summary.en: The Rav tells that the Ba'al Shem Tov secluded himself on Rosh Chodesh Nissan, and contrasts Nissan's aleph-beis in order with Tishrei's reversed order. He brings from the Bnei Yissaschar the story of the Chozeh of Lublin, who on each of the first twelve days of Nissan wrote down all that would happen in one month of the year, since each day of the Nesi'im leads a month.

title.en: Searching out the chametz of the heart

summary.en: The Rav divides Nissan's avodah into 'sur mei'ra', removing chametz, and 'aseh tov', eating matzah. He asks why the Torah is so strict with chametz and answers from the Zohar that chametz is the yetzer hara, so one must search the holes and cracks of the heart by the light of the soul. He tells how the Lechovitcher Rebbe sent a messenger to announce this on the night of bedikas chametz.

title.en: Matzah, the food of emunah, against Amalek

summary.en: The Rav explains that the Zohar calls matzah 'michla dimeheimnusa', the food of emunah. Erev Pesach is a war against Amalek, whose gematria is 'safek', doubt: burning the chametz burns the yetzer hara, and eating matzah brings in emunah. He compares matzah to a capsule whose hidden ingredient strengthens a Jew for the whole year.

title.en: Ha lachma anya: the same matzah as in Egypt

summary.en: The Rav brings the Satmar Rav on the Magen Avraham's question how one can say 'ha lachma anya': the matzah's physical form is only a container, and its inner light is the same as in Egypt, so 'this night is all matzah'. He explains 'kulanu mesubin' as everyone having cheirus, and tells of the Yismach Moshe, who was shown Eliyahu offering korbanos, and of a tzaddik who felt the korban Pesach in his afikoman.

title.en: Matzah, the holy Names, and leaning on it

summary.en: The Rav brings that matzah equals three times the Name with its milui, higher than ordinary bread, which equals three times the Name and is sanctified by netilas yadayim and hamotzi. Eating matzah takes the holy Names into oneself. He then brings the Midrash that even a poor man must recline, and asks how one may lean on the afikoman under the pillow when one may not lean on a sefer.

title.en: Leaning on Hashem: simcha and its opposite

summary.en: The Rav answers that matzah is emunah and bitachon, and a Jew leans on Hashem. Simcha, with sin that sounds like samech, comes from 'somech', leaning, while atzvus comes from 'azuv', forsaken. Rich and poor have the same Ribono shel Olam to lean on; one who relies on Him is not shamed, while 'kesufas panim', the pale face of shame, is a sign of chametz.

title.en: Avraham Avinu and the spring of every Jew

summary.en: The Rav explains that Pesach is the yom tov of Avraham Avinu, to whom everything happened on Pesach, the first of the believers. Pesach is a time of techiyas hameisim; a Jew must not be worse than a tree that blossoms, but sprout and bear fruit through the mitzvos of Pesach. He closes with a tefillah for the Nissan of the complete redemption.

catalogTitle: A Parallel Between טבת and our Generation; Darkness Preceded by Light (Connection to פרשת ויגש)

oneLiner.en: The Rav shows that Teves, the dark month of the tribe of Dan, mirrors our generation, the deaf and mute Chushim ben Dan at the end of the camp, yet the geulah is always prepared inside the darkness of galus.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with Parshas Vayigash, the descent into galus, and the days of 8, 9 and 10 Teves. Teves is the darkest month: the Torah was translated into Greek, the light of the Beis HaMikdash began to be extinguished, and the gentile festivities give off a hidden darkness. Teves belongs to Dan, the lowest tribe, whom darkness follows everywhere: the one case of immorality in Mitzrayim, Micha's idol, expulsion from the clouds of glory, the dark north side of the camp, Shimshon. Chushim ben Dan, the deaf and mute seventieth soul who beheaded Esav, is our generation: last, believing without seeing, tested as never before, yet destined to finish the work and bring Mashiach. Through Yocheved, the other seventieth, and the Atbash pairing of Pesach with Tisha B'Av, he shows that geulah is prepared before galus begins, and he closes with the combination of Hashem's name for Teves, through which all Jews will rise together.

en: Teves, with the longest nights, is the darkest month, and the eighth to tenth of Teves are three days of special darkness, culminating in the siege of Yerushalayim on the tenth.
Teves is assigned to the tribe of Dan, the lowest of the tribes, and wherever there is darkness in Jewish history Dan is found there.
Chushim ben Dan, the deaf and mute seventieth soul who went down to Mitzrayim and who beheaded Esav, signifies our generation, the last before Mashiach.
Our generation must believe without seeing; as the foundation at the bottom of the building, it carries all the generations before it and is charged with finishing the mission of Klal Yisrael.
Mitzvos done under the unprecedented temptations of this generation are valued by Hashem more than the greater deeds of earlier generations.
Galus is always rooted in geulah: Yocheved, mother of Moshe Rabbeinu, was born exactly as Yaakov's family entered Mitzrayim.
The combination of Hashem's name for Teves comes from the passuk Gadlu laShem iti, and through it all Jews, even the fallen, will rise and praise Hashem together.

title.en: Vayigash and the days of darkness in Teves

summary.en: The Rav opens with Vayigash as a sedra of melancholy, with a remez in Yiddish on its name, and introduces the eighth of Teves, when three days of darkness began, and the fast of the tenth, when the king of Bavel besieged Yerushalayim. He explains why the tenth of Teves could not be put off even for Shabbos, and why with the fixed calendar it no longer falls on Shabbos.

title.en: Hidden light and hidden darkness

summary.en: The Rav says that one whose neshama is not corroded sees a heavenly glow in the Chanukah and Shabbos candles, and that the same person should sense the hidden darkness coming from the gentile decorations of the season. He brings the Midrash that light is the deeds of the tzaddikim and darkness the deeds of the wicked.

title.en: Teves, the darkest month

summary.en: The Rav explains that Teves, with the longest nights, is the darkest month, and that the tenth marks the full strength of a thing: on the tenth of Teves the light of the Beis HaMikdash began to be put out. He discusses why the translation of the Torah into Greek on the eighth was darkness, brings Megillas Taanis on the eighth, ninth and tenth, and explains why in this leap year Teves comes earlier.

title.en: Teves belongs to Dan, the lowest tribe

summary.en: The Rav assigns the twelve months to the twelve tribes by the order of the camps in the Midbar, so that Teves falls to Dan. From Rashi on Betzalel and Oholiav he shows that Dan was the lowest of the tribes, and he lists where darkness appears in Dan: the single case of immorality in Mitzrayim, Micha's idol carried across the sea, and Dan's being cast out of the clouds of glory.

title.en: Shimshon, Yaakov's vision, and the eyes

summary.en: The Rav turns to Shimshon of Dan, of whom the Gemara says he went after his eyes, and insists that his strange episodes cannot be taken at face value, since Yaakov Avinu, seeing him with ruach hakodesh, thought he was Mashiach. He brings the Arizal that the months correspond to organs of the head, with Teves and Shvat as the two eyes, tying Shimshon's eyes to Dan's month.

title.en: Dan in the north; the seventy souls

summary.en: The Rav shows that Dan's camp traveled in the north, the side where the sun never shines, so that Dan and darkness are inseparable. He ties this to Vayigash, read near the tenth of Teves, where Hashem must reassure Yaakov about going down to Mitzrayim, and asks who is the seventieth soul when only sixty-nine are counted; one answer of Chazal is Chushim ben Dan.

title.en: Chushim ben Dan beheads Esav

summary.en: The Rav tells the Midrash: at Yaakov's burial Esav claimed a share in the Me'aras HaMachpelah, the deed of sale had been left in Mitzrayim and Naftali ran to fetch it, and Chushim ben Dan, who was deaf and mute, asked why they were waiting and struck off Esav's head, which rolled into the cave. He notes that Esav did not belong there, but his head did.

title.en: Chushim, the last one: our generation

summary.en: The Rav explains that Chushim, the seventieth, is the last, fitting for Dan, who trailed behind the whole camp among the stragglers whom Amalek could attack. Since place corresponds to time, Dan corresponds to the last period before Mashiach: our generation is Chushim ben Dan, deaf and mute, unable truly to speak in tefillah and Torah or to hear the word of Hashem, living in a perpetual Teves.

title.en: The foot of the Tav and the war with Esav

summary.en: The Rav shows that the alef-beis descends from the oneness of alef to the tav, whose foot protrudes beyond the camp into the realm of the sitra achra, and that foot represents Dan. He brings the Heichal HaBerachah that the tav is made of a dalet and a nun, which spell Dan, and concludes that Chushim ben Dan, who cut off Esav's head, stands for the generation that will finally defeat Esav.

title.en: A generation of emunah at the foundation

summary.en: The Rav describes our generation as cast out of the clouds of glory: earlier generations saw the wonders of tzaddikim, while ours must believe without seeing. Emunah is the foundation, and the foundation lies at the bottom, so everything before us depends on us; ours is a generation of return, carrying out Dan's mission of gathering in all the camps, and it defeats Esav by battling the yetzer hara under the hardest conditions.

title.en: Unprecedented tests, and the Chanukah light

summary.en: The Rav describes the unprecedented tests of the generation and brings the Gemara of the father who sets his son at the door of a house of sin: what can the son do not to sin? Mitzvos done under such conditions are valued more than the greater deeds of earlier generations, and one who fell may afterwards plead that the test was too strong, though never before a sin. Hashem gave the Chanukah light to carry through the darkness, and this is the message of Vayigash.

title.en: Yocheved: geulah at the gate of galus

summary.en: The Rav brings Rashi's other answer, that the seventieth was Yocheved, born between the walls as they entered Mitzrayim, and asks why she was born at that moment. Through the Atbash alef-beis in Midrash Eichah, which pairs the first day of Pesach with Tisha B'Av, he shows that galus is always rooted in geulah: Yocheved, mother of Moshe Rabbeinu, was born as the galus began, so the redeemer was prepared first.

title.en: The pearl in the depths, and Shaul ben haKenaanis

summary.en: The Rav says the dark months of Teves and Shvat will be raised, and brings the Midrash that called Yocheved's being the seventieth a pearl: in the depths of darkness, where galus begins, one finds the pearl of geulah, and our generation dives to depths earlier generations never reached. He then points to the one culprit among the seventy, Shaul ben haKenaanis of Shimon, whom Targum Yonasan identifies as Zimri.

title.en: Gadlu laShem iti: all will rise together

summary.en: The Rav explains that each month has a combination of Hashem's name drawn from a passuk: Nissan's from Yismechu hashamayim, and Teves's from the final letters of Gadlu laShem iti, since it is a month of din. The initial letters spell Shaul, so even the fallen of the generation, rooted in Teves or in Av, will be lifted by Hashem and join the chorus of praise, when the darkness of Teves turns into perpetual day.

catalogTitle: חודש של חידוש ואהבה

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains Nissan as the month of renewal and chesed, and matzah as the key that opens a Jew to emunah and to a bond with Hashem beyond time and place.

abstract.en: Following Rabbi Yehoshua that the world was created in Nissan, the Rav traces three Nissans of creation: the world itself, spoiled by Adam's sin; Klal Yisrael at the Exodus, spoiled by the Golden Calf; and the Mishkan, a smaller world of holiness. The final Nissan will be the redemption. Hashem did not tire of renewing, and a Jew should not either. Nissan is the month of chesed, the right side, against Tishrei's din. Spring, described in Shir haShirim, calls on the Jew to renew himself along with creation. Matzah is the key: the Targum calls it 'petira', opening, and Pesach is about opening doors and the heart. Pesach is Avraham's festival and the foundation of emunah, the time to plant faith in children. Matzah is heavenly food beyond time and place, holding the Divine names. The Rav closes with the Radbaz that chametz is the yetzer hara, two stories, and a call to pray for a kosher Pesach.

en: Nissan is the month of creation, renewed three times: the world, Klal Yisrael at the Exodus, and the Mishkan; the final renewal will be the redemption.
Nissan is the month of chesed, the right side, while Tishrei is the month of din.
Matzah is the key to Nissan: the Targum calls it 'petira', opening, and all of Pesach is about opening up.
Pesach is the festival of Avraham Avinu, the first of the believers, and so it is the foundation of emunah.
Matzah is a heavenly food above time and place, unlike chametz, which time acts on and which spreads in space.
Bread lives through the 'word of Hashem' within it; matzah carries the full Divine name three times, and the one who eats it absorbs emunah.
Pesach is the lowest of the festivals but their foundation, the bond of a Jew with Hashem, and one must pray for a kosher Pesach.

title.en: The three Nissans of creation

summary.en: Following Rabbi Yehoshua that the world was created in Nissan, the Rav shows how the world, then Klal Yisrael at the Exodus, then the Mishkan were each created in Nissan, the first two spoiled by sin, with the final Nissan of the redemption still to come. From Hashem renewing again and again, and from the Mishkan set up seven times, he learns not to give up after a failure.

title.en: Nissan, the month of chesed

summary.en: The Rav explains that the world was built with chesed and that Nissan is the month of chesed, the right side, which Jews strengthen in many customs. He contrasts Rabbi Yehoshua and Beis Hillel (chesed, Nissan) with Rabbi Eliezer and Beis Shammai (din, Tishrei).

title.en: Spring calls the Jew to renew himself

summary.en: Pesach opens with chesed, and in Nissan the whole world renews itself, as Shir haShirim describes the spring. The Rav asks the Jew why he alone should stay old when all of creation rises anew, and ties this to the haftarah of the dry bones.

title.en: Matzah, the key that opens

summary.en: The Rav calls matzah the key to Nissan: leaving the narrowness of Mitzrayim, the Targum's 'petira' meaning opening, opening the door at the seder, and the storehouses of dew opened on Pesach night. Pesach calls on a Jew to open his heart, and the Maharal explains that spring renews nature because Klal Yisrael is renewed.

title.en: Pesach, Avraham's festival of love and emunah

summary.en: On Pesach everything is renewed, house, clothes and dishes, and a Jew should ask Hashem to renew him. The Rav shows that Pesach is Avraham's festival: his bris, the angels' visit and his war with the four kings were all on Pesach, and as the root of love and of emunah he makes Pesach the foundation of emunah.

title.en: Planting emunah in the children; eating emunah

summary.en: Pesach is the festival of the children and the time to plant emunah in them, simply and in their language. Talking about emunah is not enough; one must eat it, and matzah, the 'food of faith', becomes part of the person's flesh and blood.

title.en: Matzah above time and place

summary.en: Everything in this world exists in time and place, as the laws of witnesses show. Matzah is heavenly bread that time does not rule; once eighteen minutes of time act on dough it becomes chametz and spreads in space. Emunah likewise means believing in what is beyond grasp.

title.en: The soul within bread

summary.en: The Rav asks how physical bread can give life, and answers from the passuk that a person lives by the 'word of Hashem' in the bread, its soul. Bread holds three times the name Havayah, and a Jew who washes and makes hamotzi for the sake of Heaven eats that holiness into himself.

title.en: Matzah, the full Divine name, and 'Mah'

summary.en: Matzah equals three times the name Havayah spelled out in full (45), the miraculous source of the Exodus beyond understanding. The seder is full of the word 'mah', the question with no answer, which is emunah. The Rav tells how the Divrei Chaim, after the seder, felt the holy names absorbed into his body.

title.en: Pesach the foundation; chametz is the yetzer hara

summary.en: Pesach is the lowest of the festivals but their foundation, the bond with Hashem, which is why its prohibition carries kares. The Rav brings the Radbaz that chametz is the yetzer hara, to be uprooted entirely, and tells of Baron Rothschild's 'Pesach house' and the Divrei Chaim's answer that Hashem wants the chametz removed and matzah brought into the same place.

title.en: Praying for a kosher Pesach

summary.en: Pesach cleaning is uprooting the yetzer hara, and one must pray for a kosher Pesach. The Rav tells of a tzaddik who found a wheat kernel in his soup at the seder and learned from Heaven that he had not prayed to be saved from chametz, then explains the two eatings of matzah as the past and future redemption and closes with a blessing.

catalogTitle: התעוררי "תחיית המתים" ביחד עם העולם!

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains Nissan as the month of chesed and renewal, when the world and Klal Yisrael are created anew, and calls on everyone to rise to a 'techiyas hameisim' of fresh life in learning, davening and eating mehudar matzah.

abstract.en: Opening on Shabbos Parshas HaChodesh, the Rav explains that Nissan is a time of midas hachesed, when the Name of Hashem stands in its straight order. He brings the dispute of Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua whether the world was created in Tishrei or in Nissan, and Tosafos that both are true. Next year's Birkas HaChamah will fall on erev Pesach, so great times are coming. Nissan renews all of nature, unlike Tishrei, and Pesach is a time of techiyas hameisim: one must not be 'dead' in learning and davening. The first twelve days of Nissan govern the year, as the story of the Chozeh of Lublin shows. Matzah is the food of emunah; by gematria it is three times the full Name of Hashem, three times 'adam'. Chametz is the yetzer hara, so one should eat mehudar matzah baked lishmah, ideally chaburah matzos, and be careful about every trace of chametz.

en: Nissan is a time of midas hachesed, when the letters of Hashem's Name stand in their straight order; in Tishrei they are reversed, which is midas hadin.
In Nissan all of nature is renewed, and Pesach is a time of techiyas hameisim; the Rav calls on the bochurim to rise with freshness and life in learning and davening.
Each of the first twelve days of Nissan governs one month of the year, so one should daven on them with life and enthusiasm.
Matzah is the 'food of emunah', and by gematria it equals three times the full Name of Hashem, three times 'adam', while ordinary bread equals only three times the simple Name.
Chametz is the yetzer hara, which is why the Torah is so strict about it, and burning and cleaning chametz removes the yetzer hara from a person.
Matzah must be baked lishmah because holy Names are in it, and so the Rav urges mehudar matzah, ideally chaburah matzos, at least for the sedarim.

title.en: Nissan, the month of chesed and creation

summary.en: The Rav opens with Parshas HaChodesh and Rosh Chodesh Nissan, explaining that in Nissan the Name of Hashem stands straight, which is chesed. He brings the dispute whether the world was created in Tishrei or Nissan and Tosafos' answer that both are true.

title.en: Birkas HaChamah and great times ahead

summary.en: The Rav notes that next year Birkas HaChamah will be said in Nissan, on erev Pesach, as in the year of yetzias Mitzrayim, and warns that great times are coming and life cannot go on as usual. He mentions the coming Pesach and the Purim meshulash in Yerushalayim, and urges holding on to the inspiration.

title.en: Nissan renews nature; Tishrei is its opposite

summary.en: The Rav explains that the world was built with chesed and that in Nissan Hashem created Klal Yisrael. He paints the spring: warm winds, returning birds singing new songs, green fields and flowers, contrasted with Tishrei's falling leaves, and reads 'aviv' as alef-beis in order against Tishrei's letters going backwards.

title.en: Pesach as techiyas hameisim

summary.en: The Rav describes how everything becomes new for Pesach, and brings the brachah 'mechayeh hameisim' on something not seen for twelve months. Pesach is techiyas hameisim, as the haftarah of the dry bones shows, and he calls on the bochurim to rise up with freshness in learning and davening.

title.en: The first twelve days of Nissan and the Chozeh

summary.en: The Rav brings a tzaddik's reading of 'lo amus ki echyeh' about people who are dead while alive. He explains that the first twelve days of Nissan govern the twelve months, tells the story of the Chozeh of Lublin's notebook as brought by the Bnei Yissaschar, and urges davening with chiyus on these days.

title.en: Matzah, the food of emunah, and its gematria

summary.en: The Rav brings the Zohar that matzah is the 'food of emunah', notes how rare true emunah is in our generation, and explains that eating matzah is eating holy Names. Bread equals three times the simple Name of Hashem, but matzah equals three times the full Name, three times 'adam', explaining 'lo al halechem levado yichyeh ha'adam'.

title.en: Why chametz is so strict; mehudar matzah

summary.en: The Rav brings Tosafos' question why chametz has so many stringencies, the Rishonim's disputed answers, and the Radbaz that the only answer is that chametz is the yetzer hara. From here he urges eating mehudar matzah baked lishmah, explaining why Chassidic gedolim did not allow machine matzos.

title.en: Matzah in place of tefillin; chaburah matzos

summary.en: The Rav explains that on Chol HaMoed Pesach the matzah takes the place of tefillin, so it deserves the same care. He praises chaburah matzos baked with joy, brings the Bnei Yissaschar's lesson from the dor haflagah that repeating 'l'shem' adds holiness, and says the matzah annuls the power of Klal Yisrael's enemies.

title.en: Care on Pesach and closing blessing

summary.en: The Rav says Avraham fought the kings on Pesach night with the power of matzah, then urges great care with even a trace of chametz, bringing the Arizal that this guards a person from sin all year and the Mishnah's language about the korban Pesach. He closes with a blessing for the coming blessed days and the full redemption.

catalogTitle: חטוף כח החידוש מהסיטרא אחרא

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains why the frog's song in Perek Shirah is 'Baruch shem kevod malchuso', a quiet praise from the place of mixed good and evil, and how the sitra achra has seized the power of renewal that belongs to the Jewish people in Nissan.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with Nissan, when all creation is renewed and sings, and brings Perek Shirah, where the frog tells King David that its song is greater than his. He asks why, and brings the dispute of Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah over 'one frog'. Building on the Bnei Yissaschar, who ties the frog to the attribute of yesod, he explains that the frog lives both in water and on land and is a mixture of tahor and tamei. Therefore its song is 'Baruch shem kevod malchuso', said quietly, because it declares Hashem's rule even in the place of the sitra achra. Tumah begins with 'two', as the tractates Ohalos and Negaim open with 'shnayim'. In the future, says the Imrei Emes, Baruch shem will be said aloud, and the frog merited this through mesirus nefesh. He then explains that renewal belongs to the Jews; when they neglect it the sitra achra seizes it, as seen in modern inventions that take away a Jew's peace. He calls for fresh avodah and stronger yiras shamayim.

en: The frog, which lives both in the sea and on land, is the intermediate between tahor and tamei and a mixture of good and evil.
The frog's song in Perek Shirah is 'Baruch shem kevod malchuso', praise that comes from the place of the sitra achra and is therefore said quietly.
Kedushah is oneness and tumah is division, which is why Ohalos and Negaim, the severest forms of tumah, open with the word 'shnayim'.
In the time of Moshiach Baruch shem will be said aloud, and the frog's song, earned through its mesirus nefesh, will be the highest of all.
Renewal belongs to the Jewish people; when they do not use it, the sitra achra seizes it, as with the flood of modern inventions.
Today's test cannot be escaped, so ordinary, traditional yiras shamayim is not enough; one must strengthen it and serve Hashem with freshness.

title.en: Nissan: all creation sings

summary.en: The Rav opens with Nissan, the month of renewal, when creation sings to Hashem, and describes Perek Shirah, where each creature praises Hashem with a passuk. He notes the two songs of Nissan, the Hallel in Egypt and the song at the sea, and that the future song will be a 'shir chadash'.

title.en: The frog's song and 'one frog'

summary.en: The Rav brings the opening of Perek Shirah, where a frog tells King David that its song is greater than his, and asks how that can be. He then brings the dispute of Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah over 'one frog' and asks why Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah sent him specifically to Negaim and Ohalos.

title.en: The frog and the attribute of yesod

summary.en: The Rav sharpens the question: he could have sent him to monetary law or to Kodshim. He brings the Bnei Yissaschar that the plagues correspond to the ten sefiros and the frog to yesod, and explains that Pharaoh wanted to keep the Jewish girls alive to create a mixture of good and evil, which the Avnei Nezer says is worse than evil itself.

title.en: The frog between tahor and tamei

summary.en: The Rav brings that every kind on land has a counterpart in the sea, one tahor and the other tamei, and the principle, from Rabbi Pinchas of Koretz via the Bnei Yissaschar, that between two extremes there is an intermediate. The frog, found both in the river and on land, is that intermediate, a mixture of tahor and tamei, and so it punished the Egyptians who sought to mix.

title.en: Why Baruch shem is said quietly

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara that Yaakov answered his sons' Shema with Baruch shem, and that it is said quietly like the king's daughter who craved a lowly dish. He explains that Shema is the higher unity of Hashem who is wholly holy, while Baruch shem declares that His rule extends even to the lowest places of the sitra achra, which is true but unseemly to say aloud.

title.en: The frog sings Baruch shem

summary.en: The Rav shows that in Perek Shirah the frog's song is Baruch shem. Since Hashem does not want praise from the wicked, a tamei creature's song is said by its tahor counterpart, but the frog, itself a mixture, sings quietly, and it alone sings no passuk. He adds the Midrash that the destroyers flee from Shema and whisper Baruch shem, and explains why one says Baruch shem after a needless brachah.

title.en: Tumah begins with 'two'

summary.en: From the Rambam's order of the tractates the Rav shows that Ohalos and Negaim are the severest tumah. Kedushah is oneness and tumah is division: the second day brought Gehinnom, pairs are dangerous, and Yeravam made two calves. Ohalos and Negaim open with 'shnayim', which resolves the dispute: the frog is a mixture of one and two. He adds the shuruk, the vowel of yesod, behind 'eshreka lahem'.

title.en: Baruch shem in the future

summary.en: The Rav brings the Imrei Emes that in the future Baruch shem will be a passuk and be said aloud, and explains that once all tumah is gone, as with the Midrash that the chazir will become tahor, Hashem's rule everywhere will no longer be a disgrace. The Midrash reads 'tzefardea' as 'tzipor de'ah', tied to 'the earth shall be full of knowledge', and the frog's song will then shine.

title.en: The frog's mesirus nefesh

summary.en: The Rav explains that the frogs gave their lives for Hashem by jumping into the ovens, and that the path of yesod is mesirus nefesh, as Yosef HaTzaddik earned his level through his test. He quotes the Imrei Emes and the Belzer Rebbe that before Moshiach nothing is achieved without mesirus nefesh, defines it as giving up one's will, and concludes that the frog's song will be the finest because of its mesirus nefesh.

title.en: Renewal belongs to the Jews

summary.en: The Rav explains that the avodah of Nissan, 'hachodesh hazeh lachem', is to serve Hashem every day as if for the first time. He brings the Chiddushei HaRim that renewal belongs to the Jews, and when they neglect it the sitra achra seizes it, as in 'a new king arose over Egypt', and the Avnei Nezer that the nations have festivity because the Jews did not keep Shabbos as a day of menuchah.

title.en: Rabbi Elazar ben Arach

summary.en: The Rav tells of Rabbi Elazar ben Arach, the greatest student of Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakai and a soul with a spark of Moshiach, who went to the ten tribes to bring them back, was drawn after them and forgot his learning, reading 'hachodesh hazeh lachem' as 'hacharesh haya libam'. He explains that he grasped the passuk of his root, the first mitzvah tied to Moshiach, and lamented that their hearts did not hear the call of renewal.

title.en: The sitra achra's new inventions

summary.en: The Rav applies 'a new king who did not know Yosef' to our time, when the renewal of Yosef has passed to the sitra achra through new devices such as the internet and television. He describes how the world lived unchanged for centuries until a sudden power of renewal came down, which first showed in great Torah giants and the Ba'al Shem Tov, but the Jews did not seize it and the nations did.

title.en: How the new devices steal menuchah

summary.en: The Rav describes how the telephone, then the cellphone, and the airplane took away a Jew's peace and time for learning, so that the sitra achra uses the renewal meant for chiddushim in Torah. He says the Jews must be renewed, not asleep, and points to the haftorah of the dry bones read on Pesach.

title.en: Two kinds of test

summary.en: The Rav distinguishes the test of keeping away from evil, as the nazir is told to go around the vineyard, from the greater test of being trapped inside it, as Yosef was. He tells a story from the Chazon Ish of a Jew whose ordinary yiras shamayim failed when an important guest was due on Friday night, and concludes that in our generation one must strengthen one's yiras shamayim.

title.en: Renewal in learning and davening

summary.en: The Rav calls for new 'inventions' in the war against the yetzer hara: learning with life, davening with feeling, and finding a good minyan. He notes the second day of Pesach and the haftorah of the dry bones, and closes with a tefillah to sing the new song with Moshiach and to say Baruch shem aloud.

catalogTitle: An Explanation of ניטל and the Month of טבת

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains why Teves, and not Adar, is the hardest month of the year, what lies behind the custom of Nittel, and that the remedy for the darkness of this galus is to come close to a tzaddik.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the sefarim's statement that Teves is a difficult month and asks why, since Adar, the last month, should be lowest. Adar's very lowness brings its rise, as with the queen whom the king finally lifts himself; the Ramban on Haazinu teaches that the geulah does not depend on teshuvah. Teves holds the longest night, the tekufah, which gentiles made a festival from the time of Adam Harishon; this is the root of Nittel, when Jews do not learn. He discusses the two calculations of the tekufah, the Gregorian calendar, Yosef and the wife of Potiphar, Onkelos, the Chofetz Chaim and the Chasam Sofer. Teves, as the beginning of the last degel, carries the strength of the end. Yaakov going down to galus 'in the visions of the night' is our generation, precious to Hashem. Asarah b'Teves marks how nearness to evil corrupts; the answer is nearness to a tzaddik.

en: Adar, the last month and a time of hester panim, has its salvation in its very lowness: one who has fallen to the bottom must rise.
According to the Ramban on Haazinu, the geulah is promised unconditionally, not dependent on teshuvah, and is the one part of the shirah still waiting to be fulfilled.
The tekufah of Teves, the longest and darkest night, became a festival of avodah zarah, and this is the source of the custom not to learn Torah on Nittel.
Teves is the hardest month because it begins the last degel, of Dan, and a beginning carries in it the strength of the whole.
Jews of the final, darkest galus are, according to the Rav, the most precious to Hashem, as Hashem called Yaakov twice by name when he went down to galus at night.
The danger of Asarah b'Teves is nearness, 'samach', to the king of Bavel, and the remedy is nearness to a tzaddik, as Yehudah felt kedushah when he came close to Yosef.

title.en: Why Teves is a difficult month

summary.en: The Rav opens with Vayigash, the parsha of going into galus that falls in Teves, and brings that the twelve months parallel the twelve shevatim and that Teves is the most difficult month. He asks why, since Adar, the last month and a time of hester panim, should be lowest, and explains that Adar's very lowness brings its rise.

title.en: The king who brings back his queen

summary.en: The Rav brings a mashal of a king who sent away his queen three times; the third time she refuses to return until he comes and lifts her up himself. So too in this galus Hashem must bring Klal Yisrael back in whatever state they are, and he brings the Ramban on Haazinu that the geulah does not depend on teshuvah.

title.en: The tekufah of Teves and the origin of Nittel

summary.en: The Rav explains that Teves holds the tekufah, the longest night, so dark that Jews do not learn Torah then, and that Chanukah's light comes against it. He brings the Gemara that Adam Harishon made a festival when the days began to lengthen, which the idolaters kept, and discusses the two calculations of the tekufah, of Shmuel and Rav Ada, the Gregorian calendar and why Nittel falls on different dates.

title.en: Yosef, Onkelos and the night of Nittel

summary.en: The Rav reads 'the day of their festival' in Rashi on Yosef's test with the wife of Potiphar: on that day Yosef could not protect himself by learning Torah. He brings Onkelos' rendering that Yosef came to do his accounts, the custom of the Chasam Sofer for Nittel night, and the Gemara in Gittin about Onkelos and the punishment of Yeshu.

title.en: Keeping Nittel: a time when one does not learn

summary.en: The Rav relates that the Chofetz Chaim and the Lithuanian yeshivos did not keep Nittel, while most of European Jewry did; Rabbi Yonasan Eybeshutz answered the priests that a minhag Yisrael is itself Torah, and the Chasam Sofer had his talmidim sleep early and learn from chatzos. He explains from the Sefer Yetzirah that just as there are places where one may not learn Torah, there is a time.

title.en: The beginning holds the whole: Teves and Dan

summary.en: The Rav answers his opening question: a beginning contains the strength of all that follows, as Haman was hanged on the first day of Sefirah, which already holds the fiftieth day. Teves begins the last degel, Dan, Asher and Naphtali, so it is Dan's month; Dan is always in trouble, and the Mitzri who cursed was from Dan, whose day falls in Teves, while Naphtali at the very end must rise.

title.en: Yaakov Yaakov: the precious Jews of the night

summary.en: The Rav explains why Hashem spoke to Yaakov 'in the visions of the night' when he went down to galus, and why He called 'Yaakov, Yaakov', in Rashi's words an expression of love. The Jews of the last galus, in its darkest night, are the most precious to Hashem, and the greatest danger today is living among the nations, after centuries in which Hashem kept us apart.

title.en: Asarah b'Teves and the danger of nearness

summary.en: The Rav explains that Asarah b'Teves is the climax of three days of darkness and that, according to the Abudraham, it is so severe it would be fasted even on Shabbos, though nothing was yet broken that day. The word 'samach', that the king of Bavel came near Yerushalayim, teaches that nearness to a rasha already lets his tumah in, just as standing near a tzaddik helps a tefilah; this is the galus of today.

title.en: Vayigash: come close to a tzaddik

summary.en: The Rav explains that when Yehudah approached Yosef he felt a great kedushah without knowing why, because he came near a tzaddik. The remedy for the 'samach' of Asarah b'Teves is to come close to a tzaddik and a talmid chacham, to have a Rebbe at every age and ask him questions, a bond rooted in one's soul.

catalogTitle: לעזור בבית בהכנה לפסח; להתחדש עצמו בזמן התחדשות

oneLiner.en: The Rav teaches that the lowly work of cleaning before Pesach is precious to Hashem, and that Nissan, the month in which all of creation is renewed, calls on every Jew to renew himself through emunah and to begin again.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the terumas hadeshen, the removal of the ashes at night, and explains that this humble night avodah, done in work clothes, is most dear to Hashem; so too taking a broom and helping at home before Pesach, as a story with Rav Gifter shows. He then turns to Nissan, the month of creation. Hashem tried four times in Nissan to bring the world to its tikkun: at creation, at Yetzias Mitzrayim, at the Mishkan, and the Nissan of the geulah still awaited. Hashem does not give up, and a Jew too must always begin again. In Nissan all of nature comes back to life, and the Jew is called to renew himself. The key is matzah, which is emunah: in Hashem, in the chachamim and in oneself. Nissan asks a person to become an adam by ruling over the animal of his own mazal. Avraham Avinu, whose Yom Tov is Pesach, is the spring of Klal Yisrael. The Rav closes with a story of Reb Arele Roth.

en: The terumas hadeshen, a night avodah done in work clothes, is most precious to Hashem, and it is the model for the humble work of cleaning and helping at home before Pesach.
Hashem tried in Nissan to bring the world to its tikkun at creation, at Yetzias Mitzrayim and at the Mishkan, and a fourth Nissan of geulah is still to come.
Just as Hashem does not give up, a Jew must always begin again, whenever he falls.
In Nissan all of nature is renewed, and a Jew is called to see himself as part of that renewal.
The key to renewal is matzah, which is emunah: in Hashem, in the chachamim, and in oneself.
To become an adam, each person must know which animal of his mazal he is and ride it rather than let it ride him.
Avraham Avinu, the first Jew and the spring of Klal Yisrael, has Pesach as his Yom Tov, and the emunah he began is taught to children at the seder.

title.en: Terumas hadeshen and helping before Pesach

summary.en: The Rav asks why the Torah waits until Tzav to speak of the olah, and explains that the night avodah of removing the ashes, done in work clothes, is the most precious to Hashem, like the avodah of the generation before Mashiach and like sweeping the house before Pesach. He tells how Rav Gifter came himself to take out a couple's garbage.

title.en: Nissan creation and birkas hachamah

summary.en: The Rav brings the dispute of Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua whether the world was created in Tishrei or Nissan, and that birkas hachamah follows Nissan. As an aside he brings the Ostrovtzer's calculation that it fell on erev Pesach only at the Mishkan and at the time of Purim, and will again at the geulah, and suggests why those were times with little to prepare.

title.en: Four Nissans of tikkun

summary.en: The Rav describes Hashem's plan for a perfected world, spoiled by the sin of Adam HaRishon in Nissan; the second attempt, Yetzias Mitzrayim and Matan Torah, spoiled by the eigel; the third, the Mishkan, which was later destroyed; and the fourth Nissan of geulah that Hashem has promised.

title.en: Always beginning again

summary.en: From Hashem's repeated attempts the Rav draws the lesson that a Jew must always start anew: like a jigsaw puzzle taken apart and begun again, like the tzaddik who falls seven times and rises, every Shabbos, Rosh Chodesh and morning. He adds that Hashem Himself, as it were, asks for a kaparah for diminishing the moon.

title.en: All of nature is renewed in Nissan

summary.en: The Rav describes, through Shlomo HaMelech's words in Shir HaShirim, how the dead winter gives way to buds, birdsong and fragrance in Nissan, because then Hashem renewed His bond with Klal Yisrael. A Jew who sees all of creation renewed must ask whether he is part of that song, and Hashem knocks and calls him to rise.

title.en: Matzah, emunah and the key to renewal

summary.en: The Rav calls Nissan the key to a new creation and says the key is matzah, which is emunah. He explains Moshe Rabbeinu's sin at the rock as a lack of faith in himself, and brings Rav Hirsch's three kinds of emunah. He explains why the Targum calls matzah 'petir', opening, and how the seder opens and closes with opening.

title.en: Becoming an adam: souls and mazalos

summary.en: The Rav explains that Nissan is the time of 'na'aseh adam' and demands that each person become an adam, but says each must answer for himself how. He brings the Tikkunei Zohar on Esther's plea to save her soul from the dog: souls come from different roots and mazalos, compared to animals, as the shevatim are compared to animals.

title.en: Riding one's own animal

summary.en: The Rav explains that each person's yetzer follows his mazal, and that the soul must rule over its animal like a rider. A young man born under the lion who rises easily to learn has nothing to boast about; his test is not to tear at others. Each person must assess which animal he is, ride it, and renew himself in this Nissan.

title.en: Avraham Avinu, the spring of Klal Yisrael

summary.en: The Rav shows that Avraham Avinu, the first Jew, is the spring of Klal Yisrael and that Pesach is his Yom Tov: the bris bein habesarim, his milah and his victory over the kings all fell on Pesach. Emunah, Avraham's trait, is the first of the Aseres HaDibros, is taught to small children at the seder, is eaten in the matzah, and, as the Maharal says, is the essence of tefillah.

title.en: Reb Arele and the Chanukah lights; closing

summary.en: The Rav urges using the days before Pesach for learning and davening with simchah, and brings Reb Arele Roth's teaching that there is no such thing as not being in the mood. He tells how the gravely weak Reb Arele lit the Chanukah lights with all his strength and danced before the doctor, and closes with a wish that this Nissan be the Nissan of the geulah.

catalogTitle: דרוש בענין: זמן של חודש ניסן הוא הנקודה האמצעות שבשנה

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Nissan, the month of chesed and of the Exodus, is the central point and root of the whole year, just as the Beis Hamikdash is the point from which the world grew and 'darosh darash Moshe' is the center of the Torah.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with emunah as the root of all mitzvos and with the Ramban's teaching that every mitzvah is a remembrance of the Exodus, so Pesach is the root of all the festivals and Nissan the head of the months. He brings the dispute of Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua whether the world was created in Tishrei, with din, or in Nissan, with chesed. He then explains the halacha that a rebellious elder is liable only in the Lishkas HaGazis: the world grew from one point, the foundation stone, and the Sanhedrin sitting there holds the power of the root. The middle of Sefer Devarim and the middle of the Torah, 'darosh darash Moshe', mirror this. That verse concerns the Rosh Chodesh Nissan goat that was burned, which the Rav explains through the diminished moon and the kushyos on Hashem, all to be answered in the days of Moshiach, a preview of which Aharon earned through his silence. He closes with the Chozeh of Lublin and with strengthening emunah in Nissan.

en: Since all mitzvos are a remembrance of the Exodus, Pesach is the root and 'embryo' of all the festivals, and Nissan the head of the months.
According to Rabbi Yehoshua the world was created in Nissan, a renewal of chesed, while Rabbi Eliezer holds it was created in Tishrei, with the attribute of din.

The world developed from a single point, the foundation stone in the Holy of Holies, which is why the Beis Hamikdash is called higher than all places and why the Sanhedrin's ruling has full force only there.
The Torah is the blueprint of the world, so its center, 'darosh darash Moshe', corresponds to Rosh Chodesh Nissan, as the word Bereishis corresponds to Tishrei.
The goat of Rosh Chodesh is an atonement 'for Hashem' for the diminishing of the moon, Knesses Yisrael, and for all the questions people have on Hashem's conduct.
The Rosh Chodesh Nissan goat was burned because that day was a preview of the days of Moshiach, when it will be revealed that Hashem never needed atonement.
Nissan builds the whole year through chesed and love rather than through din, and at the root of the year one should strengthen the mitzvah of emunah.
