title.en: Emunah, the Exodus and the head of the festivals

summary.en: The Rav opens with emunah as the root of all mitzvos and the Ramban's teaching that every mitzvah recalls the Exodus, which showed that Hashem runs the world. Therefore Pesach is the head and the embryo of all the festivals, and Nissan the head of the months.

title.en: Nissan, a renewal of chesed

summary.en: The Rav brings the dispute whether the world was created in Tishrei or Nissan and explains Nissan as a renewal of chesed, seen in spring and explained by the Maharal as Hashem renewing His bond with Klal Yisrael. He contrasts chesed, giving outward, with din, drawing inward, through the order of the letters, and ties Tishrei to din and Nissan to chesed.

title.en: The rebellious elder and 'the place causes'

summary.en: The Rav reads the passage of the rebellious elder in Parshas Shoftim and the Gemara's lesson that 'the place causes': the elder is liable only for defying the Sanhedrin in the Lishkas HaGazis. He stresses how central one final authority is for Klal Yisrael and asks how the Beis Hamikdash can be called higher than all places.

title.en: The world grew from one point

summary.en: Since the world is round, no point on it is simply highest; but its Maker began it from one point, the foundation stone, and wound it outward like an embryo, through the Beis Hamikdash, Yerushalayim and Eretz Yisrael. The Torah is the world's blueprint, the heads of the generations are its central souls, and the Sanhedrin sitting at the root point has the strongest power, which is why 'the place causes'.

title.en: The center of Sefer Devarim

summary.en: Sefer Devarim repeats the whole Torah and so contains the blueprint of the world; its middle verse, by the count of the Masorah, is in the passage of the Sanhedrin, corresponding to the Beis Hamikdash at the world's center. He adds Sefer Yetzirah's three dimensions of place, time and soul, whose holiest points meet when the Kohen Gadol enters the Holy of Holies on Yom Kippur.

title.en: Bereishis and 'darosh darash Moshe'

summary.en: According to Rabbi Eliezer the root of the Torah is the word Bereishis, matching Tishrei and din, whose service is that of the Kohen Gadol; according to Rabbi Yehoshua it is 'darosh darash Moshe', the middle of the Torah in words, matching Nissan and Moshe Rabbeinu the king. He adds a teaching on the word 'saraf' as the six hundred thousand interpretations of the Torah.

title.en: The burned goat and the diminished moon

summary.en: The middle of the Torah speaks of the goat brought on Rosh Chodesh Nissan, the eighth day of the Mishkan's inauguration, which was burned. The Rav explains the Gemara that the Rosh Chodesh goat is an atonement 'for Hashem' for diminishing the moon: the moon, Knesses Yisrael, receives from the sun, the earth's physicality comes between them, and Klal Yisrael will be renewed like the moon.

title.en: Kushyos on Hashem and the root of roots

summary.en: The Rav explains that the questions people raise against Hashem, while Klal Yisrael is diminished and mocked, are what the Rosh Chodesh atonement addresses. Rosh Chodesh Nissan is the root of all the months, and on that eighth day a preview of the days of Moshiach was revealed, when all questions will be answered and it will be clear that Hashem needs no atonement; therefore that goat was burned.

title.en: Aharon's silence and the Jewish renewal

summary.en: The preview was earned through Aharon's silence after his sons died: he could have asked questions but believed without understanding. The Rav contrasts the nations, who have a year of repetition, with Jews, who have a month of renewal and teshuvah, calls Rosh Chodesh Nissan a time of atonement, and explains that Nissan's new year works through chesed, a new year for the kings.

title.en: The Chozeh's pinkas and the root of the year

summary.en: The Rav tells, from the Bnei Yissaschar, how the Chozeh of Lublin would write on each of the first days of Nissan what would happen in the matching month, and one year stopped before the day of Av, the month he passed away. He concludes that Nissan, built with chesed, is the root of the whole year, holding the days of Moshiach and the center of the Torah, and calls for strengthening emunah, the root of all mitzvos.

catalogTitle: “בקש הקב"ה לעשות חזקיהו משיח...” זמן לעבוד על אמונה בהשגחה פרטיות

oneLiner.en: Starting from the Gemara that Hashem wanted to make Chizkiyahu Moshiach, the Rav explains why salvation must be met with shirah and thanks, and why Nissan and Pesach are the time to plant emunah in Hashem's hashgachah pratis behind every event.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Gemara that Hashem wished to make Chizkiyahu Moshiach, but he did not sing shirah after the fall of Sancheirib. Linking this to Chizkiyahu's intercalating Nissan on the thirtieth of Adar, he explains that Chizkiyahu felt he was fit to be Moshiach but not yet appointed, and held back for the sake of souls not yet ready, as the Ohev Yisrael said in a story. He then turns to the war against the Yishmaeli king of Bavel, which was won in Nissan while Jews read the nesi'im, and shows connections to Yosef, Yishmael and chametz. Through Achashverosh, a king who crowned himself, he shows that Hashem saves through unworthy agents, and calls for shirah and thanks, bringing the Chasam Sofer. The second half teaches that the Megillah and Pesach are for learning hashgachah pratis, contrasting it with Amalek's 'mikreh', and ends with Moshiach standing on the roof of the Beis HaMikdash once Amalek is gone.

en: Chizkiyahu did not sing shirah because he felt he was fit to be Moshiach but not yet appointed, and a shirah then would have been the tenth song of the final redemption.
The redemption waits until all souls of Klal Yisrael are ready, including the 'Adar souls' pushed out of the order.
Hashem brings salvation even through an unworthy king, like Achashverosh who crowned himself, to show that He alone is the One who saves.
After a salvation there is an obligation to say shirah and to thank Hashem, learned by kal vachomer from the shirah at the Yam Suf.
The Megillah, thirty days before Pesach, teaches hashgachah pratis: a Jew must believe now that everything is for the good of Yisrael, not only understand it afterwards.
Amalek's heresy is that everything is chance, and its poison can only be cured by hearing the story of Yetzias Mitzrayim from a true tzaddik, as Yisro did and as Jews do on Pesach night.

Yishmael in the end of days
Nissan as the month of redemption
Moshiach on the roof of the Beis HaMikdash

title.en: Why Chizkiyahu did not sing shirah

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara in Sanhedrin that Hashem wanted to make Chizkiyahu Moshiach but held back because he did not sing shirah, and asks why such a tzaddik did not. He adds the Gemara in Berachos that Chizkiyahu joined geulah to tefillah and intercalated Nissan on the thirtieth of Adar, and later regretted it.

title.en: The tenth shirah and the souls of Adar

summary.en: The Rav brings that there are ten shiros in the world, the tenth belonging to Moshiach, and explains that Chizkiyahu feared that his shirah would seize the role of Moshiach before he was appointed, just as he held that 'fit to be Nissan' is not yet Nissan. He ties this to Nissan and Moshiach both being called 'rishon', and to souls of 'Adar' who still await their tikkun.

title.en: The Ohev Yisrael and the waiting for all souls

summary.en: The Rav tells that the Ohev Yisrael said he could bring Moshiach but would not, since some souls would be lost, and answered a Rav who objected. Chizkiyahu felt the same; the redemption waits until all souls are ready, which is why the earth's wish to sing was answered with 'razi li'.

title.en: The war with the Yishmaeli king of Bavel

summary.en: The Rav describes the great salvation Jews just had from the Yishmaeli ruler in Bavel who boasted he would destroy Eretz Yisrael and spread fear everywhere. He brings the Zohar and Targum Yonasan that the twelve nesi'im subdue the twelve princes of Yishmael, and notes that the war turned in Nissan while Jews read the nasi and did bedikas chametz.

title.en: The ten makos, Yishmael and se'or

summary.en: The Rav explains that pouring out wine at the ten makos at the Seder subdues the enemies of Yisrael, and that Rabbi Yehudah's simanim also hint at the Yishmaelim, who began the galus by selling Yosef, as Rashi says about Pinchas's war with Midyan. He suggests that chametz is the other nations and se'or, which is not fit to eat, is Yishmael.

title.en: Victory on the day of Efrayim's nasi

summary.en: The Rav notes that Baghdad fell on the seventh day of Nissan, the day of the nasi of Efrayim, a descendant of Yosef, who embodies holy bris milah against Yishmael's empty milah. He brings the Ba'al HaTurim that when Yishmael falls Moshiach will come from Yitzchak's children, and concludes that Jews must say shirah on Shevi'i shel Pesach.

title.en: A king who crowned himself

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara that Achashverosh became king on his own, and the Maharal on why the Torah does not name Moshe's parents: the redemption is not because of anyone's worthiness. Hashem uses unworthy agents to show that He saves, and the Rav applies this to the American president and to the Stoliner Rebbe's prediction that America would help Jews in danger.

title.en: Shirah after a salvation: the Chasam Sofer

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara's kal vachomer that shirah after a salvation is rooted in the shirah at the sea. He tells how in the Chasam Sofer's city the battle with Napoleon's forces spared the Jews, compares it to the Gulf War's missiles, and relates how the Chasam Sofer ordered tefillos during the war and chapters of Tehillim of thanks after it, as written in his Sefer HaZikaron.

title.en: Thanking Hashem for every small thing

summary.en: The Rav teaches that thanking Hashem for every small thing is a foundation of a Jew, with the story of a Lithuanian Jew praised by the Chozeh of Lublin and of Rav Yonasan Steif thanking Hashem for a breeze. He suggests that perhaps the redemption waits for our shirah and proposes that shuls set a time on Shevi'i shel Pesach to say the Chasam Sofer's chapters of thanks.

title.en: A salvation both sweet and bitter

summary.en: The Rav tells how the Chasam Sofer, thanking the Kaiser for granting Jews freedom, wept and gave a mashal of a banished prince who cries when the king builds him a comfortable house in exile. So too the present salvation is sweet but bitter: Jews hoped the wars were Gog and Magog leading to Moshiach, and instead they have menuchah in galus.

title.en: An os l'tovah and the Megillah read backwards

summary.en: The Rav brings the Ibn Ezra that Esther delayed her request to wait for a sign for good, which came with Haman's downfall before Mordechai, and suggests the present salvation may be such a sign, a sprouting of the redemption in Nissan. Everything that happens is for the good of Yisrael; one who believes it only after the end of the story is like one who reads the Megillah backwards.

title.en: Vayikra versus vayiker: providence or chance

summary.en: The Rav explains that the Megillah, thirty days before Pesach, comes to teach hashgachah pratis against Amalek's belief in 'mikreh', chance. Through Rashi on the small aleph of Vayikra he contrasts the heretic who says the world 'happened' with the Jew who knows everything was called into being by Hashem, and he connects 'asher karcha' of Amalek with Haman's story.

title.en: The Ruzhiner and the natural Yam Suf

summary.en: The Rav asks why Yisro came after hearing of kriyas Yam Suf and Amalek, as Rashi says, if he already knew. He tells of a heretic who told the Ruzhiner that the splitting of the sea had natural causes, and the Ruzhiner's answer that such a once-in-history convergence at exactly the right moment would be an even greater nes, a hidden one like Purim.

title.en: Amalek's poison and the antidote of Pesach night

summary.en: The Rav explains that Amalek attacked because he held the sea split by itself, and that Yisro, hearing this, was poisoned by his heresy; even passing words of apikorsus are a contagious poison. The antidote was to hear Yetzias Mitzrayim from Moshe Rabbeinu, and so Pesach night, when Yetzias Mitzrayim is the root of emunah, is the time to plant emunah.

title.en: The world is a Megillah

summary.en: The Rav teaches that the whole world is a Megillah in which Hashem's name is hidden, and that Haman saw miracle after miracle and still called it chance. He brings the Chasam Sofer that the gentile chronicles credit Achashverosh's might, while Jews know Hashem did it all, and the Chasam Sofer's answer why the miracle was at the sea and not at the Nile: so that Jews could make a brachah on the place of the nes.

title.en: Moshiach on the roof; Shiloh without a roof

summary.en: The Rav brings the Pesikta that Moshiach will stand on the roof of the Beis HaMikdash, and asks why on the roof. Through the Gemara in Zevachim that Shiloh had stone walls and a roof of curtains, he explains that the roof corresponds to heaven and to keser, and that because Amalek, whose gematria is 'ram', is the head of the sitra achra, the roof could not hold kedushah.

title.en: Wiping out Amalek and the holy roof

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara that before building the Beis HaMikdash Amalek must be wiped out, and shows that each time Amalek was only weakened, so the roof remained without kedushah. In the third Beis HaMikdash, with Amalek and the pride he brings gone, Moshiach, called 'rishon', will stand on a holy roof, and the Rav closes with the hope of Nissan as the month of redemption.

catalogTitle: The Sweetness of תורה One Feels when Learning Properly

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Yaakov did not need to teach Yosef Seder Taharos because Yosef's soul was rooted in taharah, and that only through kedushah and taharah does a person taste the true sweetness of Torah, tefillah and Shabbos.

abstract.en: Opening the weeks of Shovavim with the theme of taharah, the Rav brings the Ba'al HaTurim that the word zekunim stands for five orders of the Mishnah, without Taharos, and asks why Taharos is missing and why Yaakov taught only Yosef. He also asks what Yaakov saw in the grain from Mitzrayim. He explains that the seven shepherds of Klal Yisrael, Yosef among them, stand above the tribes, and that the orders of the Mishnah correspond to them, with Taharos belonging to Yosef the tzaddik. Each tzaddik knows the Torah of his own middah by himself, as every creature knows by nature what it needs; so Yosef needed no teaching in Taharos. Because a tzaddik's possessions do not spoil, Yosef's grain kept the taste and smell that fruit lost when taharah ceased, and Yaakov sensed through it that Yosef was alive. The Rav concludes that the taste of Torah and Shabbos comes only with kedushah and taharah, the work of Shovavim.

en: According to the Ba'al HaTurim, zekunim stands for the orders of Zeraim, Kodashim, Nashim, Yeshuos (Nezikin) and Moed, which Yaakov taught Yosef; Taharos is missing.
The seven shepherds (ro'im), the Ushpizin, are higher than the tribes because they lead all of Klal Yisrael, and Yosef is one of them.
Each of the six orders of the Mishnah corresponds to one of the Avos and tzaddikim, and Taharos corresponds to Yosef, the only one called 'the tzaddik', because he withstood his test.
Each tzaddik is rooted in one middah and knows by himself the part of the Torah tied to it, just as every creature knows by nature what it needs.
Whatever belongs to a tzaddik does not deteriorate, so Yosef's grain kept the true taste and smell, and through it Yaakov sensed that Yosef was in Mitzrayim.
The Rav teaches that one can merit Torah, and feel the taste of Shabbos, only through kedushah and taharah, and that the weeks of Shovavim are the season to work on this.

candidateTopics: six orders of the Mishnah and the Avos

title.en: Ben zekunim without Taharos

summary.en: Opening the weeks of Shovavim, the Rav brings Rashi and the Ba'al HaTurim on 'ben zekunim' and asks why Taharos is missing and why Yaakov taught only Yosef. He then asks what Yaakov saw when he 'saw that there was grain in Mitzrayim', since everyone knew it.

title.en: The seven shepherds above the tribes

summary.en: The Rav explains that the seven ro'im, the Ushpizin, lead all of Klal Yisrael while each tribe's head leads only his tribe, and that in the future the river will split into seven for them. Yosef was raised from a tribe to a ro'eh, as the pesukim and Rashi on 'even Yisrael' show.

title.en: The orders of the Mishnah and the Avos

summary.en: The Rav describes the Chok LeYisrael, which assigns each weekday an order of the Mishnah matching its middah, and shows which order belongs to Avraham, Yitzchak and Yaakov. Taharos belongs to Yosef, the only one called 'the tzaddik' because he withstood his test in Mitzrayim.

title.en: Why Yosef needed no teaching in Taharos

summary.en: The Rav asks why Yaakov had to learn Torah from others while Avraham knew it by himself. He answers that each tzaddik is rooted in one of the seven middos and knows its Torah innately, like animals born knowing their craft; Avraham's chesed spans everything, while Yosef knew Taharos by himself, which answers the opening questions.

title.en: Shemiras habris, da'as and Shabbos

summary.en: The Rav explains that one who guards the bris like Yosef merits da'as, which is taharah, and Shabbos, since Yosef is Friday which prepares for Shabbos. He brings the Midrash that Shabbos is mentioned only by Yosef among the tribes, and that the nasi of Ephraim brought his offering on Shabbos.

title.en: The taste and smell of Yosef's grain

summary.en: The Rav explains that fruit lost its true taste and smell when taharah ceased, while a tzaddik's possessions do not deteriorate, so Yosef's grain did not spoil and kept its taste. Tasting that grain, Yaakov sensed a great tzaddik in Mitzrayim and hoped it was Yosef; the Rav connects this to gematrios of 'yesh shever' and 'ben zekunim'.

title.en: Taharah brings the sweetness of Torah and Shabbos

summary.en: The Rav brings the Ma'or VaShemesh that without taharah one cannot merit true Torah, and says the same holds for feeling the taste of Shabbos, which some find a burden. He mentions the Chazon Ish's instruction about boys' clothing for learning with clean hands, and ends that in Shovavim one must learn and daven with kedushah and taharah to feel their joy.

catalogTitle: חודש של זריזות והתחדשות

oneLiner.en: The Rav teaches that Nissan is a month of chesed and renewal in which Hashem's original plan for the world is tried again, and that its blessing is received only through zerizus, the alacrity of matzah, as opposed to the lazy rising of chametz.

abstract.en: Opening with Parshas HaChodesh, the Rav calls Nissan a month of chesed and of zerizus: heaven pours out kindness, and a person without alacrity is a bucket with a hole. Zerizus is learned from matzah. He then explains that the world was created in Nissan for a life of sweet closeness to Hashem, like an endless spring, and Avraham Avinu is the spring of Yiddishkeit. Adam spoiled the plan; Hashem tried again with the Exodus, spoiled by the Golden Calf, then with the Mishkan, spoiled by the foreign fire; the fourth Nissan, the final redemption, will succeed. The Mishkan set up seven times teaches that one who falls must rise again rather than let things go chametz. Pesach is a rebirth, like nature's spring. A story of a poritz who spread sugar on his field to sled in summer contrasts with the sweetness of a Jew's Shabbos. He ends urging zerizus in davening and learning.

en: Nissan is a month of chesed, and only one who receives it with zerizus keeps the blessing that pours down.
Zerizus in all mitzvos is learned from matzah, which must be baked quickly so it does not become chametz.
Hashem created the world in Nissan so that man would live in Gan Eden in the sweetness of closeness to Him, and Nissan is the month in which that plan is tried again.
The plan was tried in four Nissans: at creation, at the Exodus, at the Mishkan, and in the coming redemption, which will not be spoiled.
Chametz is the bread of laziness, puffed up with air and emptiness, while matzah is the bread of zerizus.
Pesach is the greatest Yom Tov because through it one became a Jew; it is a rebirth, like the spring that revives the dead world of winter.

candidateTopics: creation of the world in Nissan

title.en: Nissan: a month of chesed and zerizus

summary.en: The Rav opens with Parshas HaChodesh and its piyut on the blessed days that are coming, and calls Nissan a month of chesed in which a person must set out a bucket without a hole. He explains that Nissan is a month of renewal and zerizus, learned from the quick baking of matzah.

title.en: The world created in Nissan for sweetness

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara's dispute whether the world was created in Nissan and explains Hashem's intention: a world like Gan Eden where man enjoys the sweetness of closeness to Him, a sweetness Jews can taste in davening. He describes spring in detail and calls Avraham Avinu the spring of Yiddishkeit, then says Adam spoiled the plan.

title.en: The second and third Nissan: Exodus and Mishkan

summary.en: Noting that the shivas yemei hamiluim begin today, the Rav explains that Hashem tried His plan again in a smaller form with the Jewish people leaving Egypt, which was spoiled by the Golden Calf, and again with the Mishkan erected on Rosh Chodesh Nissan, which was spoiled by the foreign fire.

title.en: The fourth Nissan: the final redemption

summary.en: The Rav brings Chazal that in Nissan the future redemption will come, and says the fourth Nissan will not disappoint: the whole world will serve Hashem and the nations will stream to the third Beis HaMikdash. He says one must prepare for Nissan with kedushah and Torah.

title.en: Rising after a fall; chametz as laziness

summary.en: The Rav notes that the parshiyos of the Mishkan's inauguration are read at this season, and that the Mishkan was set up and taken down seven times before it stood, like a tzaddik who falls seven times and rises. One who falls must not let things go chametz: chametz is the bread of laziness, rising only with air, while matzah is the bread of zerizus.

title.en: Pesach: Avraham's Yom Tov and rebirth

summary.en: The Rav recalls baking matzos with joy and song, and brings the Zohar that matzah is the food of emunah. Pesach is Avraham Avinu's Yom Tov, when his great events took place, and the greatest Yom Tov because through it one becomes a Jew. He paints winter as death and spring as tchiyas hameisim, the theme of the haftarah of the dry bones, and asks why a Jew should stay asleep.

title.en: The poritz who sledded on sugar

summary.en: The Rav asks when a Jew will take up avodas Hashem with zerizus and feel a pleasure no gentile can buy. He tells of a poritz who, in August, had sacks of sugar spread over his field so he could ride his sled, and contrasts that poor pleasure with what a Jew feels saying Nishmas on Shabbos morning.

title.en: Shabbos sweetness and the call to zerizus

summary.en: The Rav describes the sweetness of Shabbos and brings the Beis Aharon that a blatt Gemara before davening is Gan Eden. He closes urging his listeners to use the time, rise early, come early to davening, and treat these days as the miluim, a training like the kohanim, who are zerizim, in preparation for the coming Nissan.

catalogTitle: צד א: הקדמה ללימוד מהר"ל. יצ"מ התגלות הקב"ה; ביאור עמוק שבנ"י הם ההיפוך של מצרים.

oneLiner.en: After introducing the Maharal as the key to Chazal's aggados, the Rav begins Gevuras Hashem: yetzias Mitzrayim is Hashem's revelation and the foundation of emunah, and Klal Yisrael, like Avraham from Ur Kasdim, had to begin from Mitzrayim, their exact opposite.

abstract.en: The Rav opens by explaining that the aggados of Shas hide deep wisdom and cannot be read by their plain meaning, citing the Ramchal. The Maharal was chosen from Heaven to explain them through pure, simple logic rather than pilpul, and all streams of Klal Yisrael built on him. The Rav describes the Maharal's sefarim, recommends starting with Nesivos Olam and Derech Chaim, and announces that he will teach the main ideas of Gevuras Hashem before Pesach. He then begins: the Ramban at the end of Parshas Bo makes yetzias Mitzrayim the foundation of all emunah, and the Maharal says Hashem chose that night to make His deeds known. Klal Yisrael reached completeness at six hundred thousand, like a body with six sides. Mitzrayim was the exact opposite of Yisrael, and only from the opposite, from zero, can a true beginning come, as with Avraham from Ur Kasdim and his break from Terach.

en: The aggados of Shas are not to be read literally; they hide deep wisdom like a code, and the Maharal was the one who opened them through clear logic.
The Maharal's way is depth and simple truth, not pilpul or clever constructions, and one must get used to it over time.
Following the Ramban at the end of Parshas Bo, yetzias Mitzrayim is the foundation of the whole Torah and of emunah, since there Hashem revealed Himself to a whole nation.
Klal Yisrael became a complete nation only at six hundred thousand, since six marks completeness, like a body with six sides.
Mitzrayim was the exact opposite of Klal Yisrael, and that is what made it the deepest galus.
A true beginning must start from zero, from the opposite; so Avraham came out of Kasdim and Yisrael out of Mitzrayim.

title.en: The hidden wisdom in Chazal's aggados

summary.en: The Rav explains that each generation's sages had their own portion in Torah, and that the aggados of Shas cannot be read by their plain meaning. Citing the Ramchal, he says they hide deep wisdom like a code, and that the secrets of the Torah lie in them.

title.en: The Maharal, key to the aggados

summary.en: The Rav presents the Maharal as the one chosen to explain the aggados through deep, simple logic rather than pilpul, accepted by Chassidim and the mussar movement alike. He lists the Maharal's sefarim, advises beginning with Nesivos Olam and Derech Chaim, and explains why gedolim called his mind a 'sechel nivdal', a mind free of personal bias.

title.en: Preparing for Pesach with Gevuras Hashem

summary.en: The Rav notes that Gevuras Hashem was the Maharal's first printed sefer and tells of a chassid whose Pesach preparation was learning hilchos Pesach and Gevuras Hashem. Since people are busy, he announces he will present a digest of the sefer before Pesach and asks for patience in getting used to the Maharal's style.

title.en: Yetzias Mitzrayim, the root of emunah

summary.en: The Rav brings the Ramban at the end of Parshas Bo that yetzias Mitzrayim is the foundation of all of Torah and emunah, and the Maharal's opening that Hashem chose that night to make His deeds known. He ties this to the mitzvah of Anochi, the zecher l'yetzias Mitzrayim of the Yamim Tovim and the daily mention of the Exodus.

title.en: Six hundred thousand: a nation complete

summary.en: The Rav explains that the Jewish people was formed at yetzias Mitzrayim once it reached six hundred thousand, since six is the number of completeness: a point, a line and a flat area are incomplete until there are six sides. He then brings 'goy mikerev goy', that Yisrael were taken out of Mitzrayim like a fetus from its mother.

title.en: Mitzrayim, the exact opposite of Yisrael

summary.en: The Rav explains that Mitzrayim, the land of immorality, was the exact opposite of the holy nation, so being strangers there was the deepest galus. He brings the story of Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai and the daughter of Nakdimon ben Gurion and the Maharal's explanation of 'ashreichem Yisrael': the lowness of their galus shows how high Yisrael are.

title.en: Beginning from zero: Avraham and Ur Kasdim

summary.en: The Rav compares yetzias Mitzrayim to Avraham leaving Ur Kasdim, a people that 'was not'. Avraham, the purpose of creation, came at the end of the two thousand years of tohu, because a beginning must start from zero; so too Yisrael, the beginning of kedushah, had to start in Mitzrayim, and the Rav suggests the same about the present galus in America. He closes with the Maharal on Rashi at the end of Noach: Avraham's tie to Terach was cut, as he began a new line.

catalogTitle: ט”ו בשבט Ushers in the Months of חסד (A Deeper Understanding of the צירופי החודש)

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains through the twelve arrangements of the Shem Havaya that Tu B'Shvat is the point where the din of the winter is sweetened and the months of chesed begin.

abstract.en: The Rav compares the Torah to a field whose flowers hide gold and diamonds below, and sets out to dig beneath the surface of Tu B'Shvat. Each month is an arrangement of the four letters of the Shem Havaya: the Yud and Vav are masculine and chesed, the two Heis feminine and din. When the masculine letter comes first, chesed sweetens din; when the feminine comes first, din dominates, as with Esav, who put his wives before his sons. Nissan and Tishrei begin the summer and winter, while Tammuz and Teves are fully or partly reversed. Their din spills into Av and Shevat until the fifteenth, when the order turns back to chesed. From Tu B'Shvat on, the gates of chesed are open until Shavuos. The gematria of seraf (580) and ilan (91) shows the side of tumah being raised into kedushah, and the Rav ties the day to davening for an esrog.

en: Each of the twelve months is a different arrangement of the four letters of the Shem Havaya.
The Yud and Vav are masculine and chesed, the Heis feminine and din; when the masculine comes first, chesed sweetens din.
Tammuz and Teves are reversed arrangements of din, and their din spills into Av and Shevat until the fifteenth of the month.
From Tu B'Shvat until Shavuos the gates of chesed are open, and these days are meant to be used for Torah and avodah.
Seraf (580) rising into the ilan (91) shows the power of tumah being raised and absorbed into kedushah.
On Tu B'Shvat one davens for the esrog, and the berachah on fruit is said with the 'pri etz hadar' in mind.

months of chesed from Tu B'Shvat to Shavuos

title.en: Digging beneath the surface; the Shem Havaya

summary.en: The Rav compares the levels of Torah to a field of flowers with gold and diamonds below, and introduces the idea that each month is an arrangement of the Shem Havaya. He presents its letters as father, mother, son and daughter, the masculine being chesed and the feminine din.

title.en: Giver and receiver: chassan and kallah

summary.en: The Rav explains that the chassan, chesed, gives and the kallah, din, receives, which is why kiddushin and the kesubah go only from him to her. He shows that the Yud and Vav are masculine letters and the Hei feminine, as in women's names, and that the four letters with two identical Heis give twelve arrangements, one per month.

title.en: In kedushah the masculine comes first

summary.en: The Rav brings Rashi that Yaakov put his sons before his wives while Esav did the reverse, and explains that the right side is chesed: we write from right to left and start with the right hand. He adds examples from the nations, from white and red, and from Achashverosh, whose deference to his wife brought him trouble.

title.en: Nissan and Tishrei, kings of the year

summary.en: The Rav shows in the siddur that each month has its arrangement and a passuk it comes from. Nissan, the pleasant month of spring, is Yud-Kei-Vav-Kei in order, from the roshei teivos of 'Yismechu hashamayim', while Tishrei, king of the winter months, comes from the Aleph-Beis backwards and turns to chesed in its second half through the avodah of Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur.

title.en: Tammuz, Teves, and the turn on the fifteenth

summary.en: The Rav explains that Tammuz, the peak of summer, has the Shem entirely backwards, from sofei teivos, which is why the meraglim's journey and the churban began then, and its din lasts into Av until the fifteenth. Likewise Teves, the brunt of winter, is reversed and its din spills into Shevat, whose first half is Hei-Yud and second half Vav-Hei, sweetened from Tu B'Shvat.

title.en: Having the arrangement in mind without mechanical davening

summary.en: The Rav discusses the sefarim's advice to have the month's arrangement in mind, warning that thinking only of letters makes davening mechanical, as Rebbe Nachman of Breslov said. Only if it truly lifts one's davening, drawing down chesed and connecting to Hashem, should one do it; in a month like Tammuz one sweetens the din by connecting to chesed.

title.en: From Tu B'Shvat to Shavuos: the gates of chesed

summary.en: The Rav brings the Divrei Chaim's observation that from Tu B'Shvat to Shavuos there are never two weeks without a Yom Tov, an ascent of growing chesed in which the gates are open and should be used for Torah and avodah. He describes the sap already rising in the roots though nothing is yet seen on the tree.

title.en: Havaya and Adnus: the union in the Mikdash

summary.en: The Rav explains that the Shem Havaya is chesed and the Shem Adnus din, the chassan and kallah, and their union is the union of Hakadosh Baruch Hu and Knesses Yisrael, whose seat is the Mikdash. He notes the passuk read the day before and the siddurim that join the two Names, then says that tumah mirrors kedushah with its own masculine and feminine, where the feminine dominates.

title.en: The two forces of tumah and the number 580

summary.en: The Rav brings the Ohr HaChaim in Vayechi, who saw the power of tumah as two dogs, male and female, and overcame the male at once but the female only with difficulty. He explains that the two names of tumah together equal 580, the number of Esav's gift animals and of Seir, while Havaya and Adnus together equal 91, the gematria of Amen.

title.en: Seraf in the ilan; davening for the esrog

summary.en: The Rav reads Rashi's phrase that on Tu B'Shvat the seraf rises in the ilan as 580 being raised into 91: the power of tumah sublimated into kedushah, as Nissan, Purim and Pesach approach. He ties the day to davening for the esrog, brings the Bnei Yissaschar and the custom to say borei pri ha'etz and perhaps shehecheyanu, and gives a remez that the berachah is said with the 'pri etz hadar' in mind.

title.en: Barren trees, and only scratching the surface

summary.en: The Rav repeats from the day before Rashi's explanation that barren trees will one day give fruit, since all trees were created fruitful before Adam's sin, and says this is a time to daven for them. He closes that all these insights only scratch the surface, a drop in the ocean of what Tu B'Shvat is, until Mashiach comes.

catalogTitle: צד ב: אברהם אבינו ראש למאמינים

oneLiner.en: Following the Maharal's answer to the Ramban, the Rav explains why Avraham Avinu's emunah was so great and why emunah, which frees a Jew from dependence on anyone but Hashem, is the foundation of Klal Yisrael.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Ramban's question on 'vehe'emin baShem': what was so praiseworthy in Avraham believing Hashem? The Maharal answers that by nature Avraham could not have children, and he feared sin might cancel the promise, yet he believed. From here the Rav shows that a Jew's bond with Hashem does not rest on merits: the Torah gives no reason for 'Lech lecha', and the Ramban's 'great sin' of going down to Egypt teaches that a Jew remains a Jew and his sins are only external. He then follows the Maharal's challenge to the Ramban: emunah is no small thing, as the Mechilta's praise of the emunah at the sea shows. Emunah means firmness; a believer is subjugated to no person, as the Maharal's explanation of the dog shows. A believer is always joyful and never angry; Moshe's anger at Mei Merivah was a lack of emunah. He ends with Yaakov's 'me'ayin yavo ezri'.

en: According to the Maharal, Avraham's emunah was great because by nature he could not have children and he feared sin might cancel the promise, yet he believed because he saw that Hashem wanted it.
The Rav teaches that a Jew's bond with Hashem does not depend on merits; this is why the Torah says 'Lech lecha' without first praising Avraham.
The first thing the Torah tells after 'Lech lecha' is what the Ramban calls Avraham's great sin, to show that a Jew remains a Jew even when he sins.
The Maharal argues against the Ramban that emunah is a great thing in itself, and Chazal say the Jews merited ruach hakodesh at the sea in reward for their emunah.
Emunah means firmness: a believer depends only on Hashem and is subjugated to no person, and the Jews left Egypt through emunah because it made them free.
One who believes in Hashem is always in simcha and does not become angry, and Moshe's anger at the rock was a lack of emunah.

candidateTopics: anger as a lack of emunah

title.en: The Ramban's question on 'vehe'emin'

summary.en: The Rav ties Pesach to the bris bein habesarim and brings the Ramban's question of what was great in Avraham's believing. He gives the Maharal's answer: by nature Avraham could have no children and he feared sin might undo the promise, yet he believed because Hashem wanted it.

title.en: Why 'Lech lecha' gives no reason

summary.en: The Rav says Klal Yisrael began with Avraham and does not rest on merits. He asks why the Torah, unlike by Noach, gives no reason for choosing Avraham, and leaves his mesiras nefesh in Ur Kasdim to the Oral Torah: a Jew is a Jew because his soul is a part of Hashem, even when he sins.

title.en: The Ramban's 'great sin' of Avraham

summary.en: The Rav brings the Ramban that Avraham sinned greatly by going down to Egypt and by Sarah being taken to Pharaoh, and asks how the Ramban could judge him so when even Korach and Zimri are judged favorably. He answers that the very first account after 'Lech lecha' shows a sin, to teach that a Jew remains a Jew and his sin is only external.

title.en: The Maharal: emunah is no small thing

summary.en: The Rav brings the Maharal's challenge to the Ramban and the Mechilta that the Jews at the sea merited ruach hakodesh for their emunah, and that one who takes on one mitzvah with emunah merits the Shechinah. He applies it: each Jew should take on one mitzvah with mesiras nefesh, such as a fixed seder after davening, illustrated by a story of a man who was 'dead' during his shiur, and Avraham withstanding the Satan at the Akeidah with pure emunah.

title.en: Emunah as firmness and foundation

summary.en: The Rav says emunah is great even if it came easily, as a segulah, like the Midrash on oneg Shabbos. Emunah means firmness, like a peg in a firm place; Avraham is the rock from which Klal Yisrael was hewn, the foundation, and as he became the first Jew through emunah, the nation left Egypt through emunah.

title.en: A believer is subjugated to no one

summary.en: The Rav explains the Maharal: one who believes depends on Hashem alone and cannot be subjugated, since subjugation is the opposite of existence; so the Jews, believing, became free and left Egypt. He brings the Maharal's explanation of why 'dog' is an insult in every language: the dog is wholly dependent on its master, a repulsive trait, while a person should depend only on Hashem.

title.en: Rooted in Hashem, always in simcha

summary.en: The Rav explains that a believer is rooted in Hashem like a tree planted by water, and answers the Ramban that emunah is a great feat, for even Moshe Rabbeinu fell short in it. He teaches that a believer is always in simcha, and tells the story of Reb Shimon of Yaroslav and his 'two cows'.

title.en: A believer never becomes angry

summary.en: The Rav teaches that a believer does not become angry, since everything is from Heaven, as Dovid said of Shimi. Following the Maharal, Moshe's anger and striking the rock was the lack of emunah for which he was punished. He ends with the Midrash on Yaakov leaving Be'er Sheva saying 'me'ayin yavo ezri', a support for Jews in golus.

catalogTitle: צד א: במה אדע - עצמיות של כנ"י טוב; מדריגת אבות' שבטים' ושבעים נפש' גאולה עצם הגלות.

oneLiner.en: Following the Maharal, the Rav explains that a Jew's sin, and so his exile, is only incidental while his goodness is his essence, which is why Avraham was promised that korbanos would bring his children back to Eretz Yisrael and why the start of every galus already holds the geulah.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with Avraham's question 'bameh eda', 'how will I know that I will inherit the land', and asks how Avraham could seem to lack faith. Hashem answered: in the merit of korbanos. Bringing the Gemara in Megillah and the Midrash, the Rav sets out the Maharal's rule: in a Jew sin is incidental, while in a gentile it is essential, illustrated by a man splashed with mud as opposed to one whose skin is dark. That is why a korban can wipe away a Jew's sin and draw him close to Hashem. Eretz Yisrael, a 'Jew in geography', spits out sin, yet it must return to the Jews, and this was Avraham's real question. The Rav then distinguishes the avos, the shevatim and the seventy souls in their bond to Mitzrayim, and shows through the atbash calendar, Yocheved and Serach bas Asher that galus begins with the geulah already inside it.

en: According to the Maharal, Avraham's question 'bameh eda' was not a lack of faith but whether his children would return to Eretz Yisrael after being exiled for their sins.
A Jew's sin is incidental (b'mikreh) and does not cling to him, while a gentile's sin becomes part of his essence (b'etzem).
Korbanos, and today the saying and learning of korbanos, show that a Jew is close to Hashem and can be cleansed, and they protect the Jews in galus.
Eretz Yisrael is the 'separated land' that, like the Jewish soul, does not tolerate sin, and every nation has a land fitted to its nature.
The avos, the shevatim and the seventy souls are three levels in their bond to Eretz Yisrael and to Mitzrayim.
Galus for Jews is only temporary while the geulah is essential, so the geulah is rooted in the very start of every galus.

title.en: Avraham's question: 'bameh eda'

summary.en: Recalling that Avraham was the foundation of Jewish emunah, the Rav asks how he could ask 'bameh eda'. He brings the Midrash that Hashem answered 'in the merit of korbanos', the objection of meforshim, and the Gemara in Megillah that korbanos would protect Avraham's children from the fate of the generations of the Flood and the Dispersion.

title.en: The Maharal's rule: sin by accident, not by essence

summary.en: The Rav sets out the Maharal's rule that a Jew's sin is incidental while a gentile's is essential, with the mashal of a man splashed with black mud as opposed to a man whose skin is black. That is why a korban, which means closeness, can wipe away a Jew's sin, while a gentile may bring only an olah.

title.en: Korbanos and Torah as a shield in galus

summary.en: The Rav explains that a korban accepted for a Jew proves his goodness is essential, while a gentile's good deeds bring no closeness. In galus, Torah, and especially the Torah of korbanos and the daily saying of korbanos, draws a Jew close to Hashem; he laments that yeshiva students treat saying korbanos lightly.

title.en: Eretz Yisrael, a Jew in geography

summary.en: Every Jew must in the end become good, through whatever cleansing is needed, while gentiles cannot be cleansed. Just as the Jewish people accept no filth, Eretz Yisrael, the 'separated land', spits out sinners; the Rav calls it a Jew by place rather than by soul, and touches on exile to the cities of refuge.

title.en: Every nation's land, and Avraham's answer

summary.en: Every nation has a land fitted to its nature, and Eretz Yisrael is the land of Klal Yisrael. The Rav returns to the Maharal: Avraham asked whether his children would come back after being exiled for their sins, and the answer, korbanos, shows their sin is incidental, so they must return.

title.en: Avos, shevatim and the seventy souls

summary.en: The Rav describes three levels in Klal Yisrael: Yaakov, who belonged wholly to Eretz Yisrael and was brought back there in full; the shevatim, branches of the tree, whose bones alone went up; and the seventy souls, Jews of galus who stayed in Mitzrayim. He brings a hint from sefarim in the word 'gevia', Yosef's goblet.

title.en: Who completed the seventy: Yocheved or Serach

summary.en: The Gemara notes that only sixty-nine are counted, and answers that Yocheved, born 'between the walls' at the border of Mitzrayim, completed the seventy. The Midrash says Serach bas Asher completed it; the Rav asks how, since she is already counted, and explains she is counted as two. He then brings the Midrash linking the first day of Pesach with Tisha b'Av.

title.en: Pesach sets Tisha b'Av: churban rooted in geulah

summary.en: By the atbash rule the first day of Pesach falls on the same weekday as Tisha b'Av. The Rav explains that Pesach, the day of geulah, determines the day of churban because a Jewish churban must be rooted in geulah; galus is incidental and geulah essential. So Yocheved, mother of Moshe Rabbeinu, was born at the very step into the first galus.

title.en: Serach bas Asher and Eliyahu, bearer of good news

summary.en: Every matter has an angel appointed over it, and Eliyahu Hanavi is appointed over good news. Serach, who told Yaakov 'od Yosef chai', took on Eliyahu's quality, so she lived on, entered Gan Eden alive and counts as two. She later confirmed Moshe as redeemer by 'pakod pakadti', and the Rav concludes that the seventy souls entering galus already hint at the geulah.

catalogTitle: צד ב: ברית בין הבתרים - אדום הוא מציאות של שוא; החומריות נעלמת לפני מקבלי התורה; ביאור ענין ששבעים נפש כנגד שבעים אומות.

oneLiner.en: Following the Maharal, the Rav explains the animals of the Bris Bein HaBesarim as the four kingdoms that Avraham's children will outlast, shows that Edom has nothing of its own, and explains why the servitude of Egypt began only once the Jews became seventy souls, corresponding to the seventy nations.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Midrash that the animals Hashem showed Avraham at the Bris Bein HaBesarim stand for the four kingdoms, ending with Edom, a galus spread across many nations. Following the Maharal, the kingdoms are mere beasts before Avraham: he passes between them and they are cut apart, a promise that the Jewish people will outlive every obstacle, and each person carries these kingdoms within himself. The bird, Edom, was not cut at all, since it is a trifle; its greatness is robbed from Yerushalayim and from the Jews. The cutting also hints at the splitting of the sea, where physicality gives way before those going to receive the Torah. He then explains that servitude begins with Yitzchak, not Avraham, the root, and becomes real only once the Jews are seventy souls, opposite the seventy nations. Every Jew keeps the point of Avraham and the level of the shevatim, tied to Hashem's four-letter Name, which no galus can touch.

en: The animals of the Bris Bein HaBesarim are the four kingdoms, and the last of them, Edom, is a galus made of many nations.
The kingdoms are beasts compared to Avraham; they are cut apart as he passes through, a promise that the Jewish people will outlive them all.
The bird, Edom, was not even cut, because it is insignificant; all its greatness is robbed from the Jews.
The cutting of the animals hints at the splitting of the sea, where nature and physicality give way before the Jewish people.
Servitude could not begin with Avraham, the root of Klal Yisroel; it begins with Yitzchak as sojourning and becomes real only after the shevatim pass on.
Seventy souls correspond to the seventy nations; only at that level do the Jews have a connection with the nations, and therefore the galus began then.
Every Jew has within him the point of Avraham and the level of the shevatim, bound to Hashem's four-letter Name, which no nation and no galus can touch.

title.en: The four kingdoms at the Bris Bein HaBesarim

summary.en: The Rav brings the Midrash that the animals at the Bris Bein HaBesarim are the four kingdoms: Bavel, Madai, Yavan and Edom. He describes Edom as a galus of many nations, which began in Rome from nothing and is hinted at in the 'melech goyim' among the four kings.

title.en: Beasts before Avraham, cut as he passes

summary.en: Following the Maharal, the Rav explains that the kingdoms are beasts compared to Avraham, obstacles that are cut apart as he passes, a promise that Klal Yisroel will outlive them. He compares the nation to a body whose cells are renewed, and adds that each person has the four kingdoms within himself.

title.en: The uncut bird: Edom the robber

summary.en: The Rav asks why the bird was not cut, and explains with the Maharal that Edom is a small bird of no importance; its greatness is not its own but robbed. Its whole culture and progress are taken from the Jews, and likewise the yetzer hara's strength is stolen from the good.

title.en: Rome filled from the ruin of Yerushalayim

summary.en: The Rav explains that Tzor, meaning Rome, is filled only from the ruin of Yerushalayim, and plays on Yerushalayim written without a yud. He repeats that Rome grew out of the sea, from nothing, and brings Esav called 'small' and 'despised'.

title.en: The nation's birth and the splitting of the sea

summary.en: The Rav explains that the Bris Bein HaBesarim was the birth of the Jewish people, when its whole destiny was shown. He brings the Midrash that the cut animals hint at the splitting of the sea: before those going to receive the Torah, nature and physicality give way.

title.en: Why servitude starts with Yitzchak

summary.en: The Rav brings Rashi that the four hundred years are counted from Yitzchak's birth, and explains that Avraham, the single root of Klal Yisroel, is above servitude. Yitzchak was only a sojourner, and even in the shevatim's lifetime there was no real servitude.

title.en: Seventy souls opposite seventy nations

summary.en: Using the image of a trunk, branches and twigs, the Rav explains with the Maharal that seventy souls correspond to the seventy nations, and only at that level do the Jews connect with the nations and the galus begins. Yaakov and the shevatim only joined the count, so they were brought back to Eretz Yisroel.

title.en: The point of Avraham in every Jew

summary.en: The Rav brings the explanation of 'Magen Avraham': every Jew has a point of Avraham that many waters cannot extinguish, and no nation can enslave it, illustrated by the Previous Lubavitcher Rebbe facing a revolver. He then explains why the nations need borders while the Jews are bound to the inner, heavenly Eretz Yisroel.

title.en: The shevatim, the Name Havaya and Shevat

summary.en: The Rav explains that the twelve shevatim correspond to the twelve months and the twelve combinations of the Name Havaya, to which the nations have no connection, unlike the seventy Names. A Jew reaches the level of shevet through his own chiddushei Torah, which are revealed especially in the month of Shevat.

catalogTitle: A Coin of Fire

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that the half-shekel is a 'coin of fire', the yud of Hashem's Name and the indestructible point in every Jew, and that this is why it defeated Haman's shekalim and why Yehoash is its haftarah.

abstract.en: For Parshas Shekalim the Rav asks why the half-shekel was the merit that saved the Jews from Haman. He starts from Rashi's 'coin of fire' and a vort that a talmid of Rebbe Reb Bunim heard in Germany: Hashem wants the fire within a mitzvah, not its metal. The Alshich's reading of the apiryon shows the Beis Hamikdash was precious for the love inside it. Avraham's 400 shekalim for Me'aras HaMachpelah were compounded above, while Efron, named from afar (earth), kept cold metal. The four parshiyos match the four letters of Hashem's Name, and Shekalim is the yud, fire. The haftarah's Yehoash, whose soul came from shekalim, killed Zechariah on Yom Kippur in the Mikdash, forgetting a kindness as Haman did. Yet shekalim is the indestructible point in every Jew, where all are equal as children; it outweighed Haman's shekalim, and through it Yehoash too will be atoned.

en: The coin of fire Hashem showed Moshe teaches that what counts in a mitzvah is the fire and devotion within it, not its outward material.
A gift given with love is multiplied as it rises; Avraham's 400 shekalim for Me'aras HaMachpelah were registered above as endless sums.
The four parshiyos correspond to the four letters of the Shem Havayah, and Shekalim is the yud, the source of fire.
Every Jew's neshama comes from a particular mitzvah, and Yehoash, who renewed the mitzvah of shekalim, has a neshama from shekalim.
Shekalim is the kotzo shel yud, the nucleus in every Jew that no aveirah can destroy, and in its merit the Jews could not be annihilated in Haman's time.
In shekalim rich and poor give alike because it touches the root where Jews are Hashem's children, all equally His, as on Yom Kippur.

title.en: Parshas Shekalim and the coin of fire

summary.en: The Rav introduces the four parshiyos and the Gemara that the Jews' shekalim came before Haman's ten thousand talents of silver. He then asks what 'this they shall give' means and brings Rashi that Hashem showed Moshe a coin of fire from under the Heavenly Throne.

title.en: The vort heard in Germany

summary.en: The Rav tells of a talmid of Rebbe Reb Bunim who heard a German preacher say that Hashem wants a coin of fire, the warmth and devotion that go with a mitzvah. He applies this to tefillin, tzitzis and tefillah, notes that shekel equals nefesh in gematria, and brings Rebbe Reb Bunim's explanation that the German Jews merited this vort through their hachnasas orchim.

title.en: The glowing love inside the Beis Hamikdash

summary.en: The Rav brings the Alshich on the apiryon of Shir Hashirim: Hashem lacks no silver or gold, and what He wanted in the Beis Hamikdash was the glowing love of the Jews inside it. He contrasts a cold Roman edifice and a bronze statue with living people who have a neshama.

title.en: Avraham's compounded shekalim

summary.en: The Rav asks what the Musaf piyut of Parshas Shekalim means by asking Hashem to remember the shekalim of Efron. A dollar given with love is multiplied as it rises, and Avraham, who knew the holiness of Me'aras HaMachpelah, gave his 400 shekalim with such love that they were registered above as endless sums.

title.en: Fire, earth and the yud of Hashem's Name

summary.en: The Rav explains the four elements, fire rising and earth falling. Efron, named for afar, kept only cold metal while Avraham's fire went up, and 'Machpelah' means compounding. The four parshiyos correspond to the four letters of the Shem Havayah, and Shekalim is the yud, the fire.

title.en: Yehoash and the mitzvah of shekalim

summary.en: The Rav explains that the haftarah tells how King Yehoash renewed the forgotten mitzvah of shekalim. Every Jew's neshama comes from a particular mitzvah, as with a tzaddik who dealt with his sukkah every day of the year, so Yehoash's neshama comes from shekalim.

title.en: Yehoash in the Kodesh HaKadashim and Zechariah's death

summary.en: The Rav tells how Yehoash, the last of the house of David, was hidden in the Kodesh HaKadashim for six years and crowned at seven. Later his servants made him a deity, and he killed Zechariah, the Kohen Gadol and Navi, on Yom Kippur in the Mikdash, forgetting Yehoyada's kindness; Zechariah's blood boiled until the Churban.

title.en: Like Haman: Kodesh HaKadashim defiled

summary.en: The Rav compares Yehoash to Haman, who did not remember Shaul's mercy to Agag. Using Sefer Yetzirah's three dimensions of world, year and soul, he shows that Yehoash killed the Kohen Gadol, the Kodesh HaKadashim of souls, in the holiest place on the holiest day.

title.en: The kotzo shel yud and the indestructible nucleus

summary.en: The Rav asks why the small mitzvah of shekalim saved the Jews from Haman. Shekalim is the yud, and the yud has a kotz, the nucleus; every Jew has an indestructible point, like the luz bone, from which he is rebuilt however deep he falls.

title.en: One root of all Jews

summary.en: The Rav explains that shekalim corresponds to that nucleus, so in its merit the Jews, who cannot be totally destroyed, were saved. He brings the Chasam Sofer that all Jews share one root to which teshuvah returns, his reading of the passuk comparing Jews to the children of Kush, and the future circle dance where every point is equally close to the center.

title.en: Equal half-shekalim: children, not servants

summary.en: The Rav contrasts other mitzvos, which each Jew performs on his own level, with shekalim, where rich and poor give the same. Shekalim, called the money of atonement, belongs to Yom Kippur, the day of the circle dance and of forgiveness, where Jews are children and not servants, and where the lot chooses without a reason, as with Purim.

title.en: Haman's shekalim against ours; Yehoash is not Haman

summary.en: The Rav explains why the Jews' shekalim came before Haman's: theirs are fire, the yud, given with the joy of Adar, while Haman's are earth. Yehoash fits the haftarah because, though guilty of Haman's crime, his neshama of shekalim cannot be destroyed, which shows every Jew that he can never be lost forever.

title.en: The rising fire and the gates of mercy

summary.en: The Rav says that even today the eagerness for the mitzvah of shekalim is fire that rises to the heavenly Beis Hamikdash. He finds a hint that Yom Kippur will atone for Yehoash, who came from the Kodesh HaKadashim, and closes with the Gemara on Mordechai ben Yair ben Shimi ben Kish, who knocked on the gates of mercy that open on Yom Kippur and Purim.

catalogTitle: משה רבינו - עצמיות של תורה שהיא מקור החידושים; שכל נבדל - כולו רוחני; נשמה כוללת

oneLiner.en: Following the Maharal, the Rav explains that Moshe Rabbeinu is pure form, a soul from the source of all renewal, set apart from the physical, and a soul that includes all of Israel.

abstract.en: The Rav begins with Rashi's teaching that Yocheved became young again before Moshe's birth, and explains that Moshe comes from the higher world from which all renewal flows; his first mitzvah was Kiddush HaChodesh, and the Torah was given in the third month to show that Torah must never grow old. He then explains why the Torah does not name Moshe's parents: Moshe was separate from all physicality, and his redemption of Israel came from Hashem, not from his lineage, though the tribe of Levi is named. The name Moshe, given by Pharaoh's daughter as a reward for kindness, shows that he is form, the opposite of water, which is pure matter; this is why the astrologers tried to drown him and why he split the sea. Finally, he describes Moshe as an all-inclusive soul who cared for his brothers, passed three tests, and faced Dasan and Aviram.

en: Moshe's soul comes from the higher world, the source of all chiddushim, so at his birth his mother Yocheved was renewed and became young again.
Torah must feel new every day, and it was given in the third month, when the newness of the redemption would naturally have faded, to show that it must never grow old.
The Torah does not name Moshe's parents because he was separate from physicality and from ordinary family ties, and because the redemption had to come regardless of lineage.
Moshe is form (tzurah) and water is matter (chomer); therefore the astrologers tried to defeat him through water, yet form must overcome matter, as he showed at the splitting of the sea.
Moshe was an all-inclusive soul who felt his brothers' suffering as his own, unlike a lowly soul that does not care.
Whoever truly serves Hashem will meet opposition, as Moshe and Aharon faced Dasan and Aviram.

title.en: Yocheved renewed: Moshe, source of renewal

summary.en: The Rav opens with Rashi's teaching that Yocheved became young again, and explains that Moshe comes from the higher world, the source of all chiddushim, which the world below lacks. He adds that Moshe's first mitzvah to Israel was Kiddush HaChodesh, and that renewal belongs to a Jew and not to a gentile.

title.en: Torah new every day; the third month

summary.en: From the pasuk of the third month and Rashi's 'let them be new in your eyes', the Rav explains that Torah is always new, like the daily prayers that each open something different. Three times makes a habit, so by the third Rosh Chodesh the newness should have faded; the Torah was given exactly then to show it must never grow old.

title.en: Why Moshe's parents are not named

summary.en: The Rav brings the Maharal's two explanations of why the Torah does not name Moshe's father and mother: Moshe was a 'nivdal', wholly separate from physical ties, as his children also left no mark; and the redemption had to come no matter whose son he was. Only the tribe of Levi is named, since Levi, bound to Hashem, was never enslaved.

title.en: The name from Pharaoh's daughter; form and matter

summary.en: The Rav brings the Midrash that the Torah uses the name Pharaoh's daughter gave Moshe as a reward for kindness, and explains that the Torah itself is a Torah of chesed. He then begins the meaning of the name, 'drawn from the water', defining form as the spiritual, lasting essence and matter as its temporary garment, with water as the most formless substance.

title.en: Moshe, the opposite of water

summary.en: The Rav explains that Moshe is pure form, so the astrologers sought to defeat him through water, yet form overcomes matter, as at the splitting of the sea; only after the sin at Mei Merivah was he punished through water. Water is always plural because it has no single essence, while Moshe is unique; his merit even held back the Flood for 120 years.

title.en: An all-inclusive soul and three tests

summary.en: On 'Moshe grew and went out to his brothers', the Rav explains that Moshe's greatness was his concern for others: a holy soul is a neshamah kelalis that feels another's pain, unlike a lowly soul. He brings the Chasam Sofer that Moshe passed three tests before being chosen to give the Torah: an Egyptian striking a Jew, a Jew striking a Jew, and injustice among gentiles in Midian.

title.en: A Torah for all; Dasan and Aviram

summary.en: The Rav explains that Moshe's Torah is for Israel and for all mankind, bringing the Rambam on the bnei Noach, and that Moshe did not give up doing good after a setback. He then teaches that whoever truly serves Hashem will face opposition, and explains that Dasan, from 'das', opposed Moshe the giver of Torah, while Aviram, 'the father is great', opposed Aharon's inherited holiness.

catalogTitle: משה רבינו - “ותרא אותו כי טוב” - אור הגנוז שנולד מהול

oneLiner.en: Building on the Maharal, the Rav explains that Moshe Rabbeinu was born circumcised and filled the house with light because he was a 'separate form' with no share in evil, and from there he develops why holiness and blessing must always stay hidden.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Midrash's readings of 'she saw that he was good' and the Maharal: the orlah is the power of physicality and evil, and Moshe, who had no connection to evil and came only to repair others, was born without it. Milah shows that man can improve on nature, as wheat becomes bread and grapes wine, which is why Malki-tzedek, born circumcised, brought Avraham bread and wine. The light hidden for the righteous lies under the orlah and is reached through toil, the work of Shovavim, until in Adar one sees that Torah is light. The Rav then explains Moshe's name, the astrologers' error about water, and why Moshe married Tzipporah, a convert tied to the heavens like a bird. From Yisro's recognition of Sarah's modesty he concludes that holiness and blessing are always covered.

en: According to the Maharal, Moshe was born circumcised because the orlah is the power of evil and physicality, and Moshe had no connection to evil.
Some souls do not come into the world to repair themselves but only to repair others, and Moshe was such a soul.
Milah shows that man can improve on what Hashem created, like wheat that becomes bread and grapes that become wine.
The hidden light for the righteous lies under the orlah and darkness, and one reaches it only through toil and self-sacrifice.
Moshe, a 'separate form' equal to all of Israel, could not find his match within Klal Yisrael and married a convert.
The holier a thing is, the more it must be covered: the world hides Hashem, and blessing rests only on what is hidden.

title.en: Why Moshe was born circumcised

summary.en: The Rav brings the Midrash's readings of 'she saw that he was good', and the Maharal's explanation that Moshe was born circumcised because the orlah is the power of evil and physicality, while Moshe came only to repair others.

title.en: Souls that come for others; the Apter Rav

summary.en: Every Jew's life work is to remove the orlah, which begins with the bris. Tzaddikim who come only for others are spared the risk; the Rav tells how the Apter Rav remembered being a king and a kohen gadol in earlier lives.

title.en: Milah, bread and wine: man perfects nature

summary.en: Milah shows that man can improve on nature, as in the Midrash's answer about wheat and bread. The Rav explains why bread and wine get higher brachos, and why Malki-tzedek, born circumcised, brought Avraham bread and wine.

title.en: The hidden light under the orlah

summary.en: The house filling with light means the goodness of serving Hashem. That light, the 'light sown for the tzaddik', is hidden under darkness and obstacles, and is reached only through hard work and self-sacrifice, the meaning of milah.

title.en: Shovavim, Terumah and Adar: Torah is light

summary.en: The weeks of Shovavim are the time to remove the orlah, today through toil in Torah and tefillah. After them comes Terumah, where the aron (from 'or') shines, and Adar, when one discovers that Torah is light and milah is joy.

title.en: Moshe and water: form against formlessness

summary.en: Following the Maharal, the Rav explains that Moshe is a 'separate form' while water has no form, so water is his opposite. The astrologers saw that Israel's savior would be struck through water but did not understand that only his sin at Mei Merivah gave water power over him.

title.en: Why Moshe married a convert

summary.en: The Rav asks why Moshe married Tzipporah, a convert, from whom a descendant became an idol priest. He answers that Moshe, equal to all of Israel, was not part of the six hundred thousand, so his match had to be someone else outside them, a convert.

title.en: Form and matter; Tzipporah the seventh

summary.en: Man is to woman as form to matter, and Moshe stands as form to all Israel; this explains why he was suspected regarding married women. The Torah notes that Tzipporah was the seventh daughter, since all sevenths are beloved, raising her to be Moshe's match.

title.en: Tzipporah: a bird tied to the heavens

summary.en: The Rav explains that Tzipporah's name shows her nature: like a bird, which belongs to the air and the heavens, her body was refined and fit for Moshe, who belonged to the heavens. The Midrash says she purified her father's house like a bird.

title.en: Yisro served every idol: the all-inclusive power

summary.en: Yisro served every idol in the world because his soul was tied to all powers and could rest only with the power that includes all, Hashem. This matches Moshe, who includes all Israel; like Moshe, Yisro had seven names.

title.en: 'Where is he?': Yisro recognizes Sarah's modesty

summary.en: The Midrash says Yisro's word 've'ayo' hinted that Moshe came from Sarah, of whom it says 'ayeh'. The Rav explains: blessing rests only on what is hidden, and when Moshe did not come home to be thanked for rescuing the daughters, Yisro saw the modesty of Sarah's children.

title.en: The world as the Artist's camouflage

summary.en: As the Ba'al Shem Tov's students teach, all holiness is hidden: the whole earth is full of His glory yet He is not seen. Through the Gemara's 'there is no artist like our G-d', the Rav compares the world to a painting and to camouflage that hides Hashem's trademark.

title.en: The holier, the more covered: Mishkan, Adar, head covering

summary.en: This world is a place where one must dig for G-dliness. The holier a thing, the more hidden: Purim and Adar, the Mishkan's coverings, the aron in the Holy of Holies, uncovered drinks, and the Jewish custom of covering the head, which the Rav says has been weakened.

title.en: Hidden deeds and covered blessing

summary.en: Through Rebbe Reb Bunim on Lavan and Sarah, who did not come out for compliments, the Rav shows that a Jew hides his mitzvos. Blessing is covered, like the challos at kiddush, and Adar is a hidden month until the reward stored for the righteous is revealed.

catalogTitle: התעוררות למצוות החג; מצה מאכל שהוא למעלה מן הזמן; קרבן פסח - בחינת אחדות ; מכת בכורות - בני בכורי ישראל.

oneLiner.en: Building on the Maharal, the Rav explains that matzah, the korban Pesach and makas bechoros all reveal Hashem's oneness, which stands above time, place and division, and he closes with a call to strengthen emunah and prepare for Mashiach.

abstract.en: The Rav opens by explaining that a Jew's eating is avodah, and that in galus matzah is the only eating left from the Torah; he speaks of the customs and chumros of Pesach, which he links to chametz being the yetzer hara. With the Maharal he explains that matzah is food above time: chametz is flour, water and time, while the exodus was above nature and time, which is why Nissan is called 'first'. He adds that chametz takes up more place than its truth, a false witness, while matzah testifies truly. The korban Pesach, eaten at bein ha'arbayim, roasted whole and in one group, shows Hashem's oneness. Makas bechoros struck the reishis of the klipah and revealed that every Jew is a bechor. A long discussion of the number two, the frog's song and R' Akiva's frog follows, and the Rav closes on the signs of Mashiach and the need for emunah.

en: In galus, eating matzah is the only eating from the Torah that remains, and every food a Jew eats with the proper intentions is part of serving Hashem.
Chametz is made of flour, water and time, while matzah is a food over which time has no hold, because the exodus was above nature and above time.
Chametz swells and takes more place than its true substance, a false testimony, while matzah takes exactly its true size and testifies to Hashem's oneness.
The korban Pesach expresses Hashem's oneness: it is slaughtered at bein ha'arbayim, a time with no partner, roasted rather than cooked, and eaten in one group.
Makas bechoros struck the reishis, the first point, of the klipah, and so revealed that the Jews are Hashem's reishis and that every Jew is a bechor.
The number two is the power of division and tumah, which is why pairs are dangerous, why Seder Taharos opens with 'two', and why on Pesach night, a time of oneness, four cups are permitted.
The Rav says the signs of Mashiach's coming are visible, and that the way to prepare is through emunah, toil in Torah and binding together with other yirei Shamayim.

candidateTopics: korban Pesach and the oneness of Hashem

title.en: Eating as avodah; the customs of Pesach

summary.en: The Rav explains that a Jew's eating, with its halachos, intentions and brachos, is part of serving Hashem, and that in galus matzah is the only eating from the Torah left. He adds that after the churban the rabbinic mitzvos and customs grew in importance, and tells of a tzaddik who handed out kneidlach on the last day of Pesach.

title.en: Why Pesach is kept with chumros

summary.en: The Rav brings the Ba'al HaTanya's ruling that on Pesach one takes on the chumros of the Rishonim, and tells how R' Yechezkel of Kuzmir hung his wheat from the ceiling. He explains with the Radbaz that the chumros of Pesach have no other reason than that chametz is the yetzer hara.

title.en: Matzah: food above time

summary.en: Following the Maharal, the Rav explains why matzah must be made quickly: chametz is flour, water and time, while the exodus was above nature and above time. This is why the exodus had to be in the month called 'first', since the first point is not yet time.

title.en: Milah, Pesach and Hashem's oneness

summary.en: The Rav explains that milah cuts a Jew off from nature, and the korban Pesach brings him into Hashem's oneness. Bein ha'arbayim is a time with no partner, the Pesach is eaten in one group, with matzah and maror together, and it is roasted, which draws a thing together, rather than cooked, which takes it apart.

title.en: Chametz, time and place: a false witness

summary.en: The Rav adds his own point: if time has no place on Pesach, why is wine, which improves with age, central to the Seder? He explains that time and place are bound together, and that chametz is a false witness because time makes it take more place than its truth, while matzah testifies truly. Wine is from kedushah and carries the matzah's quality into the world.

title.en: The Pesach at night and the mashchis

summary.en: Following the Maharal, the Rav explains why the Pesach is eaten at night: the night was the downfall of the klipah, while the redemption itself came in the morning. He then asks why the Jews had to stay inside if Hashem Himself struck Egypt, and answers that all destructive forces wanted to join in, so protection was needed from them.

title.en: Makas bechoros: every Jew is a bechor

summary.en: With the Maharal the Rav explains that makas bechoros struck the reishis of the klipah and revealed that the Jews are Hashem's reishis, so that every Jew is a bechor. He then describes Nissan as the month of reishis and chesed, when everything begins to bloom, and a good time for a Jew to make a new beginning.

title.en: Pairs, four cups and the Seder each year

summary.en: The Rav explains the Gemara in Pesachim that pairs are dangerous: two is the power of division and klipah, yet on Pesach night, a time of oneness, four cups are permitted. He brings Chad Gadya and the Rambam on the moon shown to Moshe, says that the exodus repeats every year at the Seder, and speaks of Shabbos Rosh Chodesh Nissan and the eighth day of the miluim.

title.en: How can impure animals sing shirah?

summary.en: The Rav asks how impure creatures can say shirah. Through the Mishnah in Keilim on the sea-dog, which is impure because it flees to land, he suggests that each species has a pure counterpart that serves as its shliach tzibbur. The dog has none, and he answers that its tongue was made pure when it did not bark at the Jews.

title.en: The frog's song: Baruch Shem

summary.en: The Rav asks how the frog, a mixture of good and evil, can say shirah, and points out that in Perek Shirah it alone says 'Baruch Shem kevod malchuso', not a passuk, and quietly. This is a song that rises even from the places of tumah, and he explains with a Midrash that the mazikin flee when a Jew says Shema, saying Baruch Shem as they go.

title.en: The number two as division and tumah

summary.en: The Rav brings the Midrash that the first day was 'one day', Hashem's oneness, while machlokes and Gehinnom were created on the second day. From this he explains the danger of pairs, the four cups at night, the Mishnah that ma'aseh merkavah is not taught to two, Yeravam's two calves, the two kinds of carrying on Shabbos, and why Oholos and Negaim, the gravest tumos, open with the word 'two'.

title.en: R' Akiva and R' Elazar ben Azaryah on the frog

summary.en: The Rav explains the Gemara where R' Akiva says there was one frog that bred all the others, and R' Elazar ben Azaryah tells him to go to Negaim and Oholos. Since those tractates open with 'two', the frog, a mixture of kedushah and tumah, cannot be called 'one' as a root; R' Elazar ben Azaryah holds it was one frog that whistled and the rest came, a partnership of one with many.

title.en: Shuruk, yesod and the weeks of Shovavim

summary.en: From the passuk in Zechariah and the Metzudos the Rav shows that shuruk and kubutz are the same, a gathering, which corresponds to yesod, and with the Arizal he links the frog to yesod and the weeks of Shovavim to its tikkun. He says that in this generation the tikkun is not fasting but toiling in Torah and tzedakah, and tells how R' Yechezkel of Kuzmir told a penitent not to fast.

title.en: Mashiach is in the air

summary.en: The Rav says the whole world is talking about Mashiach, and from Rashi on Leah he shows that what people say is a sign. He goes through the signs in the Gemara, especially that yirei Shamayim are mocked, and tells of a Jew in Detroit whose uncle called him 'meshuga frum' for keeping Shabbos.

title.en: An orphaned generation: Malachi's advice

summary.en: The Rav calls this an orphaned generation with no one to rely on but Hashem, and brings Malachi's advice that the yirei Hashem speak to one another. Mashiach, greater than Avraham Avinu, will come suddenly, so one must prepare with emunah; from Pharaoh's words 'divrei sheker' he explains that the Jews in Egypt drew hope from talk of the redemption, and that waiting for Mashiach is a mitzvah.

title.en: Baruch Shem: joining ourselves to Hashem

summary.en: The Rav describes today as a time when good and evil are mixed and serving Hashem is hard, and says each Jew must resolve firmly to stop stumbling and love Hashem even without desire. Yaakov Avinu, seeing the last generations, said Baruch Shem; from Sefer HaKanah he shows that its letters are the only ones that join with Hashem's name, and concludes that the advice is to bind oneself to those better than oneself.
